In March 2018, Sergei Skripal, a former Russian military intelligence (GRU) officer who had spied for Britain, and his daughter, Yulia, were found slumped on a bench in Salisbury, UK,, a military-grade nerve agent developed by the Soviet Union. The forensic evidence pointed to the Kremlin. But rather than deny the attack or offer a singular counter-story, Russia offered dozens—the agent had come from Porton Down; the British had staged it; the Skripals had poisoned themselves. Each account was implausible, but the Kremlin’s intention was never about creating belief in one thing. Its goal was to ensure that anyone encountering the story came away thinking the matter was disputed, complicated, and probably unknowable. The creation of doubt, something inherently cognitive, was the primary objective.
In this instance, London responded uncharacteristically. Rather than countering each narrative, as doctrine often prescribes, UK Prime Minister Theresa May ordered the
of classified intelligence identifying the GRU as the guilty party. Within weeks, more than 150 Russian diplomats and intelligence officers were
by almost 30 countries.
Compare this event to a similar one in 2006, when Alexander Litvinenko was murdered in London with radioactive polonium. The intelligence was substantially there, but its release took nearly a
, so the global response was muted, and no coalition materialized.
Seen side by side, it is tempting to view Salisbury as a communications success and Litvinenko as a failure, but the takeaway is doctrinal. What worked in the Salisbury case was not better messaging but a
. The UK chose the terrain and the timing, and by making the intelligence public, gave its Allies no choice but to act. Without that shift in posture, the problem is not that we respond poorly, since many Allied rebuttals are excellent. It is that responding is exactly what the adversary wants, because every rebuttal concedes the subject, the timing, and the terms to whoever spoke first. As Ronald Reagan aptly observed, “If you’re explaining, you’re losing.”
To address some of these issues, the recently approved NATO Cognitive Warfare Concept (NATO Allied Command Transformation, 2025) set out to fill gaps in Alliance thinking. The Concept defines cognitive warfare as “the fight for cognitive superiority,” noting that “contesting in this environment comprises deliberate, synchronized military and non-military activities throughout the continuum of competition designed to gain, maintain and protect cognitive advantage.” The definition’s wording is intentional and designed to address existing frictions within the wider cognitive warfare discourse that continue to muddy how we speak about it. Namely, cognitive warfare is not something we
; it is the fight itself. It is not an activity a state conducts, nor a capability fielded by a military. It is the battlespace, defined like land, air, or maritime warfare, by the contest waged within it rather than the instruments used to wage it. And like those, it can be won or lost.
Unfortunately, the current discourse does not account for this distinction because cognitive warfare is still routinely misrepresented as something a state or military does, and it is still treated as interchangeable with propaganda, disinformation, strategic communications (StratCom), or information operations (Info Ops). The question, “isn’t this just propaganda?” is ubiquitous. But cognitive warfare is not propaganda, nor is it disinformation by another name.
Take a campaign aimed at breaking an enemy’s will to fight. We might combine heavy bombardment with leaflets, broadcasts, and posts that convince the adversary’s soldiers their commanders have abandoned them. The bombardment is not there to take ground; it is there to make the abandonment feel real. The messages are propaganda, which is simply a way of delivering an idea. PsyOps is the capability that crafts and delivers those messages to that audience. Info Ops is the function that decides the effect is worth pursuing in the first place, and that lines up everything the force does to support it, including the bombardment. Strategic Communications is the doctrine governing whether we should be doing any of this at all, and the function that ensures we do it properly.
Fires, maneuvers, propaganda, disinformation, PsyOps, Info Ops, and Strategic Communications are all used
the fight. None of them
the fight, in the same way that a torpedo is an instrument used within submarine warfare rather than a synonym for it. Conflating the tool with the fight fundamentally misshapes how institutions organize themselves to respond.
In this case, the confusion runs deeper than vocabulary. Cognitive warfare is generally discussed only within the Strategic Communications family, and that placement risks narrowing it. Once the conversation turns to doctrine, cognition is often collapsed into information, and the fight incorrectly becomes a contest of messaging. But the cognitive dimension is not the information environment by another name. Messaging is merely one route in—as are troop movements, blackouts, and bridges or buildings destroyed. They all reach a human being whose perceptions and judgments are shaped by culture, memory, social identity, group belonging, and the physiological conditions under which thinking happens. This is also why disinformation is only the tip of the iceberg, though it is the tip we focus on most. As Krewson has argued
, adversaries are most effective when the material they peddle is true, when they seize a real grievance—be it individual, group, or societal—and inflame the identity beneath it. Identity-based manipulation (IBM) requires no falsehood at all, yet countering and debunking falsehoods remains our primary focus. An alliance that mechanistically perceives the fight as informational will organize to manage information, missing the criticality of everything that determines whether it lands at all.
If cognitive warfare is the fight, then what places an activity within it is whether its primary objective includes not just what people think, but
they think. A commander may destroy a bridge to disrupt a supply route, but the population, seeing their infrastructure destroyed, will conclude whether their government can protect them. That cognitive effect is a byproduct. An identical strike, chosen for what the bridge’s loss will mean to that population rather than for the supplies it shuttles, is an activity in the cognitive fight: same explosion, different logic.
This is where most institutions are struggling, and their struggle is largely structural rather than intellectual. NATO’s own defense planning bears this out. Capability codes for Strategic Communications were established through the NATO Defense Planning Process (NDPP), yet most remain unmet by member nations’ capability commitments. The requirement is agreed; the resourcing is not.
Further, since the cognitive dimension crosses every domain, militaries and governments often treat cognitive effects as something layered onto traditional military activities. Yet, as the bridge example illustrates, the same action can either produce a cognitive effect as a byproduct or constitute a deliberate action within the cognitive battlespace. The difference lies in whether the cognitive effect was the primary point from the beginning. Part of what makes this so difficult to correct—and even understand—is that cognitive effects are rarely as overt as kinetic effects. A struck building, particularly if civilians are found beneath it, is visible and emotionally palpable, while a population scrolling itself into distrust of its own institutions is less so. Thus, the add-on problem is not just organizational; it represents a failure of imagination about what “damage” actually looks like and who is responsible for mitigating or addressing it. As a result, caring about an effect and being organized to generate it—regardless of how long it takes to see the fruits of that generation—are not the same thing.
This gap between caring and being organized frames the argument of this article: to effectively deter in the cognitive dimension, NATO must transform its status quo reactive narrative defense into persistent narrative offense because an alliance organized to answer stories will always arrive after the adversary has chosen the terrain. Real narrative offense means identifying, understanding, and occupying that terrain before the adversary claims it. Easy in principle; hard in practice.
NATO’s current Strategic Communications doctrine describes a persistent battlespace contested throughout the continuum of competition, particularly below the threshold of conflict. Yet the core Allied Joint Publications governing it, principally AJP-01, AJP-10, and AJP-10.1, are often read as defensive and reactive, justified by the fact that NATO does not initiate aggression. Our adversaries have already organized this way. Russia’s
and China’s cognitive-
both build around the effect on the mind rather than the medium carrying that effect. The open question is whether the Alliance will organize around the effect as deliberately as our adversaries have theorized it.
In other domains, “defensive” rarely means “reactive.” For example, NATO
persistently rather than responding after an incursion, and it forward-deploys
against attacks that have not happened. Neither is a reactive position, since a defensive alliance that moves only after being struck possesses little deterrent value below the threshold.
The same logic is transferable to the cognitive dimension. Persistent air policing and forward-deployed land forces impose a cost by forcing an adversary to respond, limiting their ability to mass without exposing a weakness elsewhere. Pressing truth into an adversary’s information space works the same way, since it forces them to divert capability to counter the incursion. We know this because it is precisely what the Kremlin does to us, generating activity that keeps NATO and the EU chasing the narrative. Why, then, do we frame our posture in the cognitive dimension as something requiring us to move second?
To be clear, this is not a failure of doctrinal drafting; only of doctrinal reading. The Alliance too often interprets narrative-led doctrine as an instruction to counter stories rather than to create them, yet correction, rebuttal, and debunking—regardless of how well-reasoned—still cede the subject, the timing, and the terms to the adversary.
The theoretical foundation for the mindset shifts this article proposes already exists in a neighboring domain.
states that in an environment of constant contact, deterrence understood as the threat of response or punishment offers little protection, because an actor only engaging in response cedes the initiative permanently. Instead, advantage comes from persistent engagement: continuously contesting the environment rather than punishing discrete acts after the fact.
What transfers is the logic rather than the method. The principle holds wherever a domain is actively contested because a purely defensive posture cannot win; it can only wait for the adversary to lose. In cyberspace, that means contesting those conducting the attacks rather than the adversary’s networks at large. In the cognitive dimension, it means choosing where, when, and to whom we press our truths, so adversary detection and response capabilities turn inward to protect their own information space rather than outward against ours. The instruments and the staff differ, which is why this article argues for separating them. However, the underlying logic of contesting does not.
This does not mean deterrence stops mattering. It means we must be honest about which kind is still available to us, because our adversaries often work through proxies they can disown, rarely presenting a front to retaliate against. In the cognitive dimension, deterrence by denial requires an almost-utopian inoculation at scale or, perhaps more realistically, the ongoing ability to make adversary operations harder to run, easier to expose, and more politically costly at home.
Denial of that kind cannot be improvised, which exposes a structural problem. The current approach starts with the capabilities the Alliance already has and asks what objectives they can serve. The alternative, and the argument of this article, is to start with the cognitive effect required and build the capability around it. Effects-first thinking is already embedded in Alliance doctrine and planning, but force structure, budget lines, career pathways, and training pipelines are organized around platforms rather than effects, and, whether we like it or not, that machinery dictates what actually gets done.
Doctrine alone cannot close that gap, because it depends on a specialism the Alliance lacks. No Allied navy would put an officer who had never served in submarines in command of one, yet we routinely put people in charge of cognitive effects because they are “good communicators,” as though understanding cognition follows from possessing it. For example, it is common for nations to put officers with no background in psychology or the information environment in command of information capabilities, and to assign officers with the same limited foundation to senior NATO StratCom positions. This does more damage than the immediate mismatch, because filling senior posts from outside the discipline leaves the specialists who have spent careers building the expertise with nowhere to be promoted to.
This is not to say the Alliance is without capable people. NATO and allied nations have a pool of skilled Info Ops planners, military public affairs (MilPA) communicators, and PsyOps practitioners, and some nations have built serious professional pipelines around them. But this is precisely the point. Formations such as the British Army’s 77th Brigade and the US Army’s Fort Bragg PsyOps Group illustrate the problem rather than solve it, because they remain national investments in a discipline the Alliance has never built or exercised collectively. Centers of excellence, working groups, and bilateral exchanges circulate what these formations know, but no Alliance-level pathway forms practitioners in the first place. As a result, the depth available to NATO is whatever its members happen to have built at home.
The problem is not only where practitioners are formed, but what they are formed in. The discipline cannot be built out of communications expertise alone. Understanding why a narrative takes hold in one society, yet fails in another, requires cultural and anthropological knowledge that no message-testing framework supplies, and understanding why fear and sustained threat change what a population will accept and believe requires psychology alongside the physiological realities of how people process information under stress. None of this sits inside a single profession, which is why a shared standard would have to be built across several.
Before any of this can be built, narrative offense raises two governance questions: whom are we doing this to, and who is authorized to do it? The first draws a line between when we must tell the truth and when deception is legitimate. MilPA exists to tell the truth, which is not a constraint but the entire basis of its value, since credibility, once destroyed, cannot be rebuilt quickly enough to matter in a crisis. At the other end, military deception against enemy forces in the field is legitimate and sometimes decisive, as Ukraine’s 2022
showed. These extremes, telling the truth to your own populations and allies while deceiving an enemy in the field, can coexist inside one campaign without contradiction. The mistake is viewing narrative offense in reductionist black-and-white terms, when the hard questions often live in the middle ground where most communication sits. What governs that middle ground is not a wall but two principles: 1) attribution—we do not pretend to be someone else when speaking to audiences entitled to our name, and 2) audience—deception is only aimed at military opponents, never at our own publics or the press that serves them.
The second question, who is authorized to do it, asks us how the work should be divided, which gives this article its title. The defense of the domestic cognitive space is the Sovereign Shield. It must remain a national responsibility led by civilian institutions, because a military instrument that polices what its own population believes has already abandoned the democratic values it exists to defend. Yes, military resources can and should support that effort, but the rules must be clear, publicly accountable, and drawn in doctrine before the capability exists.
Taking the fight to the adversary is the Alliance Sword, and it inverts that arrangement. It must be led collectively, through integral Alliance functions and capabilities supported by national assets, orchestrating cognitive effects under rules of engagement agreed for the cognitive dimension. Where the Shield is national and civilian by necessity, the Sword is Alliance-wide and military by design, delivering deterrence by denial across peace, crisis, and conflict.
The Shield and the Sword are not rival descriptions of the same task but complementary answers to different questions, so keeping them distinct is how democracies stop frightening themselves out of competing at all.
Particularly in the space between peacetime and a formalized Article 5 declaration, which our adversaries have normalized fighting within, the cognitive contest is continuous. Yet existing Alliance decision-making requires crisis-level consensus for every below-threshold action. This is not only unsustainable; it leaves us arriving second on ground someone else has chosen. The remedy is the logic we already apply in the air: the North Atlantic Council is not convened to approve each intercept over the Baltic. The cognitive fight needs the same. Standing peacetime authorities would assess the information environment and act below the threshold under agreed rules of engagement, within boundaries set politically in advance. The
before Russia’s 2022 invasion showed what this looks like in practice, and what it costs to improvise without such authorities.
Our argument attracts five predictable objections. The first is that this is just hybrid warfare with a new label. It is not, though the two overlap. Hybrid warfare describes how instruments are combined below the threshold of armed conflict. Cognitive warfare describes what they are aimed at. For example, hybrid framing tells us an operation combined cyber intrusion, proxies, and economic pressure to disable an energy network. It does not tell us whether the objective was the network itself or the population’s confidence in the government that failed to keep the lights on.
The second objection is escalation. If we engage continuously rather than only when provoked, does that risk pushing an adversary to retaliate at a higher level? On this front, the
is genuinely
, but we do not need to resolve the debate to act. Helping populations—both ours and our adversaries’—recognize manipulation and openly disclosing what adversaries are doing sit at the de-escalatory end of the spectrum.
The third objection is that we become what we fight, but this mistakes the method for the posture. The adversary’s method is covert manipulation, meaning operations that only work because, often, no one can prove who is behind them. This article proposes the opposite: open, attributable truth that works specifically because everyone knows where it comes from. Radical transparency is not the sibling of authoritarian information control; it is its antidote. The line drawn between when we must use truth and when deception is legitimate exists precisely to preserve it.
Building upon this, the fourth objection is one of ethics. Why are we more comfortable authorizing a strike that kills people than authorizing a social media post directed at the population those people came from? This asymmetry rarely headlines the discourse, but we must scrutinize it. If we are prepared to bomb a society but not to tweet at it to avert the need for kinetic action, we should ask ourselves where our ethics actually lie. Is our discomfort genuinely principled or simply misunderstanding masquerading as righteous constraint? Narrative offense is often the more humane option, because getting accurate information into an adversary’s information space can change calculations before lives are lost. Moreover, deterrence is itself a cognitive effect. Making an adversary’s operations harder to run and more costly to sustain is not separate from the humane case, because deterring an adversary from moving to physical attack saves military and civilian lives on both sides. The question is not whether it is ethical to act offensively, but whether we can keep justifying the tangible, often human, cost of refusing to do so.
Moreover, pushing truth into an adversary’s information space is neither new nor a departure from our democratic principles; it is an application of them. Since 1948,of the Universal Declaration of Human Rights has held that the right to seek, receive, and impart information runs “regardless of frontiers.” Authoritarian governments assert a sovereign right to decide what their citizens may know, so treating their border as a line we dare not cross with the truth concedes that claim. International law prohibits coercion, and open, attributed disclosure coerces no one. Moreover, staying silent while our own populations are manipulated covertly is not neutrality; it is choosing—and make no mistake,—to let our adversaries win without contest.
The final objection asks whether any of this works. In all honesty, the
for influence operations of every flavor is
. The Salisbury disclosures and the intelligence releases before Russia’s 2022 invasion of Ukraine, for all their success in stripping deniability, did not stop Russia’s tanks. So, the case cannot rest on rapidly changing minds at scale. Instead, it must rest on disruption, cost, and initiative: forcing authoritarian regimes—more brittle than they appear—to spend finite bandwidth policing their own information space, and ensuring the contest happens on a terrain of our choosing. Measured as mass persuasion, the evidence is modest. But persuasion should not be the goal. The goal is making the adversary’s job harder and more expensive, and that is a lower bar than changing minds.
The same honesty must carry into the doctrine itself, which should state the limits of the evidence as plainly as the intent. Doctrine that overpromises persuasion will be discredited by its first assessment cycle, and credibility is what makes boldness affordable.
Nothing above asks NATO to invent a new doctrine, only to continue developing the one it already has. What follows is a practical agenda.
There is evidence that the tectonics are already shifting. NATO’s PsyOps doctrine has recently moved into the Strategic Communications family and is the first publication there to cite the Cognitive Warfare Concept by name. The move was met with resistance, but it was deliberate and consequential.
This article’s argument comes down to a single chain of reasoning: cognitive warfare is not a capability but the contest itself. It reaches past information into everything that shapes how we perceive and engage with the world, impacting who we believe we are and what we stand for. The contest is continuous, an ever-present fight within our day-to-day lives. Thus, a posture built on myopic response is merely a slow concession on the way to surrender. On the surface, there may be no blood to staunch or ground to hold, yet societies are inherently breakable. They thin from the inside, until the trust that tethered people and institutions together no longer tethers anything at all.
Combating this descent does not require the Alliance to become something it is not, because the entire design rests on a critical advantage that adversaries do not have: our ability to be seen. Closed, authoritarian systems spend enormous resources controlling what their people know, while open, democratic societies are, by their nature, on the side of more information rather than less. This is why attributable truth is our natural instrument, and using it does not betray the order we exist to defend. The Sovereign Shield and the Alliance Sword are not a contradiction; they are a uniform idea. Democracies can protect their own cognitive space with civilian and national hands, while still contesting adversarial actors with a collective military instrument pointed explicitly outward. This division is not a constraint on how we fight; to the contrary, it is how we engage in and defend against cognitive warfare without becoming a casualty of the fight itself.
Every contest for superiority is won by the side that understands what it is actually contesting. In this one, the prize is not territory, systems, or even influence. It is whether populations can still think for themselves at all, and whether the cognitive conditions for free thought and self-determination still exist. That is what we risk losing.
It is also why doctrine matters, unsexy and boring as it is. Beneath the structured language and carefully curated words, doctrine is a decision made in advance about who we will be when the next Salisbury arrives. Litvinenko produced the managed story, but Salisbury produced the coalition because Theresa May chose to act outside the established playbook. Our current doctrine is still written for the Litvinenko response, but the fight in front of us has changed. Continuing to assume a back-foot posture is no longer prudent or feasible.
Free thought is still ours to defend. We must evolve.

_source.movement_abstract: 文章针对北约在认知战领域的现状提出改革建议，指出当前北约将认知战误读为信息战或宣传战，导致防御姿态被动。2025年北约批准的《认知战概念》虽已定义认知战为争夺认知优势的斗争，但现有条令仍侧重于事后反驳。文章主张北约需从被动叙事防御转向持续叙事进攻，通过“主权盾”与“联盟剑”双轨机制重构防御体系。“主权盾”由各国文职机构主导，负责国内认知空间防御，确保民主价值不被军事化侵蚀；“联盟剑”则由北约集体军事力量主导，负责在对手信息空间实施归因明确的真相攻势，以干扰对手行动并增加其成本。文章强调，认知战的核心在于争夺思维逻辑而非单纯的信息传递，需建立跨学科专业人才培养体系，并赋予北约在和平时期低于冲突阈值下的常设行动授权，以打破对手设定的战场规则，确保持续的主动权和威慑力。

; it is the fight itself. It is not an activity a state conducts, nor a capability fielded by a military. It is the battlespace, defined like land, air, or maritime warfare, by the contest waged within it rather than the instruments used to wage it. And like those, it can be won or lost.
Unfortunately, the current discourse does not account for this distinction because cognitive warfare is still routinely misrepresented as something a state or military does, and it is still treated as interchangeable with propaganda, disinformation, strategic communications (StratCom), or information operations (Info Ops). The question, “isn’t this just propaganda?” is ubiquitous. But cognitive warfare is not propaganda, nor is it disinformation by another name.
Take a campaign aimed at breaking an enemy’s will to fight. We might combine heavy bombardment with leaflets, broadcasts, and posts that convince the adversary’s soldiers their commanders have abandoned them. The bombardment is not there to take ground; it is there to make the abandonment feel real. The messages are propaganda, which is simply a way of delivering an idea. PsyOps is the capability that crafts and delivers those messages to that audience. Info Ops is the function that decides the effect is worth pursuing in the first place, and that lines up everything the force does to support it, including the bombardment. Strategic Communications is the doctrine governing whether we should be doing any of this at all, and the function that ensures we do it properly.
Fires, maneuvers, propaganda, disinformation, PsyOps, Info Ops, and Strategic Communications are all used
the fight. None of them
the fight, in the same way that a torpedo is an instrument used within submarine warfare rather than a synonym for it. Conflating the tool with the fight fundamentally misshapes how institutions organize themselves to respond.
In this case, the confusion runs deeper than vocabulary. Cognitive warfare is generally discussed only within the Strategic Communications family, and that placement risks narrowing it. Once the conversation turns to doctrine, cognition is often collapsed into information, and the fight incorrectly becomes a contest of messaging. But the cognitive dimension is not the information environment by another name. Messaging is merely one route in—as are troop movements, blackouts, and bridges or buildings destroyed. They all reach a human being whose perceptions and judgments are shaped by culture, memory, social identity, group belonging, and the physiological conditions under which thinking happens. This is also why disinformation is only the tip of the iceberg, though it is the tip we focus on most. As Krewson has argued
, adversaries are most effective when the material they peddle is true, when they seize a real grievance—be it individual, group, or societal—and inflame the identity beneath it. Identity-based manipulation (IBM) requires no falsehood at all, yet countering and debunking falsehoods remains our primary focus. An alliance that mechanistically perceives the fight as informational will organize to manage information, missing the criticality of everything that determines whether it lands at all.
If cognitive warfare is the fight, then what places an activity within it is whether its primary objective includes not just what people think, but
they think. A commander may destroy a bridge to disrupt a supply route, but the population, seeing their infrastructure destroyed, will conclude whether their government can protect them. That cognitive effect is a byproduct. An identical strike, chosen for what the bridge’s loss will mean to that population rather than for the supplies it shuttles, is an activity in the cognitive fight: same explosion, different logic.
This is where most institutions are struggling, and their struggle is largely structural rather than intellectual. NATO’s own defense planning bears this out. Capability codes for Strategic Communications were established through the NATO Defense Planning Process (NDPP), yet most remain unmet by member nations’ capability commitments. The requirement is agreed; the resourcing is not.
Further, since the cognitive dimension crosses every domain, militaries and governments often treat cognitive effects as something layered onto traditional military activities. Yet, as the bridge example illustrates, the same action can either produce a cognitive effect as a byproduct or constitute a deliberate action within the cognitive battlespace. The difference lies in whether the cognitive effect was the primary point from the beginning. Part of what makes this so difficult to correct—and even understand—is that cognitive effects are rarely as overt as kinetic effects. A struck building, particularly if civilians are found beneath it, is visible and emotionally palpable, while a population scrolling itself into distrust of its own institutions is less so. Thus, the add-on problem is not just organizational; it represents a failure of imagination about what “damage” actually looks like and who is responsible for mitigating or addressing it. As a result, caring about an effect and being organized to generate it—regardless of how long it takes to see the fruits of that generation—are not the same thing.
This gap between caring and being organized frames the argument of this article: to effectively deter in the cognitive dimension, NATO must transform its status quo reactive narrative defense into persistent narrative offense because an alliance organized to answer stories will always arrive after the adversary has chosen the terrain. Real narrative offense means identifying, understanding, and occupying that terrain before the adversary claims it. Easy in principle; hard in practice.
NATO’s current Strategic Communications doctrine describes a persistent battlespace contested throughout the continuum of competition, particularly below the threshold of conflict. Yet the core Allied Joint Publications governing it, principally AJP-01, AJP-10, and AJP-10.1, are often read as defensive and reactive, justified by the fact that NATO does not initiate aggression. Our adversaries have already organized this way. Russia’s
and China’s cognitive-
both build around the effect on the mind rather than the medium carrying that effect. The open question is whether the Alliance will organize around the effect as deliberately as our adversaries have theorized it.
In other domains, “defensive” rarely means “reactive.” For example, NATO
persistently rather than responding after an incursion, and it forward-deploys
against attacks that have not happened. Neither is a reactive position, since a defensive alliance that moves only after being struck possesses little deterrent value below the threshold.
The same logic is transferable to the cognitive dimension. Persistent air policing and forward-deployed land forces impose a cost by forcing an adversary to respond, limiting their ability to mass without exposing a weakness elsewhere. Pressing truth into an adversary’s information space works the same way, since it forces them to divert capability to counter the incursion. We know this because it is precisely what the Kremlin does to us, generating activity that keeps NATO and the EU chasing the narrative. Why, then, do we frame our posture in the cognitive dimension as something requiring us to move second?
To be clear, this is not a failure of doctrinal drafting; only of doctrinal reading. The Alliance too often interprets narrative-led doctrine as an instruction to counter stories rather than to create them, yet correction, rebuttal, and debunking—regardless of how well-reasoned—still cede the subject, the timing, and the terms to the adversary.
The theoretical foundation for the mindset shifts this article proposes already exists in a neighboring domain.
states that in an environment of constant contact, deterrence understood as the threat of response or punishment offers little protection, because an actor only engaging in response cedes the initiative permanently. Instead, advantage comes from persistent engagement: continuously contesting the environment rather than punishing discrete acts after the fact.
What transfers is the logic rather than the method. The principle holds wherever a domain is actively contested because a purely defensive posture cannot win; it can only wait for the adversary to lose. In cyberspace, that means contesting those conducting the attacks rather than the adversary’s networks at large. In the cognitive dimension, it means choosing where, when, and to whom we press our truths, so adversary detection and response capabilities turn inward to protect their own information space rather than outward against ours. The instruments and the staff differ, which is why this article argues for separating them. However, the underlying logic of contesting does not.
This does not mean deterrence stops mattering. It means we must be honest about which kind is still available to us, because our adversaries often work through proxies they can disown, rarely presenting a front to retaliate against. In the cognitive dimension, deterrence by denial requires an almost-utopian inoculation at scale or, perhaps more realistically, the ongoing ability to make adversary operations harder to run, easier to expose, and more politically costly at home.
Denial of that kind cannot be improvised, which exposes a structural problem. The current approach starts with the capabilities the Alliance already has and asks what objectives they can serve. The alternative, and the argument of this article, is to start with the cognitive effect required and build the capability around it. Effects-first thinking is already embedded in Alliance doctrine and planning, but force structure, budget lines, career pathways, and training pipelines are organized around platforms rather than effects, and, whether we like it or not, that machinery dictates what actually gets done.
Doctrine alone cannot close that gap, because it depends on a specialism the Alliance lacks. No Allied navy would put an officer who had never served in submarines in command of one, yet we routinely put people in charge of cognitive effects because they are “good communicators,” as though understanding cognition follows from possessing it. For example, it is common for nations to put officers with no background in psychology or the information environment in command of information capabilities, and to assign officers with the same limited foundation to senior NATO StratCom positions. This does more damage than the immediate mismatch, because filling senior posts from outside the discipline leaves the specialists who have spent careers building the expertise with nowhere to be promoted to.
This is not to say the Alliance is without capable people. NATO and allied nations have a pool of skilled Info Ops planners, military public affairs (MilPA) communicators, and PsyOps practitioners, and some nations have built serious professional pipelines around them. But this is precisely the point. Formations such as the British Army’s 77th Brigade and the US Army’s Fort Bragg PsyOps Group illustrate the problem rather than solve it, because they remain national investments in a discipline the Alliance has never built or exercised collectively. Centers of excellence, working groups, and bilateral exchanges circulate what these formations know, but no Alliance-level pathway forms practitioners in the first place. As a result, the depth available to NATO is whatever its members happen to have built at home.
The problem is not only where practitioners are formed, but what they are formed in. The discipline cannot be built out of communications expertise alone. Understanding why a narrative takes hold in one society, yet fails in another, requires cultural and anthropological knowledge that no message-testing framework supplies, and understanding why fear and sustained threat change what a population will accept and believe requires psychology alongside the physiological realities of how people process information under stress. None of this sits inside a single profession, which is why a shared standard would have to be built across several.
Before any of this can be built, narrative offense raises two governance questions: whom are we doing this to, and who is authorized to do it? The first draws a line between when we must tell the truth and when deception is legitimate. MilPA exists to tell the truth, which is not a constraint but the entire basis of its value, since credibility, once destroyed, cannot be rebuilt quickly enough to matter in a crisis. At the other end, military deception against enemy forces in the field is legitimate and sometimes decisive, as Ukraine’s 2022
showed. These extremes, telling the truth to your own populations and allies while deceiving an enemy in the field, can coexist inside one campaign without contradiction. The mistake is viewing narrative offense in reductionist black-and-white terms, when the hard questions often live in the middle ground where most communication sits. What governs that middle ground is not a wall but two principles: 1) attribution—we do not pretend to be someone else when speaking to audiences entitled to our name, and 2) audience—deception is only aimed at military opponents, never at our own publics or the press that serves them.
The second question, who is authorized to do it, asks us how the work should be divided, which gives this article its title. The defense of the domestic cognitive space is the Sovereign Shield. It must remain a national responsibility led by civilian institutions, because a military instrument that polices what its own population believes has already abandoned the democratic values it exists to defend. Yes, military resources can and should support that effort, but the rules must be clear, publicly accountable, and drawn in doctrine before the capability exists.
Taking the fight to the adversary is the Alliance Sword, and it inverts that arrangement. It must be led collectively, through integral Alliance functions and capabilities supported by national assets, orchestrating cognitive effects under rules of engagement agreed for the cognitive dimension. Where the Shield is national and civilian by necessity, the Sword is Alliance-wide and military by design, delivering deterrence by denial across peace, crisis, and conflict.
The Shield and the Sword are not rival descriptions of the same task but complementary answers to different questions, so keeping them distinct is how democracies stop frightening themselves out of competing at all.
Particularly in the space between peacetime and a formalized Article 5 declaration, which our adversaries have normalized fighting within, the cognitive contest is continuous. Yet existing Alliance decision-making requires crisis-level consensus for every below-threshold action. This is not only unsustainable; it leaves us arriving second on ground someone else has chosen. The remedy is the logic we already apply in the air: the North Atlantic Council is not convened to approve each intercept over the Baltic. The cognitive fight needs the same. Standing peacetime authorities would assess the information environment and act below the threshold under agreed rules of engagement, within boundaries set politically in advance. The
before Russia’s 2022 invasion showed what this looks like in practice, and what it costs to improvise without such authorities.
Our argument attracts five predictable objections. The first is that this is just hybrid warfare with a new label. It is not, though the two overlap. Hybrid warfare describes how instruments are combined below the threshold of armed conflict. Cognitive warfare describes what they are aimed at. For example, hybrid framing tells us an operation combined cyber intrusion, proxies, and economic pressure to disable an energy network. It does not tell us whether the objective was the network itself or the population’s confidence in the government that failed to keep the lights on.
The second objection is escalation. If we engage continuously rather than only when provoked, does that risk pushing an adversary to retaliate at a higher level? On this front, the
is genuinely
, but we do not need to resolve the debate to act. Helping populations—both ours and our adversaries’—recognize manipulation and openly disclosing what adversaries are doing sit at the de-escalatory end of the spectrum.
The third objection is that we become what we fight, but this mistakes the method for the posture. The adversary’s method is covert manipulation, meaning operations that only work because, often, no one can prove who is behind them. This article proposes the opposite: open, attributable truth that works specifically because everyone knows where it comes from. Radical transparency is not the sibling of authoritarian information control; it is its antidote. The line drawn between when we must use truth and when deception is legitimate exists precisely to preserve it.
Building upon this, the fourth objection is one of ethics. Why are we more comfortable authorizing a strike that kills people than authorizing a social media post directed at the population those people came from? This asymmetry rarely headlines the discourse, but we must scrutinize it. If we are prepared to bomb a society but not to tweet at it to avert the need for kinetic action, we should ask ourselves where our ethics actually lie. Is our discomfort genuinely principled or simply misunderstanding masquerading as righteous constraint? Narrative offense is often the more humane option, because getting accurate information into an adversary’s information space can change calculations before lives are lost. Moreover, deterrence is itself a cognitive effect. Making an adversary’s operations harder to run and more costly to sustain is not separate from the humane case, because deterring an adversary from moving to physical attack saves military and civilian lives on both sides. The question is not whether it is ethical to act offensively, but whether we can keep justifying the tangible, often human, cost of refusing to do so.
Moreover, pushing truth into an adversary’s information space is neither new nor a departure from our democratic principles; it is an application of them. Since 1948,
of the Universal Declaration of Human Rights has held that the right to seek, receive, and impart information runs “regardless of frontiers.” Authoritarian governments assert a sovereign right to decide what their citizens may know, so treating their border as a line we dare not cross with the truth concedes that claim. International law prohibits coercion, and open, attributed disclosure coerces no one. Moreover, staying silent while our own populations are manipulated covertly is not neutrality; it is choosing—and make no mistake,
—to let our adversaries win without contest.
The final objection asks whether any of this works. In all honesty, the
for influence operations of every flavor is
. The Salisbury disclosures and the intelligence releases before Russia’s 2022 invasion of Ukraine, for all their success in stripping deniability, did not stop Russia’s tanks. So, the case cannot rest on rapidly changing minds at scale. Instead, it must rest on disruption, cost, and initiative: forcing authoritarian regimes—more brittle than they appear—to spend finite bandwidth policing their own information space, and ensuring the contest happens on a terrain of our choosing. Measured as mass persuasion, the evidence is modest. But persuasion should not be the goal. The goal is making the adversary’s job harder and more expensive, and that is a lower bar than changing minds.
The same honesty must carry into the doctrine itself, which should state the limits of the evidence as plainly as the intent. Doctrine that overpromises persuasion will be discredited by its first assessment cycle, and credibility is what makes boldness affordable.
Nothing above asks NATO to invent a new doctrine, only to continue developing the one it already has. What follows is a practical agenda.
There is evidence that the tectonics are already shifting. NATO’s PsyOps doctrine has recently moved into the Strategic Communications family and is the first publication there to cite the Cognitive Warfare Concept by name. The move was met with resistance, but it was deliberate and consequential.
This article’s argument comes down to a single chain of reasoning: cognitive warfare is not a capability but the contest itself. It reaches past information into everything that shapes how we perceive and engage with the world, impacting who we believe we are and what we stand for. The contest is continuous, an ever-present fight within our day-to-day lives. Thus, a posture built on myopic response is merely a slow concession on the way to surrender. On the surface, there may be no blood to staunch or ground to hold, yet societies are inherently breakable. They thin from the inside, until the trust that tethered people and institutions together no longer tethers anything at all.
Combating this descent does not require the Alliance to become something it is not, because the entire design rests on a critical advantage that adversaries do not have: our ability to be seen. Closed, authoritarian systems spend enormous resources controlling what their people know, while open, democratic societies are, by their nature, on the side of more information rather than less. This is why attributable truth is our natural instrument, and using it does not betray the order we exist to defend. The Sovereign Shield and the Alliance Sword are not a contradiction; they are a uniform idea. Democracies can protect their own cognitive space with civilian and national hands, while still contesting adversarial actors with a collective military instrument pointed explicitly outward. This division is not a constraint on how we fight; to the contrary, it is how we engage in and defend against cognitive warfare without becoming a casualty of the fight itself.
Every contest for superiority is won by the side that understands what it is actually contesting. In this one, the prize is not territory, systems, or even influence. It is whether populations can still think for themselves at all, and whether the cognitive conditions for free thought and self-determination still exist. That is what we risk losing.
It is also why doctrine matters, unsexy and boring as it is. Beneath the structured language and carefully curated words, doctrine is a decision made in advance about who we will be when the next Salisbury arrives. Litvinenko produced the managed story, but Salisbury produced the coalition because Theresa May chose to act outside the established playbook. Our current doctrine is still written for the Litvinenko response, but the fight in front of us has changed. Continuing to assume a back-foot posture is no longer prudent or feasible.
Free thought is still ours to defend. 为了解决其中的一些问题，最近批准的北约认知战概念（北约盟军司令部转型，2025）开始填补联盟思维的空白。该概念将认知战定义为“为认知优势而战”，并指出“在这种环境中的竞争包括在旨在获得、保持和保护认知优势的整个竞争过程中进行的深思熟虑的、同步的军事和非军事活动”。该定义的措辞是有意的，旨在解决更广泛的认知战争话语中的现有摩擦，这些摩擦继续混淆我们谈论它的方式。也就是说，认知战不是我们

不幸的是，当前的讨论并没有考虑到这一区别，因为认知战仍然经常被错误地描述为国家或军队所做的事情，并且它仍然被视为可以与宣传、假情报、战略通信（Stratcom）或信息作战（Info Ops）互换。“这不就是宣传吗？”这个问题无处不在。但认知战不是宣传，也不是假情报。

他们认为。一名指挥官可能会摧毁一座桥梁以中断一条补给线，但民众看到他们的基础设施被毁，会断定他们的政府是否能够保护他们。这种认知效应是一种副产品。选择同样的打击，是因为大桥的损失对人们意味着什么，而不是因为它运送的物资，这是认知斗争中的一种活动：同样的爆炸，不同的逻辑。
这是大多数机构都在挣扎的地方，而他们的挣扎主要是结构性的，而不是知识性的。北约自己的防御计划证实了这一点。战略通信的能力代码是通过北约防御计划过程（NDPP）建立的，但大多数仍未满足成员国的能力承诺。同意该要求；资源不是。
此外，由于认知维度跨越各个领域，军方和政府通常将认知效应视为传统军事活动的一部分。然而，正如舰桥的例子所示，同样的行动既可以作为副产品产生认知效果，也可以在认知作战空间内构成蓄意行动。不同之处在于认知效应是否从一开始就是主要的。认知效应很少像动力学效应那样明显，这一点很难纠正，甚至很难理解。一座被击中的建筑物，特别是如果在它下面发现了平民，是可以看到的，在情感上也是可以感受到的，而民众对自己的机构产生不信任则不那么明显。因此，附加问题不仅仅是组织问题；它代表了对“损害”实际是什么样子以及谁负责减轻或解决它的想象力的失败。因此，关心一种影响和有组织地产生这种影响——不管需要多长时间才能看到那一代人的成果——并不是一回事。
关心和有组织之间的差距构成了本文的论点：为了在认知维度上有效地威慑，北约必须将其现状从被动的叙事防御转变为持续的叙事进攻，因为一个有组织的联盟总是在对手选择了地形之后才会到来。真正的叙述性进攻意味着在对手宣称之前识别、理解和占领该地区。原则上容易；在实践中努力。
北约当前的战略通信条令描述了在整个竞争过程中，特别是在冲突门槛以下，持续争夺的作战空间。然而，管理它的核心盟军联合出版物，主要是AJP-01、AJP-10和AJP-10.1，经常被解读为防御性和反应性，理由是北约没有发起侵略。我们的对手已经这样组织了。俄罗斯的
中国的认知-
两者都是围绕着对大脑的影响而建立的，而不是承载这种影响的媒介。公开的问题是，联盟是否会像我们的对手所推测的那样，故意围绕这一效应组织起来。
在其他领域，“防御性”很少意味着“反应性”。例如，北约
而不是在入侵后做出反应，并且它是向前部署的
针对尚未发生的攻击。两者都不是被动的立场，因为只有在受到打击后才采取行动的防御联盟在阈值以下几乎没有威慑价值。
同样的逻辑可以转移到认知维度。持续的空中警戒和前沿部署的地面部队迫使对手做出反应，限制了他们的大规模作战能力，而不会暴露其他地方的弱点，从而增加了成本。将真相压入对手的信息空间也是如此，因为这迫使他们转移能力以对抗入侵。我们知道这一点，因为这正是克里姆林宫对我们所做的，它所产生的活动让北约和欧盟继续追逐这种说法。那么，为什么我们在认知维度上把我们的姿势设定为需要我们第二个移动的东西呢？
需要明确的是，这不是理论起草的失败；只是教义上的解读。联盟经常将叙事主导的教义解释为一种反驳故事的指令，而不是创造故事，然而纠正、反驳和揭穿——无论理由多么充分——仍然将主题、时机和条件让给对手。
这篇文章提出的思维转变的理论基础已经存在于邻近的领域。
指出，在不断接触的环境中，被理解为反应或惩罚的威胁的威慑提供的保护很少，因为只参与反应的行为者永久地放弃了主动性。相反，优势来自于持续的参与：不断挑战环境，而不是事后惩罚离散的行为。
传递的是逻辑而不是方法。这一原则适用于任何积极争夺的领域，因为纯粹的防御姿态不可能获胜。它只能等待对手失败。在网络空间，这意味着挑战那些进行攻击的人，而不是整个对手的网络。在认知维度上，这意味着我们选择在何处、何时以及向谁传达我们的真相，因此对手的探测和响应能力转向内部以保护他们自己的信息空间，而不是向外对抗我们的信息空间。乐器和五线谱是不同的，这就是本文主张将它们分开的原因。然而，竞争的基本逻辑却不是这样。
这并不意味着威慑不再重要。这意味着我们必须诚实地说明我们仍然可以使用哪一种，因为我们的对手经常通过他们可以否认的代理人来工作，很少提出报复的理由。在认知维度上，拒止威慑需要一种近乎乌托邦式的大规模接种，或者更现实地说，需要一种持续的能力，使对手的行动更难进行，更容易暴露，并在国内付出更高的政治代价。
这种否认不能是即兴的，这暴露了一个结构性问题。当前的方法从联盟已经拥有的能力开始，并询问它们可以服务于什么目标。另一种选择，也是本文的论点，是从所需的认知效果开始，并围绕它建立能力。效果优先的思想已经嵌入到联盟条令和规划中，但部队结构、预算线、职业途径和训练管道都是围绕平台而不是效果来组织的，而且，无论我们喜欢与否，这种机制都决定了实际要做什么。
理论本身并不能弥补这一差距，因为它依赖于联盟所缺乏的专业知识。没有哪个盟军海军会让一个从未在潜艇上服役过的军官来指挥一艘潜艇，但我们通常会让人们负责认知效果，因为他们是“优秀的沟通者”，就好像理解认知是从拥有认知开始的。例如，各国通常让没有心理学或信息环境背景的军官来指挥信息能力，并将同样基础有限的军官分配到北约战略司令部的高级职位。这比直接的不匹配造成的损害更大，因为从学科之外填补高级职位，让那些在职业生涯中积累了专业知识的专家无处晋升。
这并不是说联盟没有能人。北约和盟国拥有一批熟练的信息行动规划者、军事公共事务（MILPA）通信员和心理战从业人员，一些国家已经在他们周围建立了重要的专业管道。但这正是问题所在。英国陆军第77旅和美国陆军布拉格堡心理战大队等编队说明了这个问题，而不是解决这个问题，因为它们仍然是对联盟从未建立或集体行使的纪律的国家投资。卓越中心、工作组和双边交流传播这些组织所知道的东西，但首先没有联盟级别的途径形成实践者。因此，北约可利用的纵深是其成员国碰巧在国内建立的。
问题不仅在于从业者是在哪里形成的，还在于他们是在什么地方形成的。这门学科不能仅仅建立在通信专业知识的基础上。理解为什么一种叙事在一个社会中占据主导地位，而在另一个社会中却失败了，这需要文化和人类学知识，而信息测试框架无法提供这些知识；理解为什么恐惧和持续的威胁会改变人们接受和相信的东西，这需要心理学以及人们在压力下如何处理信息的生理现实。所有这些都不属于单一职业，这就是为什么必须在多个职业之间建立共享标准的原因。
在这一切建立之前，叙述性攻击提出了两个治理问题：我们这样做是为了谁，谁被授权这样做？第一条在我们必须说真话的时候和欺骗合法的时候之间划了一条线。米尔帕的存在是为了说出真相，这不是一种约束，而是其价值的全部基础，因为信誉一旦被摧毁，就无法迅速重建，无法在危机中发挥作用。在另一端，对战场上的敌军进行军事欺骗是合法的，有时甚至是决定性的，就像乌克兰的2022年
显示。这些极端，告诉你自己的人民和盟友真相，同时在战场上欺骗敌人，可以在一场战役中共存而不矛盾。错误在于用简化的非黑即白的术语来看待叙述性冒犯，而困难的问题往往存在于大多数交流所处的中间地带。主导这一中间地带的不是一堵墙，而是两个原则：1）归因——当我们向有权使用我们名字的听众演讲时，我们不会假装成别人；2）听众——欺骗只针对军事对手，而不是我们自己的公众或为他们服务的媒体。
第二个问题，谁被授权做这件事，问我们工作应该如何划分，这就是本文的标题。国内认知空间的防御是主权盾牌。它必须仍然是一项由文职机构领导的国家责任，因为一个管理本国人民信仰的军事工具已经放弃了它所要捍卫的民主价值观。是的，军事资源可以而且应该支持这一努力，但在能力存在之前，规则必须是明确的、公开负责的，并在理论中制定。
把战斗带给对手的是联盟之剑，它颠倒了这种安排。它必须由集体领导，通过国家资产支持的整体联盟功能和能力，根据为认知层面商定的交战规则协调认知效果。盾牌必须是国家和平民的，而剑则是联盟范围和军事设计的，通过拒绝和平、危机和冲突来提供威慑。
“盾”和“剑”不是对同一任务的对立描述，而是对不同问题的互补答案，因此，保持它们的不同是民主国家不再害怕竞争的方式。
特别是在和平时期和正式的第5条声明之间，我们的对手已经将战斗正常化，认知竞赛持续不断。然而，现有的联盟决策需要对每一个低于阈值的行动达成危机级别的共识。这不仅是不可持续的，它让我们在别人选择的地面上第二个到达。补救措施是我们已经在空中应用的逻辑：北大西洋理事会并不是为了批准在波罗的海上空的每一次拦截而召开的。认知斗争也需要同样的东西。和平时期的常设当局将评估信息环境，并根据商定的交战规则，在事先设定的政治界限内，在低于门槛的情况下采取行动。这个
在2022年俄罗斯入侵之前，这表明了这在实践中是什么样子，以及在没有这样的权力的情况下即兴发挥的代价。
我们的论点引来了五个可预见的反对意见。首先，这只是一场贴上新标签的混合战争。它不是，尽管两者是重叠的。混合战争描述了在武装冲突的门槛之下，各种手段如何结合在一起。认知战描述了他们的目标。例如，混合框架告诉我们一种结合了网络入侵、代理和经济压力的操作，以使能源网络瘫痪。它没有告诉我们，目标是网络本身，还是民众对未能维持电力供应的政府的信心。
第二个反对意见是升级。如果我们持续参与，而不是只在受到挑衅时才参与，这是否有可能促使对手进行更高级别的报复？在这方面，
是真的
但我们不需要解决辩论才能采取行动。帮助民众——包括我们的民众和我们的对手的民众——认识到操纵行为，并公开披露对手正在做的事情，这是一种不那么升级的做法。
第三个反对意见是，我们成为我们所战斗的人，但这把方法错当成了姿态。对手的方法是秘密操纵，这意味着行动只会起作用，因为通常没有人能证明谁是幕后主使。这篇文章提出了相反的观点：开放的、可归属的真理，因为每个人都知道它来自哪里，所以它特别有效。彻底透明不是专制信息控制的兄弟；这是它的解药。在我们必须使用真相和欺骗合法之间划出的界线，正是为了维护真相。
在此基础上，第四个反对意见是道德方面的。为什么我们更愿意授权一场杀人的罢工，而不是授权一篇针对这些人的社交媒体帖子？这种不对称很少成为讨论的重点，但我们必须仔细审视它。如果我们准备轰炸一个社会，而不是在推特上对它进行攻击，以避免采取积极行动，我们应该问问自己，我们的道德到底在哪里。我们的不安是真正有原则的，还是仅仅是伪装成正义约束的误解？叙述式进攻通常是更人道的选择，因为将准确的信息放入对手的信息空间可以在失去生命之前改变计算。而且，威慑本身就是一种认知效应。使对手的行动更难进行，维持成本更高，这与人道的情况是分不开的，因为阻止对手进行人身攻击可以挽救双方军人和平民的生命。问题不在于采取攻击性行动是否合乎道德，而在于我们是否能够继续证明拒绝这样做的有形代价（往往是人类的代价）是合理的。
此外，将真相推入对手的信息空间既不是什么新鲜事，也没有背离我们的民主原则。这是他们的一个应用。自1948年以来，《世界人权宣言》第条第2款规定，寻求、接受和传递信息的权利“不分国界”。威权政府坚持拥有决定其公民可能知道什么的主权权利，因此，将其边界视为一条我们不敢越过真相的界线，就等于承认了这一说法。国际法禁止胁迫，公开的、归因的披露不会胁迫任何人。此外，当我们自己的人民被暗中操纵时，保持沉默不是中立；毫无疑问，这是一种选择，让我们的对手不战而胜。
最后一个反对意见是问这些是否有效。老实说，
对于每一种味道的影响操作是
.索尔兹伯里的披露和俄罗斯2022年入侵乌克兰之前的情报发布，尽管成功地消除了否认，但并没有阻止俄罗斯的坦克。因此，这个案子不能依赖于大规模的快速变化的思想。相反，它必须依赖于破坏、成本和主动性：迫使独裁政权（比表面上看起来更脆弱）花费有限的带宽来监管自己的信息空间，并确保竞争在我们选择的领域进行。以大众说服力来衡量，证据并不充分。但说服不应该是目的。我们的目标是让对手的工作变得更难、更昂贵，这比改变主意的门槛更低。
同样的诚实必须贯彻到原则本身，它应该像意图一样清楚地说明证据的限度。过度承诺说服的教条将在其第一个评估周期中失去信誉，而信誉使大胆变得负担得起。
上面没有要求北约发明一种新的理论，只是继续发展它已经拥有的理论。接下来是一个实际的议程。
有证据表明，构造已经发生了变化。北约的心理战条令最近进入了战略通信家族，并且是第一个引用认知战概念的出版物。这一举动遭到了抵制，但这是经过深思熟虑的，也是必然的。
这篇文章的论点可以归结为一条推理链：认知战不是一种能力，而是竞赛本身。它将过去的信息延伸到塑造我们如何感知和参与世界的一切事物中，影响我们相信自己是谁以及我们代表什么。竞争是持续不断的，是我们日常生活中永远存在的斗争。因此，建立在短视反应基础上的姿态，只不过是投降道路上的缓慢让步。从表面上看，可能没有鲜血可以凝固，也没有土地可以坚守，但社会本质上是可以打破的。他们从内部变得薄弱，直到将人们和机构联系在一起的信任不再束缚任何东西。
对抗这种下降并不需要联盟成为它不是的东西，因为整个设计依赖于对手不具备的关键优势：我们被看到的能力。封闭的专制制度花费大量资源来控制人民的知识，而开放的民主社会，就其本质而言，是站在信息更多而不是更少的一边。这就是为什么可归属的真理是我们的自然工具，使用它不会背叛我们存在的秩序。主权之盾和联盟之剑并不矛盾。他们是一个统一的想法。民主国家可以用平民和国家之手保护自己的认知空间，同时仍然用明确指向外部的集体军事工具来对抗敌对势力。这种分裂并不是对我们如何作战的限制；相反，它是我们如何参与和防御认知战争，而不成为战争本身的牺牲品。
每一场争夺优势的比赛，都是由了解自己真正在争夺什么的一方赢得的。在这种情况下，奖励不是领土、系统，甚至不是影响力。而是人们是否仍然能够独立思考，以及自由思想和自决的认知条件是否仍然存在。这就是我们可能失去的东西。
这也是为什么教义很重要，尽管它既不性感又无聊。在结构化的语言和精心策划的文字之下，教义是提前做出的决定，即当下一个索尔兹伯里到来时，我们将成为什么样的人。利特维年科制作了这个有管理的故事，但索尔兹伯里制作了这个联盟，因为特蕾莎·梅选择在既定的剧本之外行动。我们目前的原则仍然是为利特维年科的回应而写的，但我们面前的战斗已经改变了。继续采取后脚姿态不再是谨慎或可行的。
自由思想仍然是我们要捍卫的。我们必须进化。

TAIPEI (Taiwan News) — Beijing is concerned about the US’ “Hellscape” drone strategy to defend Taiwan in an invasion but is convinced it has not come to fruition yet, Ian Easton, an associate professor at the US Navy’s China Maritime Studies Institute, said in a CMSI
report
.
The US Pacific Command first used the term Hellscape in August 2023 to describe what a conflict in the Taiwan Strait would look like in the future, Easton said. That same month, the command announced the Replicator Initiative, which seeks to quickly deploy thousands of drones that could make the hellscape strategy a reality.
On June 10, 2024, PACOM Commander Admiral Samuel Paparo described the hellscape strategy as massive swarms of unmanned weapons targeting Chinese forces, per the report. “I want to turn the Taiwan Strait into an unmanned hellscape using a number of classified capabilities so I can make their lives utterly miserable for a month, which buys me the time for the rest of everything,” Paparo said.
Later that month, Chinese defense ministry spokesman, Senior Colonel Wu Qian, said that “some Americans” wanted to use Taiwan to contain China and flood the Taiwan Strait with drone swarms, calling them “extremely psychotic.” Wu claimed America would end up abandoning Taiwan.
In July 2024, Ren Guozheng, an expert on Taiwan affairs at the PLA Academy of Military Science, wrote that the hellscape strategy was part of American cognitive warfare and the US was trying to scare China with its plans and operations, according to Easton.
A Taiwan affairs program in China discussed the hellscape concept and Replicator Initiative during one episode that same month. The host, Li Hong, said the US was militarily inferior and called Paparo’s remarks “full of provocative intent.” She suggested America was in decline and could not keep up with the PLA.
In August 2024, another military affairs program about the Hellscape concept and Replicator Initiative was aired. Commentators said that US unmanned systems could be easily countered with electronic jamming and cyberattacks. They claimed that PLA air defense units could shoot down the drone swarms.
Despite Chinese propaganda dismissing the Hellscape strategy, many Chinese military experts are taking it seriously and respect its basic idea of using large numbers of cheap drones, seeing it as important for future warfare, Easton said.
In August 2025, the PLA Navy’s top magazine, Navy Today, published an article linking Hellscape to several US Navy advances in different types of unmanned surface vessels. “Its current state of equipment development is comprehensive, focused on actual warfighting, and cutting edge,” it said.
In January 2025, Shipborne Weapons, a China State Shipbuilding Corporation military magazine, called the Hellscape plan a “threat” and said shipborne laser weapons could be a potential countermeasure to swarms of unmanned vessels and unmanned aerial vehicles. It argued that missiles like the Hongqi-9 and Hongqi-16 were too expensive. One shot of a solid-state laser weapon would only cost a few thousand RMB.
Additionally, lasers are not limited by ammunition and are faster and more accurate. They can also destroy anti-ship missiles that are impervious to electronic jamming, the magazine said.
In a Modern Weaponry report, authors said the Replicator Initiative was a work in progress and not yet battle-tested. They said it was “basically still conceptually immature.”
The authors said the US would need to transport huge numbers of drones close to Taiwan, which would strain limited long-distance logistics and put ships within range of PLA missiles. “This means the ‘Replicator’ plan’s large numbers of unmanned systems could be destroyed before they can even be deployed,” the report said.
Easton pointed out that while Chinese propagandists are dismissive of America’s Hellscape plan, Chinese military experts take asymmetric warfare seriously and are worried about the increased US military support to Taiwan. He added that the experts view drone swarms as integral to future warfare.

台北（台湾新闻）——美国海军中国海事研究所副教授伊恩·伊斯顿（Ian Easton）在一份CMSI中表示，北京对美国在入侵中保卫台湾的“地狱式”无人机战略感到担忧，但确信该战略尚未取得成果。
报告
.
伊斯顿说，美国太平洋司令部在2023年8月首次使用“地狱景象”一词来描述未来台湾海峡的冲突。同月，司令部宣布了“复制者计划”，该计划旨在快速部署数千架无人机，使“地狱景观”战略成为现实。
据报道，2024年6月10日，太平洋司令部司令海军上将塞缪尔·帕帕罗（Samuel Paparo）将“地狱景观”战略描述为针对中国军队的大规模无人武器。帕帕罗说：“我想把台湾海峡变成一个无人驾驶的地狱景观，使用一些机密的能力，这样我就可以让他们的生活在一个月内完全痛苦，这为我赢得了时间来做剩下的事情。”
当月晚些时候，中国国防部发言人吴谦大校表示，“一些美国人”想利用台湾来遏制中国，并用无人机群淹没台湾海峡，称他们是“极端精神病患者”。吴声称美国最终会放弃台湾。
根据伊斯顿的说法，2024年7月，解放军军事科学院台湾问题专家任国政写道，“地狱景观”战略是美国认知战的一部分，美国正试图用其计划和行动恐吓中国。
中国的一个台湾事务节目在同一个月的一期节目中讨论了“地狱景观”概念和“复制者”计划。主持人李红表示，美国在军事上处于劣势，并称帕帕罗的言论“充满挑衅意图”。她暗示美国正在衰落，无法跟上解放军的步伐。
2024年8月，另一个关于“地狱景观”概念和“复制者”计划的军事节目播出。评论人士表示，美国的无人系统很容易被电子干扰和网络攻击所反击。他们声称解放军防空部队可以击落无人机群。
伊斯顿说，尽管中国的宣传对“地狱景观”战略不屑一顾，但许多中国军事专家都认真对待这一战略，并尊重其使用大量廉价无人机的基本理念，认为这对未来战争非常重要。
2025年8月，解放军海军的顶级杂志《今日海军》（Navy Today）发表了一篇文章，将“地狱景观”（Hellscape）与美国海军在不同类型的无人水面舰艇方面的几项进展联系起来。“它目前的装备发展状态是全面的，专注于实际作战，而且是尖端的，”它说。
2025年1月，中国船舶工业集团公司旗下的军事杂志《舰载武器》（Shipborne Weapons）将“地狱景观”计划称为“威胁”，并表示舰载激光武器可能是应对大量无人船只和无人飞行器的潜在对策。它认为像红旗-9和红旗-16这样的导弹太贵了。一发固态激光武器只需要几千元人民币。
此外，激光不受弹药的限制，速度更快，精度更高。该杂志称，它们还可以摧毁不受电子干扰的反舰导弹。
在一份现代武器报告中，作者表示，复制者计划是一项正在进行的工作，尚未经过实战测试。他们说它“基本上在概念上还不成熟”。
作者表示，美国将需要在台湾附近运送大量无人机，这将使有限的长途后勤紧张，并使船只处于解放军导弹的射程之内。报告称：“这意味着'复制者'计划的大量无人系统可能在部署之前就被摧毁。”
伊斯顿指出，当中国的宣传人员对美国的“地狱式”计划不屑一顾时，中国的军事专家却严肃对待不对称战争，并对美国增加对台湾的军事支持感到担忧。他补充说，专家们认为无人机群是未来战争不可或缺的一部分。
_source.trans_title: 伊斯顿说中国怀疑美国在台湾海峡的“地狱景观”概念

A profound sense of anguish accompanies 25-year-old Taghreed Yahya during her daily commute from her town of Kafr Ra’i to the city centre of Jenin in the north of the occupied West Bank.
Along the main road connecting Jenin and Nablus, she is routinely confronted by hundreds of Israeli flags, a jarring visual imposition of Israeli domination and occupation on a route heavily used by local Palestinians.
Recommended Stories list of 4 itemslist 1 of 4Villagers vow to rebuild despite devastating mass demolition in West Banklist 2 of 4Israeli police kill Palestinian in Jerusalem as army blocks aid for Qusralist 3 of 4Israel must protect West Bank’s Palestinians amid settler pogroms: US envoylist 4 of 4Israeli campaign of West Bank destruction moves on to region’s food basketend of listYahya said it started with a flag here, an outpost there, a new road cutting through the landscape.
“[It] makes the scene that was familiar for years change; all of this naturally leaves sadness, anger and fear, in addition to a feeling of helplessness,” she told Al Jazeera. “But at the same time, it strengthens the clinging to the land, memory and identity.”
Visual sovereigntyThis aggressive visual display of Israeli occupation represents an escalating phase of colonisation, extending beyond the physical outposts and attacks to a forced disfigurement of the geographical identity of the Palestinian territory.
When dozens of olive trees owned by the Palestinian residents of Arrabeh were uprooted, groups of Israeli settlers simultaneously decked a bypass road in northeastern areas of Jenin with Israeli flags to assert their dominance.
These flag-hanging campaigns, often facilitated by Israeli military incursions to secure the area, aim to artificially alter the Palestinian landscape. This is done in conjunction with the rapid deployment of mobile homes to establish dozens of settler outposts in new areas of the occupied West Bank.
Advertisement
For Palestinians who commute through this territory to work or home, the erasure of familiar landscapes is disorienting.
Faten Abdel Hadi, a photographer who regularly travels between Qalqilya, Nablus, Tulkarem and Salfit, noted that drastic changes materialised between June and August.
“I was hit by a lack of understanding of the geography I know, if I may say so. The major change that befell the most prominent landmarks in the streets seemed as if it went through a long time period, but it actually needed less than two months,” Faten told Al Jazeera.
“This scene is very painful: the scenes of the settlers’ mobile homes and flags, and their gatherings on the sides of the main streets, return us to the truth that these people stole our right and our belonging.”
Searing the consciousnessThis phenomenon escalated after October 7, 2023, when illegal settlement expansion and Israeli military raids in the occupied West Bank escalated. Israeli forces and settlers have killed more than 1,100 Palestinians since then, while a 66th Palestinian village was ethnically cleansed, according to B’Tselem.
Israel’s tender for buildings in the E1 settlement near Jerusalem also threatens to split the occupied West Bank in two, and analysts say it will end any hope of the establishment of a Palestinian state.
The process of Israeli expansionism often begins with the hardline group Hilltop Youth erecting a single tent or grazing sheep on a Palestinian hill, before larger illegal Israeli settlements are established in the area with government backing.
The Colonization and Wall Resistance Commission (CRRC) reported that Israeli authorities reviewed 113 structural plans to expand or establish new illegal settlements during the first half of 2026. This appears to mark a strategic shift by the Israeli government to produce new settlements on a mass scale to enforce Israeli sovereignty and annex Palestinian land.
Khaldoun al-Barghouthi, head of Israeli affairs and researcher at the Palestinian Research Center (PRC), said the deployment of Israeli flags to these areas is a tactic to enforce Israel’s physical and psychological presence in Palestinian areas.
The message to Palestinians is that Israeli settlers are a permanent fixture on the land, while their presence is temporary.
This localised intimidation is echoed by the highest echelons of Israeli leadership, including Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu, who recently boasted about building 104 illegal settlements and 160 settlement farms. His far-right ministers – Bezalel Smotrich and Itamar Ben-Gvir – have also used their powers to bolster the settlers’ expansionist aims.
Advertisement
“The control they are working on is not limited to fieldwork, meaning building settlements, confiscating lands and reducing the area of land owned by Palestinians, but also aims to sear the Palestinian consciousness regarding their existence on their land,” al-Barghouthi explained to Al Jazeera.
Ultimately, this psychological warfare serves a demographic objective. The overarching plan of the Hilltop Youth and the architects of the recent settler pogroms against West Bank villages is to force Palestinians to migrate from their rural communities. The result would be Palestinians confined to isolated urban areas, while the physical and visual landscape of the West Bank is entirely consumed by Israeli settlers and the military.
_source.movement_title: 以色列加速扩建定居点并悬挂国旗强化占领心理战
_source.movement_abstract: 【卡塔尔半岛电视台2026年9月报道】2026年上半年，以色列当局审查了113项扩建或新建非法定居点的结构计划，标志着其大规模推进定居点建设的战略转变。以色列政府及极右翼部长贝扎莱尔·斯莫特里赫和伊塔马尔·本-格维尔积极推动扩张，总理内塔尼亚胡宣称已建成104个非法定居点和160个定居点农场。在约旦河西银行北部杰宁至纳布卢斯等主要道路沿线，以色列定居者频繁悬挂国旗并部署移动房屋，配合军事行动强行改变巴勒斯坦地理景观。巴勒斯坦研究中心指出，此举旨在通过视觉和心理手段确立以色列的永久存在，迫使巴勒斯坦人产生无助感并迁离农村社区。自2023年10月7日以来，以色列军队和定居者在约旦河西岸杀害超过1100名巴勒斯坦人，66个巴勒斯坦村庄遭清洗。E1定居区建设计划进一步威胁将约旦河西岸分割，终结巴勒斯坦建国希望。该行动被分析为旨在通过人口置换和领土吞并，将巴勒斯坦人限制在孤立城市区域，彻底重塑西岸物理与视觉版图。

25岁的塔格里德·叶海亚（Taghreed Yahya）每天往返于被占领的约旦河西岸北部的卡夫拉伊镇（Kafr Ra I）和杰宁（Jenin）市中心之间，她感到极度痛苦。
在连接杰宁和纳布卢斯的主要道路上，她经常遇到数百面以色列国旗，这是在当地巴勒斯坦人大量使用的道路上强加以色列统治和占领的一种不和谐的视觉效果。
推荐故事列表4个项目列表1个4个村民发誓重建，尽管在约旦河西岸进行了毁灭性的大规模拆除列表2个4以色列警察在耶路撒冷杀害巴勒斯坦人，因为军队阻止对Qusralist的援助列表3个4以色列必须在定居者大屠杀中保护约旦河西岸的巴勒斯坦人：美国Envoylist列表4个4以色列西岸破坏运动转移到该地区的食品篮Listyahya说，它开始于这里的一面旗帜，那里的一个前哨，一条新的道路穿过景观。
（它）让多年来熟悉的场景发生了变化。她告诉半岛电视台，所有这些自然会留下悲伤、愤怒和恐惧，此外还有一种无助感。“但同时也强化了对土地、记忆和身份的执着。”
视觉主权以色列占领的这一侵略性的视觉展示代表了一个不断升级的殖民阶段，超越了物理前哨和攻击，强行破坏了巴勒斯坦领土的地理特征。
当阿拉贝的巴勒斯坦居民拥有的几十棵橄榄树被连根拔起时，成群结队的以色列定居者同时用以色列国旗装饰杰宁东北部地区的一条绕行道路，以维护他们的统治地位。
以色列为确保该地区安全而进行的军事入侵往往为这些悬挂旗帜的活动提供了便利，其目的是人为地改变巴勒斯坦的面貌。这是与快速部署移动房屋同时进行的，以便在被占领的西岸新地区建立数十个定居者前哨。
广告
对于通过这片领土通勤上班或回家的巴勒斯坦人来说，熟悉的风景被抹去是令人迷惑的。
Faten Abdel Hadi是一位经常往返于盖勒吉利耶、纳布卢斯、图勒凯尔姆和萨尔费特之间的摄影师，他指出，6月至8月间发生了巨大的变化。
如果我可以这么说的话，我对我所知道的地理知识缺乏了解。法特恩告诉半岛电视台，街道上最显著的地标发生的重大变化似乎经历了很长一段时间，但实际上只需要不到两个月的时间。
“这一幕非常令人痛心：定居者的活动房屋和旗帜，以及他们在主要街道两侧聚集的场景，让我们重新认识到，这些人窃取了我们的权利和财产。”
这一现象在2023年10月7日之后升级，当时以色列在被占领的约旦河西岸的非法定居点扩张和军事袭击升级。据以色列占领区人权信息中心称，自那时以来，以色列军队和定居者已经杀害了1100多名巴勒斯坦人，而第66个巴勒斯坦村庄遭到种族清洗。
以色列对耶路撒冷附近E1定居点建筑的招标也有可能将被占领的约旦河西岸一分为二，分析人士说，这将使建立巴勒斯坦国的任何希望破灭。
以色列的扩张主义进程往往始于强硬派团体“山顶青年”在巴勒斯坦山上搭起一个帐篷或放羊，然后在政府的支持下在该地区建立更大的非法以色列定居点。
殖民和隔离墙抵抗委员会（CRRC）报告说，以色列当局审查了113项关于在2026年上半年扩大或建立新的非法定居点的结构计划。这似乎标志着以色列政府的战略转变，即大规模建立新的定居点，以加强以色列的主权并吞并巴勒斯坦土地。
巴勒斯坦研究中心（PRC）以色列事务负责人兼研究员Khaldoun al-Barghouthi说，在这些地区部署以色列国旗是一种策略，目的是加强以色列在巴勒斯坦地区的实际和心理存在。
向巴勒斯坦人传达的信息是，以色列定居者是这片土地上的永久居民，而他们的存在是暂时的。
这种局部恐吓得到了以色列最高领导层的响应，包括总理本雅明·内塔尼亚胡，他最近吹嘘建造了104个非法定居点和160个定居点农场。他的极右翼部长——贝扎莱尔·斯莫特里奇（Bezalel Smotrich）和伊塔马尔·本-格维尔（Itamar Ben-Gvir）——也利用他们的权力支持定居者的扩张主义目标。
广告
Al-Barghouthi向半岛电视台解释说：“他们正在进行的控制不仅限于实地工作，即修建定居点、没收土地和减少巴勒斯坦人拥有的土地面积，而且还旨在烧灼巴勒斯坦人对他们在自己土地上存在的意识。”
最终，这种心理战服务于一个人口统计目标。山顶青年和最近针对西岸村庄的定居者大屠杀的策划者的总体计划是迫使巴勒斯坦人离开他们的农村社区。其结果将是巴勒斯坦人被限制在孤立的城市地区，而西岸的物质和视觉景观完全被以色列定居者和军队所吞噬。

TEHRAN — Iran’s armed forces have successfully confronted the United States and Israel through an asymmetric approach to warfare, Major General Ali Abdollahi, Chief of Staff of the Iranian Armed Forces, said on Sunday.
Speaking at an event, Abdollahi said Iran was now facing an “all-out hybrid, soft and cognitive war,” involving a combination of military, economic and psychological pressure.
He said the United States had not been accustomed to hearing a “no” from other countries for more than 80 years and had wrongly assumed, before launching its war of aggression against Iran, that the Iranian people would eventually surrender.
“That illusion will never become reality,” Abdollahi said.
The senior commander stated that the United States and Israel were attempting to make up for their strategic shortcomings and setbacks by employing soft and cognitive warfare, along with economic pressure. He asserted that these efforts would ultimately fail due to the resilience of the Iranian people and the sound judgment of the country’s officials.
Abdollahi said Iran’s Armed Forces had demonstrated an ability to confront superior military powers through asymmetric means while retaining the strategic initiative in the face of threats.
He also portrayed Iran’s experience as a broader model of resistance, saying the Islamic Republic had offered the world a new approach rooted in its religious and national values.
“By God’s grace, the future world will be different from the past,” Abdollahi said. “This change will benefit the Iranian nation and will be accompanied by the definite decline of U.S. power.”
His remarks reflect Tehran’s broader narrative that military pressure alone cannot force Iran to abandon its strategic positions. Iranian officials have repeatedly emphasized the role of asymmetric capabilities, domestic defense production and national resilience in countering external military and economic pressure.

_source.movement_abstract: 伊朗武装部队总参谋长阿里·阿卜杜拉希少将周日在德黑兰发表讲话，宣称伊朗军队已成功通过非对称作战手段应对美国和以色列的军事挑战。阿卜杜拉希指出，伊朗当前正面临涵盖军事、经济及心理施压的“全面混合、软性及认知战”。他批评美国在长达80余年的霸权中习惯于他国顺从，错误预判伊朗民众会在侵略战争前屈服，并断言该幻想无法实现。阿卜杜拉希强调，美以试图利用软性认知战及经济制裁弥补战略短板，但受限于伊朗民众的韧性与政府决策的明智，这些企图终将失败。他进一步表示，伊朗武装部队已证明具备在威胁面前保持战略主动权并抗衡军事强权的能力。阿卜杜拉希将伊朗经验描述为基于宗教与民族价值观的全球抵抗新范式，预言美国权力必将衰退，世界格局将发生有利于伊朗的变革。该言论反映了德黑兰关于单纯军事压力无法迫使伊朗放弃战略立场的一贯叙事，突显非对称能力、国防自主生产及国家韧性在应对外部压力中的核心作用。

德黑兰-伊朗武装部队参谋长Ali Abdollahi少将周日表示，伊朗武装部队通过不对称的战争方式成功对抗了美国和以色列。
阿卜杜拉希在一次活动中说，伊朗现在正面临一场“全面的混合、软和认知战争”，涉及军事、经济和心理压力的结合。
他说，80多年来，美国一直不习惯听到其他国家说“不”，在发动对伊朗的侵略战争之前，错误地认为伊朗人民最终会投降。
阿卜杜拉希说：“这种幻想永远不会成为现实。”
这位高级指挥官表示，美国和以色列正试图通过软战和认知战以及经济压力来弥补其战略缺陷和挫折。他断言，由于伊朗人民的韧性和该国官员的正确判断，这些努力最终将失败。
阿卜杜拉希说，伊朗武装部队已经展示了通过不对称手段对抗优势军事力量的能力，同时在面对威胁时保持战略主动权。
他还将伊朗的经历描述为一种更广泛的抵抗模式，称这个伊斯兰共和国为世界提供了一种根植于其宗教和民族价值观的新方法。
阿卜杜拉希说：“承蒙上帝的恩典，未来的世界将与过去不同。”“这一变化将有利于伊朗民族，并将伴随着美国实力的明显下降。”
他的言论反映了德黑兰更广泛的说法，即仅靠军事压力无法迫使伊朗放弃其战略地位。伊朗官员一再强调不对称能力、国内国防生产和国家恢复力在对抗外部军事和经济压力方面的作用。

OPINION:
Taiwan is an important partner for the
United States
.
It is working to reindustrialize and onshore drone, robotics and advanced-manufacturing supply chains. It also supplies the U.S. with the advanced chips necessary for maintaining our frontier lead in artificial intelligence over China.
Taiwan is investing unprecedented amounts of money to help restore American chip fabrication capacity.
In July,Taiwan Semiconductor Manufacturing Co.
committed to investing an additional $100 billion for the construction of several advanced fabs and advanced packaging facilities in Phoenix.
These facilities would allow the U.S. to produce chips with 2-nanometer process nodes and below, as well as packaging technologies necessary for AI computing. They bring TSMC’s total investment in the U.S. to $265 billion.
The Trump administration is focused on onshoring critical industries, and with good reason, but Mr. Trump’s contentious claim that Taiwan “stole” America’s chip industry and Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent’s statement that the concentration of advanced chip production in Taiwan represents the “single greatest point of failure for the world economy” position Taiwan as a competitor in semiconductor manufacturing, not a partner.
Although these statements are often taken out of context, they amplify fears among the Taiwanese that the U.S. seeks to “hollow out” Taiwan’s advanced semiconductor industry.
By feeding into the “hollowing out” narrative, the administration is arming Taiwan’s political opposition and other skeptics with rhetorical ammunition to resist deeper U.S.-Taiwan economic cooperation.
It is also providing cannon fodder for China to undermine Taiwan’s trust in the U.S. through ongoing cognitive warfare campaigns. China began spreading the story in Taiwan’s information ecosystem as early as 2021.
The narrative is part of a broader “America skepticism” refrain, which posits that the U.S. is an unreliable partner and will ultimately abandon Taiwan should China attempt to take it by force.
There is a perception that by onshoring advanced semiconductor production, America would undermine the so-called silicon shield, which proposes that Taiwan’s chip industry secure an American commitment to Taiwan’s defense and deter Chinese aggression.
Kuomintang party leader Cheng Li-wun remarked that the Trump administration’s aim to significantly increase domestic chip production by 2028 is tantamount to “completely relocating and hollowing out” Taiwan’s “family fortune and sacred mountain.”
This skepticism is making its way into policy. KMT legislators plan to advance a bill to grant Taiwan’s legislature unprecedented authority to restrict the outbound investments of Taiwanese semiconductor companies.
If passed, the measure could directly affect TSMC’s ability to build fabs in the U.S., Japan and Germany.
The “America skepticism” narrative polarizes the Taiwanese. Opposition supporters are more likely to believe that TSMC’s investments in the U.S. erode the silicon shield, according to a survey of Taiwan’s political opposition by Academia Sinica. Conversely, those who support the ruling Democratic Progressive Party are more inclined to view these investments as a sign of deepening U.S.-Taiwan economic interdependence.
Taiwan should recognize the strategic opportunity in deepening its economic ties with America. Rather than a “hollowing out,” TSMC’s investments represent an expansion of Taiwan’s footprint on the global economy.
They mark the next phase of a derisked, “non-China-centered” globalization in which deeper interdependence between Taiwan, America and allies strengthens supply chain resilience.
Because of the surge in demand for AI chips, the U.S. is also a major contributor to Taiwan’s economic growth. Therefore, Taiwan will be a key player in the global economy for decades to come, and its continued leadership in advanced semiconductors is aligned with American interests.
Taiwan did not “steal” the American chip industry. It supplies American firms. During the 1990s, the American semiconductor industry shifted toward the “fabless-foundry” business model, resulting in a division of labor where American firms specializing in chip design outsourced chip production to foundries in Taiwan and other East Asian countries.
The model allows chip designers to focus their capital on innovation and marketing.
Taiwan is the single greatest point of productivity — not failure — for the global economy. TSMC produces more than 90% of the world’s most advanced semiconductors. More than one-fifth of global maritime trade transits through the Taiwan Strait.
These are assets, not vulnerabilities.
Taiwan is not a competitor to the
United States
; it is an indispensable partner. Unfairly characterizing the island nation gives credence to narratives that erode a strategic relationship forged by shared interests and values.
The U.S. and Taiwan stand to gain if they recognize that the partnership is deepening, not diminishing. We should keep the money flowing and the fabs humming.
• Peter V. Tozzi is a policy analyst at the Research Institute for Democracy, Society and Emerging Technology, a Taipei-based think tank.

_source.movement_title: 美智库分析台美半导体合作及特朗普言论引发的认知战风险
_source.movement_abstract: 【美国智库研究员彼得·托齐2026年9月7日撰文】美国智库研究员彼得·托齐撰文分析台美半导体合作关系。台积电承诺在亚利桑那州凤凰城追加投资1000亿美元建设先进晶圆厂，使其在美总投资达2650亿美元，旨在生产2纳米及以下制程芯片。文章指出，特朗普政府关于台湾‘窃取’美国芯片产业及台积电集中生产构成‘全球经济最大单一故障点’的言论，被解读为将台湾视为竞争对手而非伙伴。此类言论加剧了台湾内部对‘产业空心化’的担忧，被台湾在野党及中国大陆利用，作为认知战素材以削弱台湾对美信任。国民党立法机构计划推动法案限制台湾半导体企业海外投资，可能影响台积电在美、日、德建厂。调查显示，台湾在野党支持者更倾向于认为赴美投资削弱‘硅盾’，而民进党支持者则视其为深化经济互赖。文章强调，台湾是全球先进半导体生产力的核心，台积电生产全球90%以上最先进芯片，台美深化经济联系符合双方战略利益，应摒弃‘空心化’叙事，强化供应链韧性。
