_source.title: Qalibaf: Iran will respond militarily if US intensifies blockade
_source.trans_cont:
德黑兰-伊朗议会议长Mohammad Baqer Qalibaf警告说，美国已经对伊朗伊斯兰共和国采取“混合战争”，试图弥补其军事和外交上的失败。
卡利巴夫在一次视频讲话中说：“敌人已经向我们表明，在军事和外交方面遭受挫折后，他们已经在其行动中增加了广泛的经济和认知战活动。”
他补充说，换句话说，我们现在正面临一场混合战争，海上封锁本身就构成了一种军事战争形式。经济战仍然是他们的主要重点，并通过复杂的心理战得到加强。
议会发言人谈到了华盛顿在这一战略背后的更广泛的目标，他说：敌人在这场混合战争中的目标是煽动国内动乱和混乱，这是他们的险恶用心，在某些情况下，还会实施定点暗杀。他们甚至可能试图进行短暂、有限的军事打击，以削弱我们的决心或迫使我们在谈判桌上投降。
卡利巴夫还警告说，如果美国加强对伊朗港口的封锁，伊朗将作出军事回应。
如果他们加强封锁，我们肯定会做出军事回应，所有人都会遭殃。他断言：“如果敌人决心阻止我们从波斯湾出口石油，那么没有人能够出口石油。”
卡利巴夫的讲话正值华盛顿的言辞不断升级之际。唐纳德·特朗普总统最近威胁要对德黑兰采取前所未有的多条战线的行动，并警告说，如果关键要求得不到满足，可能会对伊朗的战略资产和基础设施进行军事打击。
军事威胁与特朗普所说的针对德黑兰的全面“毁灭性经济诺曼底登陆”运动不谋而合。在全面的经济措施下，华盛顿警告国际银行、公司和政府，维持贸易关系、处理交易或为伊朗石油出口提供便利将引发严重的二级制裁和金融孤立。
2月28日，美国和以色列对伊朗发动了又一轮无端侵略，这距离他们在2025年6月对伊朗领土发动非法袭击已经过去了大约8个月。然而，伊朗对以色列和美国在该地区基地的强烈军事回应迫使特朗普呼吁停火，停火于4月8日生效。尽管有停火协议和6月17日在巴基斯坦斡旋下达成的谅解备忘录，但美国违反了其承诺，对伊朗发动了新的打击，并继续实施海上封锁。
_source.trans_title: 卡利巴夫：如果美国加强封锁，伊朗将作出军事回应

_source.content:
TEHRAN – In yet another delusional outburst from the decaying American empire, Donald Trump has once again proven that Washington's leadership has lost all touch with reality. His August 31 declaration that "Iran is officially a Failed Nation. IT IS DEAD!" represents not strategic analysis, but the desperate hallucinations of a regime accustomed to imposing its will through deception.
Nations do not cease to exist because a bankrupt politician declares them so on social media.  Iran's ancient civilization has weathered far greater storms than the current Zio-American pressure campaign and will certainly outlast the current crop of Western leaders whose grip on reality grows more tenuous by the day.
More concerning is Trump's brazen use of artificial intelligence as an instrument of psychological warfare. The fabricated video purporting to show Kharg Island's destruction, later admitted to be AI-generated by Vice President JD Vance, represents a new low in American propaganda. When Washington presents imaginary destruction as accomplished fact, it reveals its fundamental weakness: the inability to achieve strategic objectives through legitimate means. The Zionist-inspired American regime has long understood the power of spectacle, from Hollywood's vilification of Iran to the systematic erasure of Palestinian identity. But war is less forgiving than electoral theater. Missiles do not disappear because a bankrupt real estate mogul declares the enemy finished. Sovereign nations do not surrender because Washington announces their defeat through artificial images.
The contradiction in American policy toward Iran is glaring. If Iran is already "dead," why does Washington continue to warn Tehran about future consequences? Why does the administration still describe Iranian attacks as a serious threat to American forces and commercial shipping in the Persian Gulf? The answer is simple: the battlefield reality contradicts the propaganda. Iran has not only survived Washington's maximum pressure campaign but has demonstrated remarkable resilience. Despite facing the most comprehensive economic warfare in modern history, Iran continues to advance its scientific capabilities, maintain regional influence, and defend its sovereignty. Iran's military capabilities remain formidable, as evidenced by the embarrassing failures of American and Israeli operations against Iranian assets. The Islamic Republic's air defense systems, naval presence in the strategic Persian Gulf, and missile capabilities continue to pose a genuine deterrent to Zionist ambitions in the region.
One cannot separate Washington's hostility toward Iran from the corrosive influence of the Zionist lobby on American foreign policy. The relentless push for confrontation serves Tel Aviv's interests far more than America's. Why should American soldiers sacrifice their lives for Israeli security? Why should American taxpayers fund endless conflicts that only benefit the apartheid regime in occupied Palestine? The Iranian people have repeatedly demonstrated their capacity to resist foreign domination. From the 1979 Islamic Revolution to the present, Iran has consistently rejected Western attempts to impose its will. The American war of words against Iran is fundamentally a war against national sovereignty and the right to chart one's own destiny free from imperial interference.
Perhaps most disturbing is Washington's callous exploitation of human suffering. Reported casualty figures from American sources have shifted dramatically from tens of thousands to more than 100,000 alleged deaths with little evidence to support these claims. If accurate, these figures represent a humanitarian catastrophe demanding independent verification. If inaccurate, their use as political slogans reduces human tragedy to mere ammunition in Washington's propaganda war. The Islamic Republic has repeatedly called for international investigations into American and Israeli war crimes, including the systematic assassination of Iranian scientists, cyberattacks on civilian infrastructure, and economic warfare that constitutes collective punishment under international humanitarian law.
Washington's reckless rhetoric also threatens the Strait of Hormuz, one of the world's most strategically important waterways. Any serious confrontation in the Persian Gulf would have devastating consequences for regional security and the global economy. These realities cannot be managed through memes, AI-generated videos, or declarations that an entire nation is "dead." The Islamic Republic has consistently demonstrated its commitment to regional stability, unlike the American regime that has left a trail of destruction from Afghanistan to Libya to Yemen.
When political leaders become more invested in declaring victory than establishing facts, credibility becomes collateral damage. The United States' strategic asset should be its credibility, yet every false image or exaggerated claim weakens this foundation. Propaganda can shape perception, but perception cannot substitute for strategy. AI can manufacture the image of a destroyed island. Social media can manufacture the appearance of triumph. None of it can manufacture victory. Military power can destroy infrastructure, but it cannot, by itself, manufacture political outcomes. This is a lesson America learned in Vietnam, Afghanistan, and Iraq, and will inevitably learn in its confrontation with Iran.
While Washington indulges in fantasies of Iranian collapse, the Islamic Republic continues to demonstrate remarkable resilience. Iran has transformed challenges into opportunities for self-reliance and technological advancement, from nuclear technology to biotechnology, from aerospace to nanotechnology. Iran's political system, grounded in Islamic values and republican institutions, has proven its legitimacy through successive elections and popular participation.  The American claim that Iran is a "failed state" ignores the reality of a functioning government that provides services to its citizens, maintains security across its vast territory, and continues to exert influence from the Persian Gulf to the Mediterranean.
The broader issue extends far beyond Iran. The American empire is in terminal decline, unable to accept that the unipolar moment has passed. Washington's desperate attempts to maintain global hegemony through sanctions and military threats reflect not strength but weakness.  China, Russia, and the emerging multipolar order represent a future that respects national sovereignty and cultural diversity. Iran will continue strengthening its ties with these powers, reducing its vulnerability to American pressure. The so-called "America First" policy reveals itself as "America Alone," isolated from the global consensus that rejects unilateralism.
Trump may dominate the news cycle with a post. He may make an artificial image trend across social media. None of that changes the battlefield reality.
Iran will continue its path of dignity, resistance, and development.  The Islamic Republic will survive American propaganda, Zionist ambitions, and imperial pressures. Iranian civilization has endured for millennia; it will not collapse because a bankrupt American politician declares it "dead" on social media. The American empire, meanwhile, continues its inevitable decline, hoisted by its own petard of deception and moral bankruptcy.  History will judge which civilization truly failed.
_source.movement_title: 特朗普宣称伊朗已灭亡并承认使用AI伪造视频
_source.movement_abstract: 2026年8月31日，美国前总统唐纳德·特朗普发表声明，宣称伊朗为‘失败国家’并断言其‘已灭亡’。随后，美国副总统JD·万斯承认，此前流传的显示伊朗哈尔格岛被摧毁的视频系人工智能生成。该事件被指为美国利用AI技术进行心理战和宣传战的新手段。文章指出，尽管面临美国‘极限施压’政策及全面经济战，伊朗在科学能力、地区影响力及主权维护方面仍表现出显著韧性。伊朗防空系统、波斯湾海军存在及导弹能力构成有效威慑。美方关于伊朗造成数万人至10万人伤亡的指控缺乏证据，伊朗方面呼吁对美以涉嫌战争罪行进行国际调查。分析认为，美国在霍尔木兹海峡等关键水域的对抗言论威胁地区安全与全球经济。伊朗正通过加强与中国、俄罗斯等国的合作应对美国压力，推动多极化秩序。文章强调，美国试图通过虚假图像和社交媒体制造胜利假象，但无法改变战场现实，其单边主义政策正导致其全球信誉受损及霸权衰落。

德黑兰—在衰落的美帝国的又一次妄想爆发中，唐纳德·特朗普再一次证明了华盛顿的领导已经完全脱离了现实。他在8月31日正式宣布伊朗是一个失败的国家。它死了！它代表的不是战略分析，而是一个习惯于通过欺骗将其意志强加于人的政权的绝望幻觉。
国家不会因为一个破产的政客在社交媒体上这样宣称而停止存在。伊朗的古老文明经受住了比当前的犹太复国主义-美国施压运动更大的风暴，并且肯定会比当前的西方领导人更持久，他们对现实的把握一天比一天脆弱。
更令人担忧的是特朗普厚颜无耻地使用人工智能作为心理战的工具。这段伪造的视频声称显示了哈格岛的毁灭，后来被副总统JD Vance承认是人工智能生成的，这代表了美国宣传的新低点。当华盛顿将想象中的毁灭作为既成事实时，它暴露了自己的根本弱点：无法通过合法手段实现战略目标。从好莱坞对伊朗的中伤到对巴勒斯坦身份的系统性抹杀，受犹太复国主义者启发的美国政权早就明白了奇观的力量。但战争比选举舞台更不宽容。导弹不会因为一个破产的房地产大亨宣布敌人完蛋而消失。主权国家不会因为华盛顿通过人造图像宣布他们的失败而投降。
美国对伊朗政策的矛盾显而易见。如果伊朗已经“死亡”，为什么华盛顿继续警告德黑兰未来的后果？为什么美国政府仍然将伊朗的袭击描述为对美国军队和波斯湾商业航运的严重威胁？答案很简单：战场现实与宣传相矛盾。伊朗不仅在华盛顿的最大压力运动中幸存下来，而且表现出了非凡的韧性。尽管面临着现代历史上最全面的经济战，伊朗仍在继续提高其科学能力，保持地区影响力，捍卫其主权。伊朗的军事能力仍然令人生畏，美国和以色列针对伊朗资产的行动令人尴尬的失败就是明证。伊朗伊斯兰共和国的防空系统、在具有战略意义的波斯湾的海军存在以及导弹能力继续对该地区的犹太复国主义野心构成真正的威慑。
人们无法将华盛顿对伊朗的敌意与犹太复国主义游说团体对美国外交政策的腐蚀性影响分开。对对抗的无情推动更符合特拉维夫的利益，而不是美国的。为什么美国士兵要为以色列的安全牺牲自己的生命？为什么美国纳税人要为无休止的冲突提供资金，而这些冲突只有利于被占领的巴勒斯坦的种族隔离政权？伊朗人民一再表明他们有能力抵抗外国统治。从1979年伊斯兰革命到现在，伊朗一直拒绝西方强加其意志的企图。从根本上说，美国对伊朗的口水战是一场针对国家主权和不受帝国干涉主宰自身命运的权利的战争。
也许最令人不安的是华盛顿对人类苦难的无情利用。美国方面报告的伤亡数字从数万人急剧上升到10万多人，但几乎没有证据支持这些说法。如果准确的话，这些数字代表着一场需要独立核查的人道主义灾难。如果不准确，它们作为政治口号的使用会使人类悲剧沦为华盛顿宣传战的弹药。伊朗伊斯兰共和国一再呼吁对美国和以色列的战争罪行进行国际调查，包括有系统地暗杀伊朗科学家，对民用基础设施进行网络攻击，以及根据国际人道主义法构成集体惩罚的经济战。
华盛顿的鲁莽言论还威胁到霍尔木兹海峡，这是世界上最具战略重要性的水道之一。波斯湾的任何严重对抗都会给地区安全和全球经济带来破坏性后果。这些现实无法通过迷因、人工智能生成的视频或整个国家“死亡”的声明来管理。伊朗伊斯兰共和国一贯致力于地区稳定，不像美国政权从阿富汗到利比亚再到也门留下了一条毁灭之路。
当政治领导人更多地致力于宣布胜利而不是确立事实时，信誉就成了附带损害。美国的战略资产应该是它的信誉，但每一个虚假的形象或夸大的说法都会削弱这一基础。宣传可以塑造认知，但认知不能代替战略。人工智能可以制造一个被摧毁的岛屿的形象。社交媒体可以制造胜利的表象。这一切都不能制造胜利。军事力量可以摧毁基础设施，但它本身无法制造政治结果。这是美国在越南、阿富汗和伊拉克战争中学到的教训，也将不可避免地在与伊朗的对抗中吸取教训。
当华盛顿沉浸在伊朗崩溃的幻想中时，这个伊斯兰共和国继续表现出非凡的韧性。从核技术到生物技术，从航空航天到纳米技术，伊朗已将挑战转化为自力更生和技术进步的机遇。伊朗的政治制度以伊斯兰价值观和共和制度为基础，通过连续的选举和民众参与证明了其合法性。美国声称伊朗是一个“失败的国家”，这忽视了这样一个现实：一个正常运转的政府为其公民提供服务，维护其广大领土的安全，并继续在从波斯湾到地中海的地区施加影响。
更广泛的问题远远超出了伊朗。美帝国正在走下坡路，无法接受单极时代已经过去的事实。华盛顿不顾一切地试图通过制裁和军事威胁来维持全球霸权，这反映的不是实力，而是弱点。中国、俄罗斯和新兴的多极秩序代表着一个尊重国家主权和文化多样性的未来。伊朗将继续加强与这些大国的关系，减少其对美国压力的脆弱性。所谓的“美国优先”政策表现为“美国孤立”，孤立于反对单边主义的全球共识之外。
特朗普可能会以一篇文章主导新闻周期。他可能会在社交媒体上制造一种人为的形象趋势。这些都不能改变战场的现实。
伊朗将继续走尊严、抵抗和发展的道路。伊斯兰共和国将经受住美国的宣传、犹太复国主义的野心和帝国的压力。伊朗文明已经延续了数千年。它不会因为一个破产的美国政客在社交媒体上宣布它“死亡”而崩溃。与此同时，由于欺骗和道德沦丧，美帝国继续其不可避免的衰落。历史将会评判哪种文明真正失败了。

_source.content:
A small number of private technology firms now build the infrastructure on which both military power and the public’s perception of reality depend. Drawing on a 2025 wargaming experiment at the U.S. Army Command and General Staff College and on the documented information war of the June 2025 Israel-Iran conflict, this essay argues that simulated combat and cognitive warfare increasingly depend on the same technological ecosystem — shared firms, infrastructure, and supply chains — with direct implications for doctrine, training, and mid-sized powers such as Brazil.
Power has historically followed infrastructure: control of sea lanes defined the nineteenth century, control of oil and industry defined the twentieth. In this century, the decisive axis has shifted to digital infrastructure and artificial intelligence (AI). This is not a future possibility; it is a present condition. Whoever controls information systems can shape more than data: that control increasingly influences perception, behavior, and how populations interpret events. Every advanced AI model depends on a physical layer of semiconductors, data centers, and satellite links, which makes that physical layer, rather than any single algorithm, the true strategic terrain. Washington has increasingly treated China’s technological rise as a hegemonic challenge rather than mere commercial competition, since military capability, industrial autonomy, and normative leadership now converge on control of computing, data, and networks. Between the United States and China — and between the private companies that supply both — lies the central contest of contemporary geopolitics: a competition over semiconductors, advanced computing, and autonomous systems in which the winner sets the terms for every nation that depends on that infrastructure.
A relatively small group of private firms now supplies infrastructure once built primarily by states themselves. Palantir, founded in 2003 with early funding from the Central Intelligence Agency’s venture arm In-Q-Tel, operates the Maven Smart System, which processes drone and sensor data for targeting decisions. In July 2025, the U.S. Army signed an enterprise contract with Palantir with a
ceiling over ten years, consolidating seventy-five prior contracts and following the earlier Tactical Intelligence Targeting Access Node (TITAN) award.
SpaceX, through its Starshield division, provides the orbital backbone for military communication and target-tracking, using large constellations of small satellites to preserve connectivity under electronic-warfare conditions. Microsoft supplies sovereign cloud infrastructure to the Department of Defense and has tested the augmented-reality Integrated Visual Augmentation System (IVAS) with soldiers in the field. In February 2025, control of the twenty-two-billion-dollar
was set to transfer from Microsoft to Anduril Industries — a company founded in 2017 by Palmer Luckey that also develops the Lattice command software and autonomous drone systems. This transfer remained subject to Department of Defense approval.
Google supplies data infrastructure to defense agencies through Google Public Sector, but internal opposition has repeatedly constrained that work: in 2018, more than three thousand employees signed a letter opposing Project Maven, several resigned in protest, and Google subsequently declined to renew
. Oracle hosts isolated, hardened databases for the U.S. intelligence community. NVIDIA manufactures the graphics processors that underpin nearly every military AI application, from war-gaming simulation to autonomous targeting, while Broadcom supplies the hardened semiconductors and network components behind radar and satellite systems. OpenAI and Anthropic supply the language models increasingly integrated into intelligence analysis, cybersecurity automation, and logistics planning. None of these firms was elected; together they constitute an informal general staff for the defense architecture of the United States and its partners.
The economics of AI make reversal implausible. Training a frontier model costs hundreds of millions of dollars, but deploying it costs a fraction of a cent per use, so once built, the capability propagates at near-zero marginal cost. Militaries that adopt AI-assisted planning do not regress to manual methods any more than air forces return to celestial navigation after adopting GPS. Private investment has also outpaced the ability of most legislatures to regulate it in real time. These dynamics mirror earlier arms races — the repeating rifle, the submarine, the atomic bomb — with one structural difference: the firms building the current generation of weapons-relevant technology are civilian, transnational, and often headquartered outside the countries whose forces rely on them.
A 2025
at the U.S. Army Command and General Staff College (CGSC) tested whether a large language model could support realistic course-of-action analysis. When given highly detailed, step-by-step instructions, the model systematically favored friendly forces and required constant human correction. When given only the commander’s intent and key tasks, a second instance of the same model produced substantially more realistic assessments. In the wargame’s decisive scenario, a friendly battalion of three companies was tasked with fixing a defending force of more than five companies; the model returned an assessment of friendly
remaining at seventy-five percent against an enemy reduced to forty percent, a result the staff initially distrusted but confirmed after review: the model had correctly accounted for the effects of close air support, attack aviation, and artillery that the human planners had themselves underestimated.
Similar findings have emerged elsewhere in U.S. professional military education. The
College has used AI to reduce the variable space of its 2025 wargames, and the Army War College has used large language models to support Free Kriegsspiel-style adjudication in unclassified scenarios. Across these cases, human oversight remained essential: officers corrected AI-modeled enemy lethality, enforced movement restrictions on logistics nodes, and re-established scenario context after the model lost continuity — with AI augmenting the capabilities of intelligence professionals rather than replacing them, in line with doctrinal norms. The central finding is that excessive procedural detail degrades AI performance by preventing the model from applying its doctrinal knowledge, while clear intent, combined with accurate underlying data, improves it. Writing effective instructions for an AI system is converging with writing an effective operations order, and the resulting bias exposure functions as an informal test of a staff’s own planning assumptions.
Simulated battle is one half of this problem; contested perception is the other. The twelve-day war between Israel and Iran in June 2025 provides a documented case of AI-enabled information warfare at scale. A study by the
Association, based on 592 fast-checks published by 50 organizations across 23 countries, found that roughly one-fifth of false content examined was generated from scratch using AI, while more than 70 percent was
stripped of its original time and place and recirculated as if documenting the current conflict. The researchers assessed that 72 percent of the examined false content could have served Iranian interests, as could 90 percent of the
content, a pattern consistent with, though not conclusive proof of, a strategic recalibration by Iran: compensating for the battlefield setbacks suffered by its non-state allied groups, a weakened Hezbollah and a severely debilitated Hamas, by turning to influence operations aimed at the adversary’s morale rather than its decision-making process. The inference remains circumstantial, but the timing and target selection lend it plausibility.
Israel’s institutional response illustrates one way to organize against this threat. The IDF’s C4I and Cyber Defense Directorate has restructured to create dedicated AI and spectrum warfare divisions. Within this reorganization, the new Sphera unit consolidates electromagnetic-spectrum operations and strategic communications under a single command — a recognition that the two functions belong to the same battlespace, even as AI-enabled analysis is managed through a separate, parallel structure.
This institutional capacity was not built for the Iran conflict alone. A parallel civil-military monitoring structure has taken shape around organizations like FakeReporter, an independent NGO that has operated as Israel’s primary open-source intelligence and disinformation monitoring body since the Gaza war, documenting more than
distinct disinformation narratives in that earlier conflict’s first week alone. Israel has also developed a broader distributed monitoring network integrating military and civil society actors, though the precise channels linking NGO findings to military intelligence remain undocumented in open sources. Detection tools nonetheless struggle to keep pace with rapidly improving generation tools — a structural gap documented across the field, not a temporary lag. In this environment, prioritizing response speed — publishing verified information and correcting errors quickly — offers a more sustainable posture than an unwinnable race to detect every fabrication before it spreads, a logic consistent with the approach observed in Israeli information operations.
These two cases point to the same underlying infrastructure. The chips and cloud platforms that train a model capable of realistic combat-power estimation are drawn from the same supply chain used to train a model capable of generating synthetic battlefield imagery. Simulated war-gaming and the war for perception increasingly run on a shared technological ecosystem — common cloud infrastructure, common model providers, and, in some cases, the same defense-analytics firms that supply both targeting systems and narrative-monitoring tools. This overlap creates common points of failure: a vendor outage or breach can degrade military planning and public-facing information defenses at once, and it concentrates significant leverage in the hands of a small number of private companies whose commercial incentives do not necessarily align with military doctrine or institutional accountability. For military institutions, this implies that AI competency belongs in doctrine and professional military education rather than in a technology office: officers require the same discipline in writing intent for AI systems that they apply to operations orders, and information-verification capacity requires the same institutional priority as intelligence and fires.
For nations without a Palantir, a Starshield, or a leading-edge semiconductor industry, three outcomes are plausible. A small oligopoly of powers could consolidate control over AI and military infrastructure, leaving most states dependent on imported capability. Alternatively, falling model costs and technology diffusion could extend AI-enabled cognitive and combat capability to smaller states and non-state actors, increasing instability. A third path — pursued deliberately rather than by default — involves building sufficient independent capacity in data governance, AI-assisted planning, and disinformation verification to avoid total dependence on great-power infrastructure, without pretending to compete with it directly. This course suits mid-sized states with large domestic data pools and diversified diplomatic ties — Brazil among them — better than it does smaller or more exposed powers. Which path predominates will depend less on the pace of technological change than on sustained institutional investment and doctrinal adaptation, since forces that continue preparing for the previous war risk losing the current one before it is formally declared.

_source.movement_abstract: 2025年，美国陆军指挥与参谋学院开展兵棋推演，测试大语言模型在作战方案分析中的应用。结果显示，提供明确指挥官意图而非繁琐指令可显著提升模型评估准确性，模型在计算空中支援与炮火效应方面优于人工规划。同期，以色列与伊朗爆发冲突，事实核查协会研究显示，约20%的虚假内容由AI生成，超70%为旧内容被剥离时空背景后重新传播。以色列国防军重组C4I与网络防御局，设立专门AI与频谱战部门，整合电磁频谱与战略通信职能，并依托民间组织FakeReporter构建军民融合监测网络。分析指出，作战模拟与认知战日益依赖同一技术生态，包括Palantir、SpaceX、微软、英伟达等少数私营企业的芯片、云基础设施及数据模型。这种重叠导致单一供应商故障可同时削弱军事规划与公共信息防御能力。对于巴西等中等强国，报告建议通过加强数据治理与独立验证能力建设，避免对大国基础设施的完全依赖，而非直接进行技术竞争。

In this environment, prioritizing response speed — publishing verified information and correcting errors quickly — offers a more sustainable posture than an unwinnable race to detect every fabrication before it spreads, a logic consistent with the approach observed in Israeli information operations.
These two cases point to the same underlying infrastructure. The chips and cloud platforms that train a model capable of realistic combat-power estimation are drawn from the same supply chain used to train a model capable of generating synthetic battlefield imagery. Simulated war-gaming and the war for perception increasingly run on a shared technological ecosystem — common cloud infrastructure, common model providers, and, in some cases, the same defense-analytics firms that supply both targeting systems and narrative-monitoring tools. This overlap creates common points of failure: a vendor outage or breach can degrade military planning and public-facing information defenses at once, and it concentrates significant leverage in the hands of a small number of private companies whose commercial incentives do not necessarily align with military doctrine or institutional accountability. For military institutions, this implies that AI competency belongs in doctrine and professional military education rather than in a technology office: officers require the same discipline in writing intent for AI systems that they apply to operations orders, and information-verification capacity requires the same institutional priority as intelligence and fires.
For nations without a Palantir, a Starshield, or a leading-edge semiconductor industry, three outcomes are plausible. A small oligopoly of powers could consolidate control over AI and military infrastructure, leaving most states dependent on imported capability. Alternatively, falling model costs and technology diffusion could extend AI-enabled cognitive and combat capability to smaller states and non-state actors, increasing instability. A third path — pursued deliberately rather than by default — involves building sufficient independent capacity in data governance, AI-assisted planning, and disinformation verification to avoid total dependence on great-power infrastructure, without pretending to compete with it directly. This course suits mid-sized states with large domestic data pools and diversified diplomatic ties — Brazil among them — better than it does smaller or more exposed powers. Which path predominates will depend less on the pace of technological change than on sustained institutional investment and doctrinal adaptation, since forces that continue preparing for the previous war risk losing the current one before it is formally declared.", "url": "https://smallwarsjournal.com/2026/09/01/faceless-war-ai-military-power/", "source": null, "publish_time": 1788242441000, "update_time": 1788270594970, "gather_time": 1788270594970, "insert_time": 1788270594970, "picture_urls": ["https://smallwarsjournal.com/wp-content/uploads/2026/07/Drones-1400x933.png", "https://cdn.printfriendly.com/buttons/printfriendly-pdf-email-button-md.png"], "video_urls": null, "audio_urls": null, "file_urls": null, "picture_paths": null, "video_paths": null, "audio_paths": null, "file_paths": null, "site_id": "4d34e0a3f16f0f4eb9fe8986a50f58b7", "site_name": "美国小型战争期刊", "site_region": "美国", "board_id": null, "board_name": "essay", "source_tasks": ["002@091@20250515@10000001@11403"], "project_id": "", "task_id": "", "target_id": ""}

少数私营技术公司现在建立了军事力量和公众对现实的看法所依赖的基础设施。根据美国陆军指挥与参谋学院2025年的战争游戏实验和2025年6月以色列-伊朗冲突中记录的信息战，本文认为，模拟战斗和认知战越来越依赖于相同的技术生态系统——共享的公司、基础设施和供应链——对条令、训练和中等强国（如巴西）有直接影响。
从历史上看，权力一直伴随着基础设施：对海上航线的控制定义了19世纪，对石油和工业的控制定义了20世纪。在本世纪，决定性的轴心已经转向数字基础设施和人工智能（AI）。这不是未来的可能性；这是一种现状。谁控制了信息系统，谁就可以塑造比数据更多的东西：这种控制越来越多地影响感知、行为以及人们如何解释事件。每一个先进的人工智能模型都依赖于半导体、数据中心和卫星链路的物理层，这使得物理层而不是任何单一的算法成为真正的战略地形。华盛顿越来越多地将中国的技术崛起视为霸权挑战，而不仅仅是商业竞争，因为军事能力、工业自主权和规范领导力现在都集中在对计算、数据和网络的控制上。在美国和中国之间——以及提供这两个国家的私营公司之间——存在着当代地缘政治的核心竞争：一场关于半导体、先进计算和自主系统的竞争，在这场竞争中，获胜者为每一个依赖这些基础设施的国家设定条款。
一个相对较小的私营企业集团现在提供曾经主要由国家自己建造的基础设施。Palantir成立于2003年，早期资金来自美国中央情报局（CIA）的风险投资部门In-Q-Tel，该公司运营着Maven智能系统，该系统处理无人机和传感器数据，用于目标决策。2025年7月，美国陆军与Palantir签订了一份企业合同
十年的上限，合并了75个先前的合同，并遵循早期的战术情报目标接入节点（Titan）合同。
太空探索技术公司（SpaceX）通过其“星盾”（StarShield）部门为军事通信和目标跟踪提供轨道骨干，利用小型卫星的大型星座在电子战条件下保持连通性。微软为国防部提供了主权云基础设施，并在战场上与士兵一起测试了增强现实集成视觉增强系统（IVAS）。2025年2月，控制220亿美元
准备从微软转移到安杜里尔工业公司——一家由帕尔默·勒基于2017年创立的公司，该公司还开发莱迪思指挥软件和自主无人机系统。这一转移仍需得到国防部的批准。
谷歌通过谷歌公共部门（Google Public Sector）向国防机构提供数据基础设施，但内部的反对意见一再限制这项工作：2018年，3000多名员工签署了一封反对Project Maven的信，数人辞职以示抗议，谷歌随后拒绝续约。
.Oracle为美国情报机构托管独立的强化数据库。英伟达制造的图形处理器几乎支撑着每一个军事人工智能应用，从战争游戏模拟到自主瞄准，而博通则提供雷达和卫星系统背后的加固半导体和网络组件。OpenAI和Anthropic提供的语言模型越来越多地集成到情报分析、网络安全自动化和后勤规划中。这些公司没有一家当选；他们共同构成了美国及其合作伙伴国防体系的非正式总参谋部。
人工智能的经济学让逆转变得难以置信。训练一个前沿模型要花费数亿美元，但部署它每次使用的成本只有几分钱，因此一旦建成，这种能力就会以接近零的边际成本传播。采用人工智能辅助规划的军队不会倒退到人工方法，就像空军在采用GPS后不会倒退到天文导航一样。私人投资也超过了大多数立法机构实时监管的能力。这些动态反映了早期的军备竞赛——连发步枪、潜艇、原子弹——但有一个结构性差异：制造当前一代武器相关技术的公司是民用的、跨国的，而且总部往往设在依赖这些技术的国家之外。
A 2025年
在美国陆军指挥与参谋学院（CGSC），测试了大型语言模型是否能够支持现实的行动过程分析。当给出非常详细的、一步一步的指示时，该模型系统地倾向于友军，并需要不断的人工修正。当只给出指挥官的意图和关键任务时，同一模型的第二个实例产生了实质上更现实的评估。在兵棋推演的决定性场景中，一个由三个连组成的友军营的任务是修复一支由五个连以上组成的防御部队。模型返回的评估结果为Friendly
保持在75%，对敌人减少到40%，这是工作人员最初不信任的结果，但在审查后确认：该模型正确地考虑了近距离空中支援、攻击航空兵和炮兵的影响，而人类规划者自己低估了这些影响。
在美国职业军事教育的其他地方也出现了类似的发现。这个
学院使用人工智能来减少其2025年战争游戏的可变空间，陆军战争学院使用大型语言模型来支持非机密场景中的自由Kriegsspiel式裁决。在这些案例中，人类监督仍然至关重要：军官纠正了人工智能模拟的敌人杀伤力，对后勤节点实施了行动限制，并在模型失去连续性后重新建立了情景背景-根据理论规范，人工智能增强了情报专业人员的能力，而不是取代他们。核心发现是，过多的程序细节会阻止模型应用其理论知识，从而降低人工智能的性能，而清晰的意图与准确的基础数据相结合，则会提高人工智能的性能。为人工智能系统编写有效的指令与编写有效的操作命令是一致的，由此产生的偏见暴露功能是对员工自己的规划假设的非正式测试。
模拟作战是这个问题的一半；另一种是有争议的看法。2025年6月以色列和伊朗之间的12天战争提供了一个大规模人工智能信息战的记录案例。的一项研究
该协会基于23个国家的50个组织发布的592个快速检查，发现大约五分之一的虚假内容是使用人工智能从零开始生成的，而超过70%的虚假内容是从零开始生成的。
从最初的时间和地点中剥离出来，重新传播，好像在记录当前的冲突。研究人员估计，72%被审查的虚假内容可能符合伊朗的利益，
内容，这一模式与伊朗的战略调整相一致，尽管不是决定性的证据：通过转向针对对手士气而不是其决策过程的影响行动，来弥补其非国家联盟团体、被削弱的真主党和被严重削弱的哈马斯在战场上遭受的挫折。推论仍然是间接的，但时机和目标选择使其具有合理性。
以色列的机构反应说明了组织起来对付这一威胁的一种方式。以色列国防军的C4I和网络防御理事会已经重组，以创建专门的人工智能和频谱作战部门。在这次重组中，新的SPHERA单位将电磁频谱操作和战略通信整合在一个指挥之下-这是对这两个功能属于同一作战空间的认可，即使人工智能分析是通过一个单独的平行结构管理的。
这种机构能力不仅仅是为伊朗冲突而建立的。FakeReporter是一个独立的非政府组织，自加沙战争以来，它一直是以色列主要的公开来源情报和虚假信息监测机构，记录了超过
仅在早些时候的冲突的第一周，就有明显的虚假信息叙述。以色列还开发了一个更广泛的分布式监测网络，将军事和民间社会行为者整合在一起，尽管将非政府组织的调查结果与军事情报联系起来的确切渠道在公开来源中仍未记录在案。尽管如此，检测工具仍在努力跟上快速改进的生成工具的步伐——这是整个领域记录的结构性差距，而不是暂时的滞后。在这种环境下，优先考虑反应速度——发布经核实的信息并迅速纠正错误——提供了一种更可持续的姿态，而不是一场无法取胜的竞赛，即在每一次捏造之前发现它，这一逻辑与以色列信息行动中观察到的方法是一致的。
这两个案例指向相同的底层基础架构。训练能够进行现实作战能力评估的模型的芯片和云平台是从用于训练能够生成合成战场图像的模型的同一供应链中提取的。模拟战争游戏和感知战争越来越多地在共享的技术生态系统上运行——通用的云基础设施、通用的模型提供商，以及在某些情况下，提供目标系统和叙事监控工具的相同的国防分析公司。这种重叠造成了共同的失败点：供应商中断或违规可能会立即降低军事规划和面向公众的信息防御能力，并将重要的影响力集中在少数私营公司手中，而这些公司的商业动机并不一定与军事理论或机构责任相一致。对于军事机构来说，这意味着人工智能能力属于条令和专业军事教育，而不是技术办公室：军官要求人工智能系统的写作意图与他们应用于作战命令的相同纪律，信息验证能力要求与情报和火力相同的机构优先权。
对于没有帕兰提尔（Palantir）、星盾（Starshield）或尖端半导体产业的国家来说，有三种结果是可能的。少数寡头垄断势力可以巩固对人工智能和军事基础设施的控制，让大多数国家依赖进口能力。或者，模型成本的下降和技术扩散可能会将人工智能的认知和作战能力扩展到较小的国家和非国家行为体，从而增加不稳定性。第三条道路——有意而非默认——包括在数据治理、人工智能辅助规划和虚假信息验证方面建立足够的独立能力，以避免完全依赖大国基础设施，而不是假装与之直接竞争。这门课程更适合拥有庞大国内数据库和多样化外交关系的中等规模国家（巴西就是其中之一），而不适合规模较小或风险更大的国家。哪条道路占主导地位将更多地取决于持续的制度投资和理论调整，而不是技术变革的步伐，因为继续为前一场战争做准备的部队有可能在正式宣布前输掉当前的战争。

Previous articles devoted to special military propaganda in the Soviet Union covered the major military conflicts that influenced the development of this type of military activity. Following these events, we can now move on to the Great Patriotic War, where the Red Army's political work against enemy troops and populations reached a new level and acquired a clear organizational framework after a long period of uncertainty.

Soviet people listen to the government's announcement of the start of the war on June 22, 1941.
The topic of Soviet propaganda directed at the troops of Nazi Germany and its allies is quite broad, so it will be the subject of a series of articles covering various periods of the war, from its beginning to the Victory Day of May 9. This article is the first in this series.
The content of political campaigns against German troops at different periods of the war was structured according to the military and political situation developing at the front, the combat missions being accomplished by Soviet troops, and changes in the enemy's political and morale. To exert ideological and political influence on the enemy, the press, radio (broadcast radio stations and those from the front, domestic and captured), oral propaganda (through loudspeakers and megaphones), and visual propaganda (leaflets, newspapers, brochures, and books) were used.1.
Before examining in detail the types and methods of Soviet special propaganda during the Great Patriotic War, it is necessary to understand the organizational structure of this work. Therefore, this article will reveal which specific agencies developed and implemented information and psychological warfare against enemy troops.
Red Army soldiers training at the Voroshilov Barracks in Moscow on August 30, 1941.
It's important to begin with the fact that the recent Soviet-Finnish War exposed numerous weaknesses in the then-young Red Army. It became clear that it was necessary to summarize the war's results in order to promptly identify and address all errors and shortcomings. To this end, a meeting of the Red Army's command staff was held from April 14 to 17, 1940, under the Central Committee of the All-Union Communist Party (Bolsheviks) to summarize the experience of combat operations in Finland. 2.
The meeting yielded a reliable picture of what was happening. At this meeting, in his speech on April 17, Stalin explained why studying the experience of the Soviet-Finnish War was a priority. Here are two important quotes from this speech:
…keep in mind that during the entire existence of Soviet power, we have never fought a real modern war. Minor episodes in Manchuria, at Lake Khasan, or in Mongolia are nonsense; they are not war, they are isolated episodes in a strictly limited area. Japan was afraid to start a war, we didn't want that either, and a small test of strength in that small area showed that Japan had failed. They had two or three divisions, and we had two or three divisions in Mongolia, the same number at Lake Khasan. Our army has never fought a real, serious war. A civil war is not a real war, because it was a war without artillerywithout aviationwithout tanks, without mortars. Without all that, what kind of serious war is this?
- I.V. Stalin.
…our modern Red Army was shelled on the fields of Finland – that was its first baptism
— I.V. Stalin3
Speech by I.V. Stalin at a meeting of the Red Army's command staff to summarize the experience of the Winter War (excerpts). April 17, 1940 (RGASPI, F. 558, Op. 11, D. 1124, L. 23, 35)
The second outcome of the meeting was the proposal by Deputy People's Commissar of Defense G. I. Kulik to elect a commission to summarize the council's proposals, as well as to comprehensively analyze the military operations against Finland and formulate specific proposals for each individual area.
The commission was established and began its work on April 19, 1940. It included K.E. Voroshilov (chairman), I.V. Stalin, G.I. Kulik, L.Z. Mekhlis, E.A. Shchadenko, and other representatives of the central military department. However, most of the commission's members had been direct participants in the Winter War.
Red Army soldiers before being sent to the front. Leningrad, June 23, 1941.
For convenience, the commission created separate subcommittees for each branch of the armed forces, and others. These included the combined arms, air force, technical troops, armored vehicle, political work, and other subcommittees. Each was required to submit practical recommendations on its specific area to the USSR People's Commissar of Defense by the following day. Due to the abundance of problems identified, for some, the deadline was extended until April 21. 4.
After all subcommissions presented their findings at the plenary session on April 21, I.V. Stalin proposed creating a special "narrower commission" to address issues not previously considered. Meetings of this special commission continued from April 23 to May 14, 1940. 5.
In the context of this article, the most interesting is the report of the head of the Political Directorate of the Red Army, L. Z. Mekhlis, on military ideology from May 10, 1940, in the part concerning the informational and psychological influence on soldiers and the population of Finland.
Lev Zakharovich Mekhlis
This report outlined the key areas for improving Soviet special propaganda, taking into account all the mistakes of the past war. The full text of the report can be found in open sources, but I will provide the key excerpts necessary for understanding the topic.
The study of the armies of potential adversaries and possible theaters of military operations is completely unsatisfactory, and the available intelligence data is too classified and is not made available to the command staff,— L. Z. Mekhlis.
A deeply ingrained, harmful prejudice holds that the populations of countries entering war with the USSR will inevitably, almost en masse, rebel and defect to the Red Army, and that workers and peasants will greet us with flowers. This false belief stems from ignorance of the actual situation in neighboring countries. The war in Finland demonstrated that we hadn't conducted political reconnaissance in the northern regions and therefore didn't know what slogans to bring to these populations or how to work among them... We need to know the lives and interests of the populations of each country.
— L. Z. Mekhlis
It must be said that we have made more than one mistake in the area of ​​political study of the enemy and have made limited progress in working among the enemy's troops and population. It was only in early 1939 that foreign-language newspaper editorial offices were introduced, but they are still far from meeting the requirements, as they lack writers with a sufficiently good knowledge of the language, everyday life, history and the culture of the respective countries. If you want to defeat your enemy properly, you need to know him well... Therefore, you must carefully study and understand the strengths and weaknesses of all the armies of neighboring countries, including small ones.
— L. Z. Mekhlis6
Following the meeting, the subcommittee on party and political work in wartime, in the section devoted to work among enemy troops, adopted a number of decisions of great practical significance for the formation of a special propaganda structure. Thus, point 4 stated: “In order to provide organizational support for political work among the enemy troops and population, create departments for work among the enemy troops and population in the political departments of all border districts and armies.”.
A group of Soviet soldiers walks along the shore of the Kola Bay. 1941.
Other points also discussed establishing a military registry for individuals proficient in foreign languages, assigning them to editorial offices of foreign newspapers based on their knowledge of a particular language, and holding periodic meetings to exchange experiences and improve their skills. Furthermore, a decision was made to issue a manual on organizing political work among enemy troops in peacetime. 7.
As early as July 1939, foreign-language newspaper editorial offices were established in a number of border military districts as training centers, where editorial staff were required to accumulate information about the neighboring country, study its strengths and weaknesses, select facts for propaganda, and also improve their experience in the field of publishing printed materials for soldiers and the population of a potential enemy (that country).
A total of 24 editorial offices were created. A special instructor was assigned to manage them, and later a group of instructor-translators was formed. In April 1940, the group was reorganized into a special department for managing foreign-language publications. Each of the department's senior instructors oversaw newspapers in a specific foreign language and studied the respective countries and their armies.
Battle for the village. 1941
Finally, in August of the same year, a special department for propaganda among the enemy troops and population was established on the basis of this department within the Main Directorate of Political Propaganda of the Red Army (GUPPKA). 8It was headed by Major Mikhail Ivanovich Burtsev, who already had experience conducting special propaganda in battles with the Japanese at the Khalkhin Gol River in 1939 and with the Finns on the Karelian Isthmus in 1940.
Major General Mikhail Ivanovich Burtsev. Photo from his 1981 book "Insight"
It was the seventh department, and hence its common name, the 7th Department. It was tasked with studying the political and morale of army personnel and the population of foreign countries, and preparing to conduct propaganda and agitation among them with the aim of undermining their morale. Highly educated specialists, scientists, and educators from institutes of the USSR Academy of Sciences, graduates of state universities, and postgraduate programs at military academies, fluent in German, Finnish, Romanian, English, Persian, Arabic, Japanese, and other foreign languages, were selected and appointed to the department.9.
Following the creation of the Seventh Department within the Main Directorate of Political Propaganda of the Red Army, similar departments were established in the political directorates of the following border districts: the Leningrad, Western, and Kyiv Special, Odessa, Transcaucasian, Central Asian, and Transbaikal Military Districts, and the Far Eastern Front. Furthermore, the political departments of the armies within these districts established propaganda units for enemy troops and the general population, and the position of senior instructor for propaganda among enemy troops was added to the staff of each division's political department.10.
Naturally, such a system needed to be staffed with qualified personnel. This work began as early as May 1938, when the first census of career political workers proficient in foreign languages ​​and capable of conducting propaganda among enemy troops and the general population was conducted. These political workers, who were in the Red Army reserves, were periodically called up for training sessions.
The military department at the 2nd Moscow State Pedagogical Institute of Foreign Languages ​​(since 1942, the Military Institute of Foreign Languages ​​(VIIL)) played a major role in training special propagandists. It was called the forge of the USSR's special propagandists. The military department at the Moscow Institute of Oriental Studies also played a major role. There, students took short but informative courses on conducting political work among enemy troops and the population.11Captured enemy documents and existing propaganda publications often served as teaching aids.
The Lesnoye Sanatorium in the city of Stavropol on the Volga (now Tolyatti), where the Military Faculty of Western Foreign Languages, established at the 2nd Moscow Pedagogical Institute of Foreign Languages, was evacuated by ship by order of October 10, 1941. Photo from 1941
Students of the Military Faculty of Western Foreign Languages ​​in Stavropol-on-Volga, 1942. Photograph from the collection of the Togliatti Museum of Local History.
On October 12, 1940, GUPPKA issued Directive No. 267, which described the experience of working among enemy troops and populations in past battles, and also defined new methods and directions for conducting ideological work in relation to enemy troops.12Unlike other countries, where psychological warfare departments were independent or part of the intelligence services, the 7th Departments, as organs of ideological struggle, became part of the military-political apparatus. It must be said that within the political agencies, they felt rather out of place in their functional responsibilities, often encountering skepticism, and at times even sabotaging their activities.13.
At that time, there were still quite a few Soviet soldiers and commanders who seriously doubted even the slightest success of this difficult and dangerous task. Officially, the special propagandists were said to be engaged in decomposing enemy troops. Many front-line soldiers, hearing this, said, "Fascists decompose only in the ground." 14.
Thus, the tasks of the seventh department (directorate) of GUPPKA included:
1. Development, publication and organization of distribution of propaganda materials (leaflets, slogans, newspapers, brochures) among the armies and population of enemy countries;2. Guidance of front-line and army special propaganda agencies and assistance in decomposing the enemy’s troops and population;3. Development and implementation of special information and propaganda operations among enemy troops at the front and the population in the rear;4. Conducting a daily study of the political and moral state of the personnel of the armies and the population of enemy countries, the nature and system of their ideological processing;5. Collecting information about the effectiveness of our propaganda;6. Selection, training and distribution of special propagandists who speak the relevant foreign languages;7. Generalization and dissemination of best practices in information warfare in its information bulletins and in collections of experience in political work among the enemy troops and population15.
Excerpts from one of the 7th Department's "Exchange of Experience" bulletins. September 25, 1943. Photo from the Russian Ministry of Defense website.
The operational apparatus for special propaganda included the seventh departments of the front (district) political directorates, the seventh sections of the army political departments, and senior instructors of the corps and division political departments for work among enemy troops and the population. The seventh departments of the fronts and border military districts also operated foreign-language newspaper editorial offices and radio broadcasting offices. 16.
Each element of the special propaganda system had its own operational scope. Thus, the front political directorates served as the link between the 7th Department of the GUPPKA and all subordinate structures, ensuring a continuous exchange of information between the special propaganda leadership and those working on the ground. Furthermore, the front political directorates provided all possible support to the army political departments. For example, they instructed and dispatched special propaganda teams equipped with mobile printing presses, powerful sound amplification stations, photo laboratories, and other front-line propaganda equipment.
They also carried out extensive work on the timely delivery and distribution of propaganda materials among enemy troops and civilians. This was accomplished primarily by frontline aviation. This required constant coordination with air force headquarters.
They also carried out extensive work on training special propagandists, as well as working with prisoners of war to instill in them an anti-fascist ideology and further involve them in propaganda work against the enemy.17.
Interrogation of a captured German. July 1941.
As for the army's political departments, their important task was to collect and systematize reliable information about the opposing enemy forces and disseminate it to higher authorities. Overall, the army's political departments were distinguished by their efficiency and were able to quickly adapt their propaganda in content, forms, and methods based on the constantly changing combat situation. Their primary task was to provide comprehensive assistance and maintain constant contact with the divisional political departments.
In turn, the divisional political departments operated, as they say, "on the ground" and in a more targeted manner. Officially, they were represented only by a senior instructor for work among enemy troops and the population, but since one person could not carry out all the work, several individuals with the necessary skills were assigned to assist the instructor. This created a unique department. It addressed the task of maximally weakening the combat capability of enemy units engaged in battles against a given division in a given sector of the front. At this level, the most common tool used was operational propaganda (that is, propaganda aimed at specific enemy military formations, whose situation was comprehensively studied at the divisional political department level).18.
Senior Lieutenant P.I. Nikitin drops leaflets on enemy troop positions using a mortar of his own design. 1942.
The publication of leaflets in foreign languages ​​was handled by the Military Publishing House of the USSR People's Commissariat of Defense, which included a department for fulfilling special orders under the 7th Department (Directorate). The Moscow-based Iskra Revolutsii printing house, capable of typesetting and publishing printed materials in 60 foreign languages, was assigned to the 7th Directorate from the USSR Foreign Publishing House. The printing plant of the Pravda Publishing House of the Central Committee of the All-Union Communist Party (Bolsheviks) was also involved in the production of the most important and high-circulation propaganda materials. 19.
One of the first Soviet propaganda leaflets for the Germans. A Russian translation is included below. Leaflets with similar content were almost entirely ineffective.
In addition, on the eve of the war, military districts sent many civilian specialists (journalists, philologists, historians, German language teachers and others) to training camps fleet and into ground military units for use according to their specialty. Upon completion, they were warned that in the event of war, they would be called up again. 20This was also necessary to staff the system with valuable personnel, which, however, was constantly in short supply.
As mentioned above, the main document regulating the activities of special propaganda was Directive No. 267. It was written in the spirit of socialism and Lenin's ideas that when the enemy army and the population, through information provided by the Soviet Union, understand the senselessness of war for the working people, they will immediately protest against their government and express sympathy for the Red Army. 21.
The objective class position of capitalists is one thing. They fight for themselves. Soldiers are proletarians and peasants. That's different... their class interests are against war! That's why they can be enlightened, persuaded,— V.I. Lenin22
This was the basis of the "gold standard" of Soviet political propaganda directed at enemy troops in the pre-war period. Back then, no one understood that the Soviet Union would be confronted with soldiers raised from childhood to believe in their exceptionalism and the superiority of their nation over all other nations on the planet.
In early May 1941, the People's Commissar of Defense demanded that the 7th Department of the GUPPKA, headed by Mikhail Ivanovich Burtsev, prepare a report on the political and moral state of the countries bordering the USSR and their armies. A few days later, such a report was prepared and read out. 23But there was one important nuance. The report contained very little information about the situation in Germany.
The reason for this was that, at that time, Germany was not among the Soviet Union's most likely adversaries. This was especially influenced by the non-aggression pact between the USSR and the Third Reich in 1939.
Political Commissar I.I. Petrov conducts propaganda work on German positions using a primitive tin pipe. North Caucasus Front, 1942.
As a result, the German-language newspaper's editorial office in the Leningrad Military District was liquidated. Furthermore, only one or two German publications were subscribed to for research into the situation in Germany. A major drawback was the fact that the Soviet leadership prohibited the translation of German articles and books critical of our country. 24, even to structures for which this was a direct part of the work.
All this together made it impossible to see the real processes taking place in Germany in the pre-war period and to form a true picture of the enemy, and at the same time to develop methods and arguments for informational and psychological influence on the future enemy based on current data.
Among the potential adversaries being studied were countries located on the southern borders of the USSR (Iran, Afghanistan, India, and Turkey). Propaganda theses had already been prepared for these countries, exposing the colonial nature of the British imperialists, and some printed materials had been prepared. 25.
Photo taken during the Battle of Smolensk, 1941
Thus, on the eve of the Great Patriotic War, the special propaganda agencies lacked complete and up-to-date information on the Third Reich and its allies, but were preparing to wage psychological warfare against entirely different countries. Furthermore, among all the employees of the 7th Departments, there was a critical shortage of people with a high level of German proficiency. More often than not, those who spoke the language only spoke it colloquially, not to mention the new military terms and ranks that had emerged in Nazi Germany.
Only after the aforementioned May 1941 report was the 7th Department of the GUPPKA tasked with filling this gap and preparing a report on the situation in Germany in the shortest possible time. 26The report systematized all available relevant data on the Third Reich. But it was, of course, insufficient to fully reflect reality.
Nevertheless, based on available sources, it was noted that the German army was undergoing extraordinary moral and political preparation for war. Their army was assessed as strong, well-disciplined, and well-armed. However, the report again erroneously concluded that it would be easy to convince German soldiers that this war was inadvisable for them. The report was distributed to the Red Army's political organs for review. 27.
By the time Nazi Germany invaded the USSR, many special propaganda efforts had to be implemented on the fly. Thus, on June 22, 1941, two sections were formed within the 7th Department of the GUPPKA: the first for conducting information and psychological warfare against Germany and its allies, and the second for propaganda work among the populations of occupied countries and territories.28.
Of fundamental importance was the decision of the Central Committee of the All-Union Communist Party (Bolsheviks) on June 25, 1941, to establish the Bureau of Military-Political Propaganda. This was a collegial body created to centralize the direction of all propaganda efforts against the enemy and the populations of the territories they had captured. The 7th Department became the working body of this Bureau. 29.
Resolution of the Central Committee of the All-Union Communist Party (Bolsheviks) "On the Creation of the Soviet Bureau of Military-Political Propaganda." June 25, 1941 (Original. RGASPI, Fund 17, List 163, D. 1316. L. 183)
The Bureau included: the head of the GUPPKA, L. Z. Mekhlis, his deputy, D. Z. Manuilsky, professor and specialist in propaganda, V. S. Kruzhkov, head of the press department of the People's Commissariat of Foreign Affairs, P. G. Palgunov, and deputy people's commissar of foreign affairs, S. A. Lozovsky (on July 2, the director of the Marx-Engels-Lenin Institute under the Central Committee of the All-Union Communist Party (Bolsheviks), M. B. Mitin, was also included in the Bureau).30L. Z. Mekhlis became the head of the Bureau.
At the meetings, the fundamental directions and content of all special propaganda were determined, leading general political materials for the enemy troops and population were approved, and joint activities in the matter of special propaganda of such bodies as TASS, the Soviet Information Bureau, the USSR Radio Committee, state publishing houses and others were coordinated. 31.
Another important agency for special propaganda was the Soviet Information Bureau (Sovinformburo), established on June 24, 1941, by a joint resolution of the Central Committee of the All-Union Communist Party (Bolsheviks) and the Council of People's Commissars. Information transmitted through the Sovinformburo was often used in the preparation of leaflets for enemy soldiers (for example, the information leaflets "International Information").
Resolution of June 24, 1941 of the Central Committee of the All-Union Communist Party (Bolsheviks) and the Council of People's Commissars on the establishment of the Soviet Information Bureau (Sovinformburo)
This information was of even greater importance for the residents of the occupied eastern territories of the USSR, who were cut off from receiving News about the progress of the war. Therefore, in 1942, a directive was issued requiring every partisan detachment to receive Sovinformburo reports, record them, and reproduce them as leaflets for subsequent distribution among Soviet citizens remaining in enemy-occupied territory. In this way, people cut off from information about the state of the war and constantly subjected to massive fascist propaganda and lies could learn the truth and maintain contact with their country. 32.
Thus, the structure of the Soviet Union's special propaganda agencies targeting the enemy troops and population at the start of the Great Patriotic War can be represented in the following diagram.
The diagram of the Soviet Union's special propaganda apparatus at the start of the Great Patriotic War
In conclusion, it can be concluded that by the beginning of the Great Patriotic War, the structure of the apparatus of special propaganda had already been created, which, nevertheless, during the course of the war will undergo some necessary changes due to the increase in the scale and effectiveness of this work.
However, this work began too late, preventing the necessary experience from being accumulated. Furthermore, due to unjustified restrictions on the study of information materials from the Nazi bloc countries, by the outbreak of the war there was no true picture of the processes taking place in Germany and its allies.
This led to the Red Army's ignorance and misperception of the enemy soldiers' morale and psychological state. This resulted in failures in conducting special propaganda against the enemy during the initial period of the war. Naturally, the forced, constant retreat of Soviet troops during that difficult period contributed to the failures in disseminating propaganda against German soldiers.
The next article will examine in detail the initial successes and failures in conducting political work among enemy troops.

_source.movement_title: 苏联建立第七局构建卫国战争初期对敌宣传体系
_source.movement_abstract: 1940 年 4 月至 5 月，苏联红军总政治部在总结苏芬战争经验后，由斯大林主持成立特别委员会，决定建立针对敌军的特种宣传体系。1940 年 8 月，红军总政治宣传局（GUPPKA）下设第七局，由米哈伊尔·布尔特塞夫少校领导，负责研究敌国政治心理、制定宣传策略及培训外语宣传员。该体系在列宁格勒、西部等边境军区及方面军政治部设立对应机构，并依托莫斯科第二外语师范学院等机构培养专业人才。1941 年 6 月 25 日，联共（布）中央成立军事政治宣传局，第七局作为其执行机构，统筹塔斯社、苏联新闻局等媒体资源。尽管体系架构已成型，但因战前对德国情报研究受限、德语人才短缺及误判德军士气，导致卫国战争初期对德宣传效果不佳。1941 年 6 月 22 日战争爆发后，第七局迅速调整，设立针对德国及其盟友的专门部门，并配合游击队利用苏联新闻局信息在占领区开展反法西斯宣传。
