Soviet people listen to the government's announcement of the start of the war on June 22, 1941.
The topic of Soviet propaganda directed at the troops of Nazi Germany and its allies is quite broad, so it will be the subject of a series of articles covering various periods of the war, from its beginning to the Victory Day of May 9. This article is the first in this series.
The content of political campaigns against German troops at different periods of the war was structured according to the military and political situation developing at the front, the combat missions being accomplished by Soviet troops, and changes in the enemy's political and morale. To exert ideological and political influence on the enemy, the press, radio (broadcast radio stations and those from the front, domestic and captured), oral propaganda (through loudspeakers and megaphones), and visual propaganda (leaflets, newspapers, brochures, and books) were used.1.
Before examining in detail the types and methods of Soviet special propaganda during the Great Patriotic War, it is necessary to understand the organizational structure of this work. Therefore, this article will reveal which specific agencies developed and implemented information and psychological warfare against enemy troops.
Red Army soldiers training at the Voroshilov Barracks in Moscow on August 30, 1941.
It's important to begin with the fact that the recent Soviet-Finnish War exposed numerous weaknesses in the then-young Red Army. It became clear that it was necessary to summarize the war's results in order to promptly identify and address all errors and shortcomings. To this end, a meeting of the Red Army's command staff was held from April 14 to 17, 1940, under the Central Committee of the All-Union Communist Party (Bolsheviks) to summarize the experience of combat operations in Finland. 2.
The meeting yielded a reliable picture of what was happening. At this meeting, in his speech on April 17, Stalin explained why studying the experience of the Soviet-Finnish War was a priority. Here are two important quotes from this speech:
…keep in mind that during the entire existence of Soviet power, we have never fought a real modern war. Minor episodes in Manchuria, at Lake Khasan, or in Mongolia are nonsense; they are not war, they are isolated episodes in a strictly limited area. Japan was afraid to start a war, we didn't want that either, and a small test of strength in that small area showed that Japan had failed. They had two or three divisions, and we had two or three divisions in Mongolia, the same number at Lake Khasan. Our army has never fought a real, serious war. A civil war is not a real war, because it was a war without artillerywithout aviationwithout tanks, without mortars. Without all that, what kind of serious war is this?
- I.V. Stalin.
…our modern Red Army was shelled on the fields of Finland – that was its first baptism
— I.V. Stalin3
Speech by I.V. Stalin at a meeting of the Red Army's command staff to summarize the experience of the Winter War (excerpts). April 17, 1940 (RGASPI, F. 558, Op. 11, D. 1124, L. 23, 35)
The second outcome of the meeting was the proposal by Deputy People's Commissar of Defense G. I. Kulik to elect a commission to summarize the council's proposals, as well as to comprehensively analyze the military operations against Finland and formulate specific proposals for each individual area.
The commission was established and began its work on April 19, 1940. It included K.E. Voroshilov (chairman), I.V. Stalin, G.I. Kulik, L.Z. Mekhlis, E.A. Shchadenko, and other representatives of the central military department. However, most of the commission's members had been direct participants in the Winter War.
Red Army soldiers before being sent to the front. Leningrad, June 23, 1941.
For convenience, the commission created separate subcommittees for each branch of the armed forces, and others. These included the combined arms, air force, technical troops, armored vehicle, political work, and other subcommittees. Each was required to submit practical recommendations on its specific area to the USSR People's Commissar of Defense by the following day. Due to the abundance of problems identified, for some, the deadline was extended until April 21. 4.
After all subcommissions presented their findings at the plenary session on April 21, I.V. Stalin proposed creating a special "narrower commission" to address issues not previously considered. Meetings of this special commission continued from April 23 to May 14, 1940. 5.
In the context of this article, the most interesting is the report of the head of the Political Directorate of the Red Army, L. Z. Mekhlis, on military ideology from May 10, 1940, in the part concerning the informational and psychological influence on soldiers and the population of Finland.
Lev Zakharovich Mekhlis
This report outlined the key areas for improving Soviet special propaganda, taking into account all the mistakes of the past war. The full text of the report can be found in open sources, but I will provide the key excerpts necessary for understanding the topic.
The study of the armies of potential adversaries and possible theaters of military operations is completely unsatisfactory, and the available intelligence data is too classified and is not made available to the command staff,
— L. Z. Mekhlis.
A deeply ingrained, harmful prejudice holds that the populations of countries entering war with the USSR will inevitably, almost en masse, rebel and defect to the Red Army, and that workers and peasants will greet us with flowers. This false belief stems from ignorance of the actual situation in neighboring countries. The war in Finland demonstrated that we hadn't conducted political reconnaissance in the northern regions and therefore didn't know what slogans to bring to these populations or how to work among them... We need to know the lives and interests of the populations of each country.
— L. Z. Mekhlis
It must be said that we have made more than one mistake in the area of ​​political study of the enemy and have made limited progress in working among the enemy's troops and population. It was only in early 1939 that foreign-language newspaper editorial offices were introduced, but they are still far from meeting the requirements, as they lack writers with a sufficiently good knowledge of the language, everyday life, history and the culture of the respective countries. If you want to defeat your enemy properly, you need to know him well... Therefore, you must carefully study and understand the strengths and weaknesses of all the armies of neighboring countries, including small ones.
— L. Z. Mekhlis6
Following the meeting, the subcommittee on party and political work in wartime, in the section devoted to work among enemy troops, adopted a number of decisions of great practical significance for the formation of a special propaganda structure. Thus, point 4 stated: “In order to provide organizational support for political work among the enemy troops and population, create departments for work among the enemy troops and population in the political departments of all border districts and armies.”.
A group of Soviet soldiers walks along the shore of the Kola Bay. 1941.
Other points also discussed establishing a military registry for individuals proficient in foreign languages, assigning them to editorial offices of foreign newspapers based on their knowledge of a particular language, and holding periodic meetings to exchange experiences and improve their skills. Furthermore, a decision was made to issue a manual on organizing political work among enemy troops in peacetime. 7.
As early as July 1939, foreign-language newspaper editorial offices were established in a number of border military districts as training centers, where editorial staff were required to accumulate information about the neighboring country, study its strengths and weaknesses, select facts for propaganda, and also improve their experience in the field of publishing printed materials for soldiers and the population of a potential enemy (that country).
A total of 24 editorial offices were created. A special instructor was assigned to manage them, and later a group of instructor-translators was formed. In April 1940, the group was reorganized into a special department for managing foreign-language publications. Each of the department's senior instructors oversaw newspapers in a specific foreign language and studied the respective countries and their armies.
Battle for the village. 1941
Finally, in August of the same year, a special department for propaganda among the enemy troops and population was established on the basis of this department within the Main Directorate of Political Propaganda of the Red Army (GUPPKA). 8It was headed by Major Mikhail Ivanovich Burtsev, who already had experience conducting special propaganda in battles with the Japanese at the Khalkhin Gol River in 1939 and with the Finns on the Karelian Isthmus in 1940.
Major General Mikhail Ivanovich Burtsev. Photo from his 1981 book "Insight"
It was the seventh department, and hence its common name, the 7th Department. It was tasked with studying the political and morale of army personnel and the population of foreign countries, and preparing to conduct propaganda and agitation among them with the aim of undermining their morale. Highly educated specialists, scientists, and educators from institutes of the USSR Academy of Sciences, graduates of state universities, and postgraduate programs at military academies, fluent in German, Finnish, Romanian, English, Persian, Arabic, Japanese, and other foreign languages, were selected and appointed to the department.9.
Following the creation of the Seventh Department within the Main Directorate of Political Propaganda of the Red Army, similar departments were established in the political directorates of the following border districts: the Leningrad, Western, and Kyiv Special, Odessa, Transcaucasian, Central Asian, and Transbaikal Military Districts, and the Far Eastern Front. Furthermore, the political departments of the armies within these districts established propaganda units for enemy troops and the general population, and the position of senior instructor for propaganda among enemy troops was added to the staff of each division's political department.10.
Naturally, such a system needed to be staffed with qualified personnel. This work began as early as May 1938, when the first census of career political workers proficient in foreign languages ​​and capable of conducting propaganda among enemy troops and the general population was conducted. These political workers, who were in the Red Army reserves, were periodically called up for training sessions.
The military department at the 2nd Moscow State Pedagogical Institute of Foreign Languages ​​(since 1942, the Military Institute of Foreign Languages ​​(VIIL)) played a major role in training special propagandists. It was called the forge of the USSR's special propagandists. The military department at the Moscow Institute of Oriental Studies also played a major role. There, students took short but informative courses on conducting political work among enemy troops and the population.11Captured enemy documents and existing propaganda publications often served as teaching aids.
The Lesnoye Sanatorium in the city of Stavropol on the Volga (now Tolyatti), where the Military Faculty of Western Foreign Languages, established at the 2nd Moscow Pedagogical Institute of Foreign Languages, was evacuated by ship by order of October 10, 1941. Photo from 1941
Students of the Military Faculty of Western Foreign Languages ​​in Stavropol-on-Volga, 1942. Photograph from the collection of the Togliatti Museum of Local History.
On October 12, 1940, GUPPKA issued Directive No. 267, which described the experience of working among enemy troops and populations in past battles, and also defined new methods and directions for conducting ideological work in relation to enemy troops.12Unlike other countries, where psychological warfare departments were independent or part of the intelligence services, the 7th Departments, as organs of ideological struggle, became part of the military-political apparatus. It must be said that within the political agencies, they felt rather out of place in their functional responsibilities, often encountering skepticism, and at times even sabotaging their activities.13.
At that time, there were still quite a few Soviet soldiers and commanders who seriously doubted even the slightest success of this difficult and dangerous task. Officially, the special propagandists were said to be engaged in decomposing enemy troops. Many front-line soldiers, hearing this, said, "Fascists decompose only in the ground." 14.
Thus, the tasks of the seventh department (directorate) of GUPPKA included:
1. Development, publication and organization of distribution of propaganda materials (leaflets, slogans, newspapers, brochures) among the armies and population of enemy countries;
2. Guidance of front-line and army special propaganda agencies and assistance in decomposing the enemy’s troops and population;
3. Development and implementation of special information and propaganda operations among enemy troops at the front and the population in the rear;
4. Conducting a daily study of the political and moral state of the personnel of the armies and the population of enemy countries, the nature and system of their ideological processing;
5. Collecting information about the effectiveness of our propaganda;
6. Selection, training and distribution of special propagandists who speak the relevant foreign languages;
7. Generalization and dissemination of best practices in information warfare in its information bulletins and in collections of experience in political work among the enemy troops and population15.
Excerpts from one of the 7th Department's "Exchange of Experience" bulletins. September 25, 1943. Photo from the Russian Ministry of Defense website.
The operational apparatus for special propaganda included the seventh departments of the front (district) political directorates, the seventh sections of the army political departments, and senior instructors of the corps and division political departments for work among enemy troops and the population. The seventh departments of the fronts and border military districts also operated foreign-language newspaper editorial offices and radio broadcasting offices. 16.
Each element of the special propaganda system had its own operational scope. Thus, the front political directorates served as the link between the 7th Department of the GUPPKA and all subordinate structures, ensuring a continuous exchange of information between the special propaganda leadership and those working on the ground. Furthermore, the front political directorates provided all possible support to the army political departments. For example, they instructed and dispatched special propaganda teams equipped with mobile printing presses, powerful sound amplification stations, photo laboratories, and other front-line propaganda equipment.
They also carried out extensive work on the timely delivery and distribution of propaganda materials among enemy troops and civilians. This was accomplished primarily by frontline aviation. This required constant coordination with air force headquarters.
They also carried out extensive work on training special propagandists, as well as working with prisoners of war to instill in them an anti-fascist ideology and further involve them in propaganda work against the enemy.17.
Interrogation of a captured German. July 1941.
As for the army's political departments, their important task was to collect and systematize reliable information about the opposing enemy forces and disseminate it to higher authorities. Overall, the army's political departments were distinguished by their efficiency and were able to quickly adapt their propaganda in content, forms, and methods based on the constantly changing combat situation. Their primary task was to provide comprehensive assistance and maintain constant contact with the divisional political departments.
In turn, the divisional political departments operated, as they say, "on the ground" and in a more targeted manner. Officially, they were represented only by a senior instructor for work among enemy troops and the population, but since one person could not carry out all the work, several individuals with the necessary skills were assigned to assist the instructor. This created a unique department. It addressed the task of maximally weakening the combat capability of enemy units engaged in battles against a given division in a given sector of the front. At this level, the most common tool used was operational propaganda (that is, propaganda aimed at specific enemy military formations, whose situation was comprehensively studied at the divisional political department level).18.
Senior Lieutenant P.I. Nikitin drops leaflets on enemy troop positions using a mortar of his own design. 1942.
The publication of leaflets in foreign languages ​​was handled by the Military Publishing House of the USSR People's Commissariat of Defense, which included a department for fulfilling special orders under the 7th Department (Directorate). The Moscow-based Iskra Revolutsii printing house, capable of typesetting and publishing printed materials in 60 foreign languages, was assigned to the 7th Directorate from the USSR Foreign Publishing House. The printing plant of the Pravda Publishing House of the Central Committee of the All-Union Communist Party (Bolsheviks) was also involved in the production of the most important and high-circulation propaganda materials. 19.
One of the first Soviet propaganda leaflets for the Germans. A Russian translation is included below. Leaflets with similar content were almost entirely ineffective.
In addition, on the eve of the war, military districts sent many civilian specialists (journalists, philologists, historians, German language teachers and others) to training camps fleet and into ground military units for use according to their specialty. Upon completion, they were warned that in the event of war, they would be called up again. 20This was also necessary to staff the system with valuable personnel, which, however, was constantly in short supply.
As mentioned above, the main document regulating the activities of special propaganda was Directive No. 267. It was written in the spirit of socialism and Lenin's ideas that when the enemy army and the population, through information provided by the Soviet Union, understand the senselessness of war for the working people, they will immediately protest against their government and express sympathy for the Red Army. 21.
The objective class position of capitalists is one thing. They fight for themselves. Soldiers are proletarians and peasants. That's different... their class interests are against war! That's why they can be enlightened, persuaded,
— V.I. Lenin22
This was the basis of the "gold standard" of Soviet political propaganda directed at enemy troops in the pre-war period. Back then, no one understood that the Soviet Union would be confronted with soldiers raised from childhood to believe in their exceptionalism and the superiority of their nation over all other nations on the planet.
In early May 1941, the People's Commissar of Defense demanded that the 7th Department of the GUPPKA, headed by Mikhail Ivanovich Burtsev, prepare a report on the political and moral state of the countries bordering the USSR and their armies. A few days later, such a report was prepared and read out. 23But there was one important nuance. The report contained very little information about the situation in Germany.
The reason for this was that, at that time, Germany was not among the Soviet Union's most likely adversaries. This was especially influenced by the non-aggression pact between the USSR and the Third Reich in 1939.
Political Commissar I.I. Petrov conducts propaganda work on German positions using a primitive tin pipe. North Caucasus Front, 1942.
As a result, the German-language newspaper's editorial office in the Leningrad Military District was liquidated. Furthermore, only one or two German publications were subscribed to for research into the situation in Germany. A major drawback was the fact that the Soviet leadership prohibited the translation of German articles and books critical of our country. 24, even to structures for which this was a direct part of the work.
All this together made it impossible to see the real processes taking place in Germany in the pre-war period and to form a true picture of the enemy, and at the same time to develop methods and arguments for informational and psychological influence on the future enemy based on current data.
Among the potential adversaries being studied were countries located on the southern borders of the USSR (Iran, Afghanistan, India, and Turkey). Propaganda theses had already been prepared for these countries, exposing the colonial nature of the British imperialists, and some printed materials had been prepared. 25.
Photo taken during the Battle of Smolensk, 1941
Thus, on the eve of the Great Patriotic War, the special propaganda agencies lacked complete and up-to-date information on the Third Reich and its allies, but were preparing to wage psychological warfare against entirely different countries. Furthermore, among all the employees of the 7th Departments, there was a critical shortage of people with a high level of German proficiency. More often than not, those who spoke the language only spoke it colloquially, not to mention the new military terms and ranks that had emerged in Nazi Germany.
Only after the aforementioned May 1941 report was the 7th Department of the GUPPKA tasked with filling this gap and preparing a report on the situation in Germany in the shortest possible time. 26The report systematized all available relevant data on the Third Reich. But it was, of course, insufficient to fully reflect reality.
Nevertheless, based on available sources, it was noted that the German army was undergoing extraordinary moral and political preparation for war. Their army was assessed as strong, well-disciplined, and well-armed. However, the report again erroneously concluded that it would be easy to convince German soldiers that this war was inadvisable for them. The report was distributed to the Red Army's political organs for review. 27.
By the time Nazi Germany invaded the USSR, many special propaganda efforts had to be implemented on the fly. Thus, on June 22, 1941, two sections were formed within the 7th Department of the GUPPKA: the first for conducting information and psychological warfare against Germany and its allies, and the second for propaganda work among the populations of occupied countries and territories.28.
Of fundamental importance was the decision of the Central Committee of the All-Union Communist Party (Bolsheviks) on June 25, 1941, to establish the Bureau of Military-Political Propaganda. This was a collegial body created to centralize the direction of all propaganda efforts against the enemy and the populations of the territories they had captured. The 7th Department became the working body of this Bureau. 29.
Resolution of the Central Committee of the All-Union Communist Party (Bolsheviks) "On the Creation of the Soviet Bureau of Military-Political Propaganda." June 25, 1941 (Original. RGASPI, Fund 17, List 163, D. 1316. L. 183)
The Bureau included: the head of the GUPPKA, L. Z. Mekhlis, his deputy, D. Z. Manuilsky, professor and specialist in propaganda, V. S. Kruzhkov, head of the press department of the People's Commissariat of Foreign Affairs, P. G. Palgunov, and deputy people's commissar of foreign affairs, S. A. Lozovsky (on July 2, the director of the Marx-Engels-Lenin Institute under the Central Committee of the All-Union Communist Party (Bolsheviks), M. B. Mitin, was also included in the Bureau).30L. Z. Mekhlis became the head of the Bureau.
At the meetings, the fundamental directions and content of all special propaganda were determined, leading general political materials for the enemy troops and population were approved, and joint activities in the matter of special propaganda of such bodies as TASS, the Soviet Information Bureau, the USSR Radio Committee, state publishing houses and others were coordinated. 31.
Another important agency for special propaganda was the Soviet Information Bureau (Sovinformburo), established on June 24, 1941, by a joint resolution of the Central Committee of the All-Union Communist Party (Bolsheviks) and the Council of People's Commissars. Information transmitted through the Sovinformburo was often used in the preparation of leaflets for enemy soldiers (for example, the information leaflets "International Information").
Resolution of June 24, 1941 of the Central Committee of the All-Union Communist Party (Bolsheviks) and the Council of People's Commissars on the establishment of the Soviet Information Bureau (Sovinformburo)
This information was of even greater importance for the residents of the occupied eastern territories of the USSR, who were cut off from receiving News about the progress of the war. Therefore, in 1942, a directive was issued requiring every partisan detachment to receive Sovinformburo reports, record them, and reproduce them as leaflets for subsequent distribution among Soviet citizens remaining in enemy-occupied territory. In this way, people cut off from information about the state of the war and constantly subjected to massive fascist propaganda and lies could learn the truth and maintain contact with their country. 32.
Thus, the structure of the Soviet Union's special propaganda agencies targeting the enemy troops and population at the start of the Great Patriotic War can be represented in the following diagram.
The diagram of the Soviet Union's special propaganda apparatus at the start of the Great Patriotic War
In conclusion, it can be concluded that by the beginning of the Great Patriotic War, the structure of the apparatus of special propaganda had already been created, which, nevertheless, during the course of the war will undergo some necessary changes due to the increase in the scale and effectiveness of this work.
However, this work began too late, preventing the necessary experience from being accumulated. Furthermore, due to unjustified restrictions on the study of information materials from the Nazi bloc countries, by the outbreak of the war there was no true picture of the processes taking place in Germany and its allies.
This led to the Red Army's ignorance and misperception of the enemy soldiers' morale and psychological state. This resulted in failures in conducting special propaganda against the enemy during the initial period of the war. Naturally, the forced, constant retreat of Soviet troops during that difficult period contributed to the failures in disseminating propaganda against German soldiers.
The next article will examine in detail the initial successes and failures in conducting political work among enemy troops.

以前的文章致力于苏联的特殊军事宣传，涵盖了影响这类军事活动发展的主要军事冲突。在这些事件之后，我们现在可以继续讨论伟大的卫国战争，在这场战争中，红军对敌军和人民的政治工作达到了新的水平，并在长期不确定之后获得了明确的组织框架。

1941年6月22日，苏联人民聆听政府宣布战争开始。
苏联针对纳粹德国及其盟国军队的宣传主题相当广泛，因此它将成为一系列文章的主题，这些文章涵盖了战争的各个时期，从战争开始到5月9日胜利日。本文是本系列的第一篇文章。
在战争的不同时期，针对德国军队的政治战役的内容是根据前线军事和政治形势的发展、苏联军队完成的作战任务以及敌人政治和士气的变化而构建的。为了对敌人施加思想和政治影响，使用了报刊、电台（广播电台和来自前线、国内和被俘的电台）、口头宣传（通过扩音器和扩音器）和视觉宣传（传单、报纸、小册子和书籍）。
在详细考察卫国战争时期苏联特种宣传的类型和方法之前，有必要了解这项工作的组织结构。因此，本文将揭示哪些特定机构开发和实施了针对敌军的信息战和心理战。
1941年8月30日，红军士兵在莫斯科伏罗希洛夫军营训练。
重要的是，最近的苏芬战争暴露了当时年轻的红军的许多弱点。显然，有必要总结战争的结果，以便迅速查明和解决所有错误和缺点。为此，1940年4月14日至17日，在全联盟共产党（布尔什维克）中央委员会的领导下，召开了红军指挥参谋部会议，总结在芬兰作战行动的经验。2.
这次会议对正在发生的事情有了可靠的了解。在这次会议上，斯大林在4月17日的讲话中解释了为什么研究苏芬战争的经验是一个优先事项。以下是这篇演讲中的两段重要引言：
…请记住，在苏联政权存在的整个时期，我们从未打过一场真正的现代战争。在满洲、喀山湖或蒙古发生的小插曲都是无稽之谈。它们不是战争，而是在严格限制的区域内发生的孤立事件。日本害怕发动战争，我们也不想这样，在那一小块地方进行的一次小规模的实力测试表明，日本失败了。他们有两个或三个师，我们在蒙古有两个或三个师，在喀山湖也有同样的数字。我们的军队从未打过一场真正的、严肃的战争。内战不是真正的战争，因为它是一场没有大炮、没有飞机、没有坦克、没有迫击炮的战争。如果没有这些，这算哪门子战争？
-I.V.斯大林
…我们的现代红军在芬兰的战场上遭到炮击——那是它的第一次洗礼。
-静脉注射斯大林3
斯大林在红军指挥机关总结冬季战争经验会议上的讲话（节选）。1940年4月17日（RGASPI，F.558，op.11，D.1124，L.23，35）
会议的第二项成果是国防部副人民委员G.I.Kulik提议选举一个委员会来总结委员会的建议，以及全面分析对芬兰的军事行动，并为每个单独的地区制定具体的建议。
该委员会于1940年4月19日成立并开始工作。它包括K.E.Voroshilov（主席）、I.V.Stalin、G.I.Kulik、L.Z.Mekhlis、E.A.Shchadenko和中央军事部的其他代表。然而，委员会的大多数成员都是冬季战争的直接参与者。
红军战士在被派往前线之前。列宁格勒，1941年6月23日。
为方便起见，委员会为武装部队的每个分支和其他分支设立了单独的小组委员会。其中包括联合兵种、空军、技术部队、装甲车辆、政治工作和其他小组委员会。每个国家都必须在第二天之前向苏联国防人民委员提交关于其具体领域的实际建议。由于发现了大量问题，对一些人来说，最后期限被延长到4月21日。4.
在所有小组委员会于4月21日的全体会议上提交了他们的调查结果后，I.V.斯大林提议成立一个特别的“狭义委员会”来解决以前没有考虑过的问题。这个特别委员会的会议从1940年4月23日持续到5月14日。5.
在这篇文章的背景下，最有趣的是1940年5月10日红军政治理事会主席梅赫利斯（L.Z.Mekhlis）关于军事意识形态的报告，其中涉及对芬兰士兵和民众的信息和心理影响。
列夫·扎哈罗维奇·梅赫利斯
考虑到过去战争的所有错误，这份报告概述了改进苏联特别宣传的关键领域。该报告的全文可以在公开来源中找到，但我将提供理解该主题所需的关键摘录。
对潜在对手的军队和可能的军事行动战区的研究完全不能令人满意，可用的情报数据过于机密，不能提供给指挥人员，-L.Z.Mekhlis.
一种根深蒂固的、有害的偏见认为，与苏联交战的国家的人民将不可避免地、几乎全体地造反并投靠红军，工人和农民将用鲜花迎接我们。这种错误的信念源于对邻国实际情况的无知。芬兰的战争表明，我们没有在北部地区进行政治侦察，因此不知道该向这些人提出什么口号，也不知道如何在他们中间开展工作……我们需要了解每个国家人民的生活和利益。
-L.Z.Mekhlis
应该说，在研究敌人的政治方面，我们犯了不止一次的错误，在敌人的军队和人民中，我们的工作进展不大。直到1939年初，才引进了外文报纸编辑部，但由于缺乏对各国语言、日常生活、历史和文化有足够了解的作者，这些编辑部还远远不能满足要求。如果你想正确地打败你的敌人，你需要很好地了解他。因此，你必须仔细研究和了解邻国所有军队的长处和短处，包括小的。
-L.Z.Mekhlis6
会议之后，战时党的工作和政治工作小组委员会在专门研究敌军工作的部分中，通过了一些具有重大现实意义的决定，以形成一个特殊的宣传结构。。因此，第四点指出：“为了给敌军和人民的政治工作提供组织上的支持，在各边区和各军的政治部设立敌军和人民的工作部。”。
一群苏联士兵走在科拉湾的岸边。1941.
其他要点还讨论了为精通外语的个人建立军事登记册，根据他们对特定语言的了解将他们分配到外国报纸的编辑部，并定期举行会议以交流经验和提高他们的技能。并决定印发《和平时期敌军政治工作组织手册》。7.
早在1939年7月，一些边境军区就设立了外文报纸编辑部，作为培训中心，要求编辑人员积累邻国的信息，研究邻国的优势和劣势，选择事实进行宣传，并提高他们在为潜在敌人（该国）的士兵和民众出版印刷品方面的经验。
共创建了24个编辑部。指派了一名专门的讲师来管理他们，后来又成立了一组讲师兼翻译。1940年4月，该小组改组为一个专门管理外语出版物的部门。国防部的每一位高级教官都负责监督一种特定外语的报纸，并研究各自的国家及其军队。
村庄争夺战。1941
最后，同年8月，在红军政治宣传总局（GUPPKA）内，在这个部门的基础上，成立了一个在敌军和民众中进行宣传的特别部门。它由米哈伊尔·伊万诺维奇·布尔采夫少校领导，他在1939年与日本人在喀尔欣郭勒河的战斗中和1940年与芬兰人在卡累利阿地峡的战斗中已经有了进行特别宣传的经验。
米哈伊尔·伊万诺维奇·布尔采夫少将。照片来自他1981年的书《洞察》
它是第七个部门，因此它的通用名称是第七个部门。它的任务是研究军队人员和外国人民的政治和士气，并准备在他们中间进行宣传和鼓动，目的是打击他们的士气。来自苏联科学院各研究所的受过高等教育的专家、科学家和教育家，国立大学的毕业生和军事院校的研究生，精通德语、芬兰语、罗马尼亚语、英语、波斯语、阿拉伯语、日语和其他外语，被挑选并任命到该部门。
在红军政治宣传总局内设立第七部之后，在下列边境地区的政治部也设立了类似的部门：列宁格勒、西部和基辅特别区、敖德萨、外高加索、中亚和外贝加尔军区以及远东前线。此外，区内各军政治部还设立了对敌宣传队和宣传队，并在各师政治部工作人员中增设了对敌宣传高级指导员。
当然，这样一个系统需要配备合格的人员。这项工作早在1938年5月就开始了，当时对精通外语、能够在敌军和普通民众中进行宣传的职业政治工作者进行了第一次普查。这些在红军预备队中的政治工作者，定期被征召参加训练。
莫斯科第二国立外语教育学院军事系（自1942年起为军事外语学院（VIIL））在培训特殊宣传员方面发挥了重要作用。它被称为苏联特别宣传员的熔炉。莫斯科东方学院的军事系也发挥了重要作用。在那里，学生们参加了关于在敌军和民众中开展政治工作的简短但内容丰富的课程。11缴获的敌方文件和现有的宣传出版物经常被用作教具。
根据1941年10月10日的命令，位于伏尔加河（现在的陶里亚蒂）斯塔夫罗波尔市的列斯诺耶疗养院（Lesnoye Sanatorium）的莫斯科第二外国语教育学院（Second Moscow Educational Institute of Foreign Languages）的西方外语军事学院（Military Faculty of Western Foreign Languages）被用船撤离。照片拍摄于1941年
1942年，伏尔加河畔斯塔夫罗波尔的西方外语军事学院的学生。照片来自陶里亚蒂地方历史博物馆的收藏。
1940年10月12日，古普卡发布了第号指令。它描述了在过去的战斗中在敌军和民众中工作的经验，并确定了开展与敌军有关的意识形态工作的新方法和新方向。12与其他国家不同，在其他国家，心理战部门是独立的或情报部门的一部分，第七部门作为意识形态斗争机构，成为军事政治机构的一部分。必须指出的是，在政治机构内部，他们感到与自己的职责格格不入，经常遭到怀疑，有时甚至破坏他们的活动。
当时，仍有不少苏联士兵和指挥官严重怀疑这项艰巨而危险的任务能否取得哪怕是最轻微的成功。官方的说法是，特别宣传员从事分解敌军的工作。许多前线士兵听到后说：“法西斯只会在地下腐烂。”14.
因此，古普卡第七局的任务包括：
1.在敌国军队和民众中制作、出版和组织分发宣传材料（传单、标语、报纸、小册子）；2。（二）指导前线和军内特种宣传机构，协助分解敌军兵力和人口；在前线敌军和后方民众中发展和实施特殊的信息和宣传行动；4.每天研究军队人员和敌国人民的政治和道德状况、其意识形态的性质和制度；5.收集有关我们宣传效果的信息；6.挑选、培训和分配会讲相关外语的专门宣传员；7.在其信息公告中以及在敌军和民众中收集政治工作经验的过程中，推广和传播信息战的最佳做法15。
节选自第七部门的“经验交流”简报之一。1943年9月25日。图片来自俄罗斯国防部网站。
特殊宣传的工作机构包括前线（区）政治部第七部、军政治部第七科、军和师政治部的高级指导员，负责对敌军和民众的工作。前线军区和边防军区第七部还设有外文报纸编辑部和广播电台。16.
特殊宣传系统的每个元素都有自己的操作范围。因此，前线政治事务局充当了古普卡第7部与所有下属机构之间的纽带，确保特别宣传领导层与实地工作人员之间不断交流信息。此外，前线政治事务局向军队政治部门提供了一切可能的支持。例如，他们指示并派遣了专门的宣传小组，配备了移动印刷机、强大的扩音站、照片实验室和其他前线宣传设备。
他们还广泛开展了在敌军和平民中及时发送和分发宣传品的工作。这主要是由前线航空完成的。这需要与空军总部不断协调。
他们还广泛开展了培训专门宣传员的工作，并与战俘一起向他们灌输反法西斯思想，进一步让他们参与对敌宣传工作。
审问一个被俘的德国人。1941年7月。
至于军队的政治部门，他们的重要任务是收集和整理有关敌对部队的可靠情报，并将其传播给上级。总体而言，军队政治部门以效率见长，能够根据不断变化的作战形势，迅速调整宣传内容、形式和方法。他们的主要任务是提供全面协助，并与师政治部保持经常联系。
反过来，正如他们所说的那样，分区政治部门“在实地”以更有针对性的方式开展工作。官方规定，只有一名高级教官代表他们在敌军和民众中开展工作，但由于一个人无法完成所有工作，因此指派了几个具有必要技能的人协助教官。这创造了一个独特的部门。它解决的任务是最大限度地削弱敌方部队在前线特定地区与特定师作战的作战能力。在这一级，最常用的工具是作战宣传（即针对特定敌方军事编队的宣传，其情况由师政治部一级全面研究）。
高级中尉P.I.尼基丁用他自己设计的迫击炮向敌军阵地散发传单。1942.
外文传单的出版由苏联国防人民委员部军事出版社负责，该出版社包括第7部（董事会）下的一个执行特别命令的部门。设在莫斯科的Iskra Revolutsii印刷厂能够排版和出版60种外语的印刷材料，由苏联外国出版社分配给第七局。全联盟共产党（布尔什维克）中央委员会真理报出版社的印刷厂也参与了最重要和发行量最大的宣传材料的制作。19.
苏联给德国人的第一批宣传传单之一。俄文翻译如下。类似内容的传单几乎完全无效。
此外，在战争前夕，各军区将许多文职专家（记者、语言学家、历史学家、德语教师等）派往训练营舰队和地面军事单位，根据他们的专业使用。完成后，他们被警告说，如果发生战争，他们将再次被征召。20这对于为该系统配备有价值的人员也是必要的，但这些人员一直短缺。
正如上文所述，规范特别宣传活动的主要文件是第5/2000号指令。267.它是根据社会主义精神和列宁的思想写成的，即当敌军和民众通过苏联提供的信息了解到战争对劳动人民的无意义时，他们会立即向他们的政府提出抗议，并对红军表示同情。21.
资本家的客观阶级地位是一回事。他们为自己而战。军人是无产者，是农民。那是不同的..他们的阶级利益是反对战争！这就是为什么他们可以被启发，被说服。-V.I.列宁22
这是战前苏联政治宣传针对敌军的“黄金标准”的基础。当时，没有人明白，苏联将面对的是从小就相信自己的例外主义和自己国家优于地球上所有其他国家的士兵。
1941年5月初，国防人民委员要求以米哈伊尔·伊万诺维奇·布尔采夫为首的古普卡第七部准备一份关于与苏联接壤的国家及其军队的政治和道德状况的报告。几天后，准备并宣读了这样一份报告。23但有一个重要的细微差别。报告中关于德国情况的信息很少。
其原因是，当时德国并不是苏联最可能的对手之一。这尤其受到1939年苏联和第三帝国之间互不侵犯条约的影响。
政委I.I.Petrov使用原始的锡管在德军阵地上进行宣传工作。北高加索前线，1942年。
结果，这家德语报纸在列宁格勒军区的编辑部被清算。此外，只订阅了一两份研究德国情况的德国出版物。一个主要的缺点是，苏联领导人禁止翻译批评我国的德文文章和书籍。24，甚至对结构来说，这是工作的直接部分。
所有这些加在一起，使人们无法看到战前德国发生的真实过程，无法形成对敌人的真实描述，同时也无法根据当前的数据制定对未来敌人产生信息和心理影响的方法和论据。
正在研究的潜在对手包括位于苏联南部边境的国家（伊朗、阿富汗、印度和土耳其）。已经为这些国家准备了宣传论文，揭露英帝国主义的殖民本质，并准备了一些印刷材料。25.
照片拍摄于1941年的斯摩棱斯克战役。
因此，在伟大卫国战争前夕，特别宣传机构缺乏关于第三帝国及其盟国的完整和最新信息，但却准备对完全不同的国家发动心理战。此外，在第7部门的所有员工中，德语水平较高的人员严重短缺。更多的时候，那些说这种语言的人只是在口头上说这种语言，更不用说纳粹德国出现的新的军事术语和军衔了。
只有在上述1941年5月的报告之后，古普卡第七部门才负责填补这一空白，并在最短的时间内准备一份关于德国局势的报告。26该报告将第三帝国的所有现有相关数据系统化。但这当然不足以充分反映现实。
然而，根据现有的资料，人们注意到，德国军队正在为战争进行非同寻常的道德和政治准备。他们的军队被认为是强大的，纪律严明的，装备精良的。然而，该报告再次得出错误的结论，即很容易让德国士兵相信这场战争对他们来说是不明智的。报告分发给红军政治机关审阅。27.
到纳粹德国入侵苏联时，许多特殊的宣传工作不得不在飞行中实施。因此，1941年6月22日，在古普卡第七部内成立了两个部门：第一个部门负责对德国及其盟国进行信息战和心理战，第二个部门负责在被占领国家和领土的民众中开展宣传工作。
具有根本重要性的是全联盟共产党（布尔什维克）中央委员会于1941年6月25日作出的成立军事政治宣传局的决定。这是一个合议机构，其设立是为了集中指挥反对敌人和他们占领的领土上的人民的所有宣传努力。第七司成为该局的办事机构。29.
全联盟共产党（布尔什维克）中央委员会“关于建立苏维埃军事政治宣传局”的决议。1941年6月25日（原件。RGASPI，基金17，清单163，D.1316。第183号法律）
主席团成员包括：古普卡主席梅赫利斯（L.Z.Mekhlis），副主席马努伊尔斯基（D.Z.Manuilsky），教授兼宣传专家克鲁日科夫（V.S.Kruzhkov），外交人民委员部新闻司司长帕尔古诺夫（P.G.Palgunov）和外交副人民委员洛佐夫斯基（S.A.Lozovsky）（7月2日，全联盟共产党（布尔什维克）中央委员会下属的马克思-恩格斯-列宁研究所所长。M.B.Mitin，也包括在主席团中）.30L.梅赫利斯成为该局局长。
在这些会议上，确定了所有特别宣传的基本方向和内容，批准了针对敌军和民众的主要一般政治材料，并协调了塔斯社、苏联新闻局、苏联无线电委员会、国家出版社和其他机构在特别宣传方面的联合活动。31.
另一个重要的特殊宣传机构是苏联新闻局（Sovinformburo），根据全联盟共产党（布尔什维克）中央委员会和人民委员委员会的联合决议，于1941年6月24日成立。通过Sovinformburo传递的信息经常用于为敌方士兵准备传单（例如，信息传单“国际信息”）。
全联盟共产党（布尔什维克）中央委员会和人民委员理事会1941年6月24日关于建立苏维埃新闻局（Sovinformburo）的决议
对于被占领的苏联东部领土的居民来说，这一信息更为重要，因为他们无法获得有关战争进展的消息。因此，1942年发布了一项指令，要求每个游击队分遣队接收Sovinformburo报告，记录这些报告，并将其复制为传单，以便随后在留在敌占区的苏联公民中分发。通过这种方式，人们被切断了有关战争状况的信息，并不断受到大规模法西斯宣传和谎言的影响，从而能够了解真相并与自己的国家保持联系。32.
因此，在伟大卫国战争开始时，苏联针对敌军和民众的特别宣传机构的结构可以用下图表示。

总之，可以得出结论，在伟大卫国战争开始时，特别宣传机构的结构已经建立，然而，在战争过程中，由于这项工作的规模和效力的增加，这种结构将发生一些必要的变化。
然而，这项工作开始得太晚，无法积累必要的经验。此外，由于对来自纳粹集团国家的信息材料的研究受到不合理的限制，到战争爆发时，对德国及其盟国发生的进程没有真实的了解。
这导致了红军对敌军士气和心理状态的无知和误解。这导致了在战争初期对敌人进行特殊宣传的失败。当然，在那个困难时期，苏联军队被迫不断撤退，导致了针对德国士兵的宣传失败。

that a central challenge of cognitive warfare is governing the relationship between institutional cognition and an operational environment in which informational, behavioral, and social dynamics evolve continuously and often independently of military decision timelines. To meet this challenge, we propose that future command architectures should emphasize and integrate mechanisms for the adaptive synchronization of human judgment, AI, and the cognitive ecosystem being engaged. This approach augments extant theories of command by recognizing that operational advantage emerges from maintaining temporal alignment between institutional decision-making and the environment in which decisions are executed and incur effects.
One method of constructing such an architecture is to reconsider the roles of humans and AI across the decision cycle. If a temporal gap arises because human-paced observation, decision, and execution cannot keep pace with an environment that continues to evolve in the interim, the relevant question becomes which functions must remain human and which can be delegated to AI systems better capable of synchronizing with the cognitive environment. This reframing shifts the challenge from one of tempo alone to one of function reallocation. We posit that the resulting approach entrusts speed-bound functions to AI systems operating under human direction while preserving human judgment, accountability, situational interpretation, and
.
. This figure consists of two panels depicting a decision cycle along a left-to-right temporal axis. Red segments denote machine-executed functions and blue segments denote human judgment and authority. Dotted vertical lines mark points of ecosystem sampling and downward arrows indicate human discretion exercised over machine-executed functions. The current model (top) confines machine execution to the front and back ends of the cycle, whereas the proposed model (bottom) relocates the human to a supervisory position above the cycle.
Figure 2 illustrates both a current and proposed model of human-machine teaming with two panels depicting a decision cycle (i.e., observe, orient, decide, act) along a temporal axis. In doing so, Figure 2 contrasts the current distribution of engagement with the proposed reallocation of human and machine function across the decision cycle. In the regnant loop, machine systems perform the front-end functions of the observe and orient stages by analyzing the operational environment and processing the resulting data for human interpretation. At the back end of the decision cycle, they execute the functions of the action stage by implementing orders issued by human decision-makers. Between these nodes, humans sustain a continuous arc of involvement. Consequently, ecosystem sampling occurs only at the boundaries of these stages, such that institutional understanding is dependent upon a small number of episodic observations acquired early in the cycle. As the cycle advances at human tempo, assessments generated upon initial observation risk losing relevance before decisions can be executed.
The proposed model addresses this misalignment by relocating human involvement from within the decision cycle to a supervisory position across it. Here, the human directs and bounds machine systems that execute functions at a tempo the human observer could not achieve unaided. As noted, the vertical arrows indicate how human discretion is exercised continuously over machine function by establishing command intent, parameters, and engagement criteria within which sensing, orientation, and execution proceed. Because these functions are no longer rate-limited by human throughput, the cognitive ecosystem is sampled at a higher frequency, as indicated by the increased density of sampling lines beneath the observe, orient, and act stages.
Institutional understanding under this model thereby tracks the evolving environment rather than capturing a series of static snapshots. Decision authority, however, remains a wholly human function in both configurations. As illustrated in the lower panel of Figure 2, the reintroduction of direct human control at the decisional point functions as a guardrail, preserving human judgment, accountability, and responsibility for the use of force even as other functions are executed at machine speed. Delegation of the decisional point to machine interfaces would achieve synchronization at the cost of accountability for the use of force, which we regard as an
.
The operational implications of this analysis extend beyond the optimization of decision speed and refinement of existing C2 processes. Cognitive environments should therefore not be regarded as static operational conditions to be episodically observed and acted upon. Instead, the object of decision evolves continuously through (1) persistent human interaction, (2) algorithmically mediated information exchange, and (3) increasingly autonomous computation. The operational relevance of any decision is therefore determined both by its velocity and by the extent to which institutional cognition remains synchronized with the evolving
.
Consequently, temporal synchronization should stand as a complementary principle of military decision theory that extends Boyd's OODA construct. Whereas Boyd demonstrated that adaptive orientation and competitive tempo are central to operational advantage, we argue that this understanding should be broadened to recognize cognition as a biopsychosocial and institutional process in which operational consequences recursively shape future decision-making. Within this framework, the ongoing evolution of the cognitive ecosystem during the execution of each decision cycle emerges as an additional operational variable. Decisional superiority will thus depend increasingly upon preserving coherence between institutional understanding and an operational environment in constant flux.
AI assumes importance within this context because it enables persistent observation, continuous contextual integration, predictive analysis, and adaptive decision support across
. Properly governed, these capabilities position human-AI teaming to sustain alignment between evolving operational conditions and institutional understanding while preserving the indispensable human roles of judgment, strategic reasoning, ethical deliberation, accountable command, and missional responsibility. Within this paradigm, human cognition and AI are best regarded and engaged as reciprocally complementary capabilities within an adaptive
.
More broadly, we perceive that this relationship reflects an evolution in the character of command. As military operations become increasingly data-intensive, distributed, and AI-enabled, command advantage will derive less from accelerating individual decision cycles in isolation than from the sustained governance of cognition across interconnected human-machine
. Accordingly, future C2 architectures should increase computational speed while preserving alignment among command intent, institutional understanding, computational processes, and environmental change. We believe that decision superiority in AI-enabled warfare will increasingly depend upon this capacity for synchronized cognition and therefore regard temporal synchronization as an essential element of cognitive governance through which military organizations can integrate and sustain AI while preserving accountable human authority.
The views and opinions expressed in this essay are those of the authors and do not necessarily reflect those of the United States government, Department of War, or the National Defense University.
Mr. John Murray is a Research Intern in the Program for Disruptive Technology and Future Warfare at the Institute for National Strategic Studies at the National Defense University and a graduate candidate in the Master of Public Administration program at Auburn University.
Dr. Elise Annett is a Research Fellow in the Program for Disruptive Technology and Future Warfare of the Institute for National Strategic Studies at the National Defense University.
Dr. James Giordano is Head of the Center for Strategic Deterrence and Weapons of Mass Destruction Studies of the Institute for National Strategic Studies at the National Defense University and serves as NDU Special Advisor to the Office of the Assistant Secretary of War (CBRN).
_source.movement_title: 美国国防大学提出人机协同认知同步指挥架构
_source.movement_abstract: 美国国防大学国家战略研究所研究人员约翰·默里、伊莉丝·阿内特和詹姆斯·吉奥尔达诺提出，认知战的核心挑战在于治理机构认知与持续演变的作战环境之间的关系。文章建议未来指挥架构应强调并整合机制，以实现人类判断、人工智能与认知生态系统的自适应同步。该方案主张将受速度限制的功能委托给人工智能系统，同时保留人类在判断、问责、情境解释及决策权威方面的核心作用。研究对比了当前模型与提议模型：当前模型中人类处于决策循环内部，导致环境采样频率低且易滞后；提议模型将人类置于监督位置，通过设定意图和参数持续指导机器执行，从而在保持人类问责的前提下实现高频环境采样。文章指出，决策优势将取决于机构理解与动态环境之间的连贯性，时间同步应作为军事决策理论的补充原则。在人工智能赋能的战争中，指挥优势将源于对互联人机系统的认知持续治理，而非单纯加速单个决策循环。

_source.title: Decision Advantage in Cognitive Warfare, Part 2
_source.trans_cont:
认知战的核心挑战是控制机构认知与作战环境之间的关系，在作战环境中，信息、行为和社会动态不断发展，并且通常独立于军事决策时间表。为了应对这一挑战，我们建议未来的指挥架构应强调并整合人类判断、人工智能和认知生态系统的自适应同步机制。这种方法通过认识到保持机构决策与执行决策并产生效果的环境之间的时间一致性而产生的作战优势，增强了现存的指挥理论。
构建这种架构的一种方法是重新考虑人类和人工智能在整个决策周期中的角色。如果由于人类节奏的观察、决策和执行不能跟上在此期间继续发展的环境而出现时间差距，那么相关的问题就变成了哪些功能必须保持为人类的，哪些功能可以委托给能够更好地与认知环境同步的人工智能系统。这种重新规划将挑战从单纯的节奏转变为功能重新分配。我们假设，由此产生的方法将速度约束功能委托给在人类指导下运行的人工智能系统，同时保留人类的判断、责任、情景解释和
.
.该图由两个面板组成，描绘了沿从左到右时间轴的决策周期。红色部分表示机器执行的功能，蓝色部分表示人的判断和权限。垂直虚线表示生态系统采样点，向下箭头表示人类对机器执行功能的判断。当前模型（顶部）将机器执行限制在循环的前端和后端，而所提出的模型（底部）将人重新定位到循环上方的监督位置。
图2示出了当前和提议的人机协作模型，其中两个面板描绘了沿时间轴的决策周期（即，观察、定向、决定、行动）。在此过程中，图2将参与的当前分布与整个决策周期中人和机器功能的建议重新分配进行了对比。在统治循环中，机器系统通过分析操作环境和处理结果数据以供人类解释来执行观察和定向阶段的前端功能。在决策周期的后端，它们通过执行人类决策者发布的命令来执行行动阶段的功能。在这些节点之间，人类维持着一个连续的参与弧。因此，生态系统取样只发生在这些阶段的边界，因此机构的理解依赖于在周期早期获得的少量偶发观察。随着周期以人类的节奏推进，在执行决策之前，最初观察产生的评估可能会失去相关性。
所提出的模型通过将人的参与从决策周期内重新定位到整个决策周期的监督位置来解决这种不一致。在这里，人类指导和限制机器系统以人类观察者在没有帮助的情况下无法实现的速度执行功能。如所指出的，垂直箭头指示如何通过建立命令意图、参数和接合标准来连续地对机器功能行使人的判断力，在所述命令意图、参数和接合标准内进行感测、定向和执行。由于这些功能不再受人类吞吐量的速率限制，认知生态系统以更高的频率进行采样，如“观察”、“定向”和“行动”阶段下的采样线密度增加所示。
因此，该模型下的机构理解跟踪不断变化的环境，而不是捕捉一系列静态快照。然而，在这两种配置中，决策权仍然完全是人的功能。如图2的下面板所示，在决策点重新引入直接人工控制起到了护栏的作用，即使在以机器速度执行其他功能时，也保留了人工判断、责任和使用武力的责任。将决策点委托给机器接口将以使用武力的责任为代价实现同步，我们认为这是一种
.
该分析的作战含义超出了决策速度的优化和现有指挥控制过程的改进。因此，认知环境不应被视为静态的操作条件，以进行情景观察和操作。相反，决策的对象通过（1）持续的人类交互，（2）以算法为中介的信息交换，以及（3）日益自主的计算而不断发展。因此，任何决策的操作相关性都是由其速度和机构认知与演变保持同步的程度决定的
.
因此，时间同步应该作为军事决策理论的补充原则，扩展Boyd的OODA结构。尽管博伊德证明了适应性取向和竞争节奏是操作优势的核心，但我们认为，这种理解应该扩大到认识到认知是一个生物心理社会和制度过程，在这个过程中，操作结果会递归地影响未来的决策。在这个框架内，在每个决策周期的执行过程中，认知生态系统的持续演变成为一个额外的操作变量。因此，决策优势将越来越依赖于保持机构理解和不断变化的作战环境之间的一致性。
人工智能在这一背景下具有重要意义，因为它能够实现持续观察、持续情境整合、预测分析和自适应决策支持
.在适当的管理下，这些能力使人类-人工智能团队能够在不断变化的作战条件和机构理解之间保持一致，同时保持判断、战略推理、道德审议、负责任的指挥和任务责任等不可或缺的人类角色。在这一范式中，人类认知和人工智能最好被视为适应性中相互补充的能力
.
更广泛地说，我们认为这种关系反映了指挥性质的演变。随着军事行动日益成为数据密集型、分布式和人工智能驱动的行动，指挥优势将更少地来自于加快孤立的个体决策周期，而更多地来自于互联人机之间认知的持续治理
.因此，未来的指挥控制体系结构应提高计算速度，同时保持指挥意图、机构理解、计算过程和环境变化之间的一致性。我们相信，人工智能战争中的决策优势将越来越依赖于这种同步认知能力，因此将时间同步视为认知治理的一个基本要素，通过认知治理，军事组织可以整合和维持人工智能，同时维护负责任的人类权威。
本文所表达的观点和意见是作者的观点和意见，并不一定反映美国政府、战争部或国防大学的意见。
约翰·默里（John Murray）先生是美国国防大学（National Defense University）国家战略研究所（Institute for National Strategic Studies）破坏性技术与未来战争项目（Program for Disruptive Technology and Future Warfare）的研究实习生，也是奥本大学（Auburn University）公共管理硕士项目的研究生。
埃莉斯·安内特博士是国防大学国家战略研究所破坏性技术和未来战争项目的研究员。
詹姆斯·乔尔达诺博士是国防大学国家战略研究所战略威慑和大规模杀伤性武器研究中心的负责人，并担任国防大学助理战争部长办公室（CBRN）的特别顾问。

_source.content:
Every competitive or conflictive human activity wields some form of power in attempt to affect
. Diplomacy seeks to influence it through politics; economic sanctions seek to modify it through the distribution and access of goods; military operations seek to compel it through the threat or use of force; and information operations seek to shape it through exerting influence upon thought, attitudes, values and emotion.  In all cases, whether acting upon policy makers, civilian populations, warfighters, and/or their commanders, all such strategic endeavors ultimately engage and operate through the human nervous system. Thus, the brain serves as the mediator of all enterprises of cooperation,or
.
Cognitive warfare certainly operates in and upon psychological and social dimensions of human action, but differs from historical forms of influence in the increasing ability to understand and exploit the neural substrates and mechanisms that contribute to, if not directly subserve thought, emotion, judgment, and
. Contemporary neuroscience provides an iteratively expanding set of intelligence, surveillance and reconnaissance (ISR) data of the biological “terrain and conditions” in which cognitive warfare could be
. We opine that the emergence of the brain-as-battlespace can be seen as a significant evolution in tactical nuance and strategic competition, as near future conflicts are likely to be defined and determined by who best employs such ISR to understand and influence the cognitive processes that shape human perception and action.
Neuroscientific studies have demonstrated that cognition occurs through dynamic interactions among distributed, networked systems of the brain, which coordinate activity to continuously integrate internal and
(for overview, see DiEuliis and Giordano). As schematically depicted in Figure 1, several neural systems are particularly relevant to cognitive warfare. Particularly, the salience network (which involves the anterior insula and anterior cingulate cortex) functions to identify information deemed important for survival and action. The default mode network supports self-referential thought, identity formation, memory integration, and narrative construction. Executive control networks (of the prefrontal cortex) are involved in planning, judgment, behavioral regulation, and decision-making; and limbic structures (e.g., the amygdala, hippocampus, and fornix) contribute to memory consolidation, threat detection, emotional processing, and affective learning, all of which evolved to support adaptive survival.
: Diagrammatic representation of major functional networks in the human brain. Note that while defined aggregates of neural nodes and assemblies subtend types of cognitive functions and activities, there is some overlap of different networks’ involvement of brain structures and regions.
Human cognition relies upon mental heuristics, biases, assumptions, and predictive mechanisms that frequently substitute accuracy for
. These adaptive features can be targeted as exploitable vulnerabilities, and cognitive warfare seeks to identify these substrates and leverage such susceptibilities.
One of the more influential models in contemporary neuroscience is predictive processing and coding theory, which establishes that the brain functions as an active prediction
. Accordingly, the brain continuously generates representations of reality and compares incoming information against those expectations such that perception becomes an act of prediction. Thus, individuals actively filter incoming information according to dispositions formed by prior experiences, extant beliefs, emotions, expectations, and sociocultural frameworks. When incoming information confirms dispositional biases and expectations, cognitive “flow” is consonant and perceptions remain stable; when information conflicts with expectations, a condition of cognitive dissonance occurs, and existing schemas of reality must be modified, and/or incoming information (and decision trajectories) must be adapted. This reflects the well-known
, and expands the construct to entails prior dispositions and biases, and the interpretive function of consequential effects of behavior (viz., a
; see Figure 2). This process is fundamental to understanding cognitive warfare.
Effect(s) of biases (B) and consequences (C) on patterns of observation (O), orientation (O) contributory to
neurocognitive processes of decision making (D) and resultant actions (A).  neurocognitive processes of decision making (D) and resultant actions (A). Iterative experience(s) establish dispositional cognitions (i.e., biases) against which cognitive engagements of present factors are compared and appraised (via Bayesian dynamics) to influence initiation, extent and type of observation(s) and evaluative orientation(s). Relative valence of orienting processes as relevant to current factors, and reflective of prior value-based (cognitively biased) recollections  (casuistically) inform and afford purchase to decisional options (that are weighted against prior experiential cognitions/memories, and their attendant emotional register) to (1) predict possible outcomes of different action effects and trajectories, and (2) compel action selection and execution. The (immediate and latent) consequences of action(s) are cognitively appraised relative to cognitive and emotional valences of prior experiences and actions. Consequences that are aligned with prior biases and expectations are positively reinforced, while those that are not prompt discordance. Additional details in text.
Influence operations succeed because information (positively or negatively) interacts with pre-existing cognitive architectures. Narratives that align with existing beliefs (i.e., which are cognitively consonant) can propagate rapidly. Information that challenges core constructs, values and/or identities (i.e., which are cognitively dissonant) may be rejected regardless of objective accuracy. Thus, successful cognitive engagement depends upon (1) understanding how brains construct reality, and (2) by controlling the information itself.
Trust determines whether information is accepted, rejected, amplified, or ignored, and thus one of the most important variables in cognitive warfare. Neuroscientific studies have demonstrated that feelings of trust occur through interactions of the brain’s mechanisms involved in social affiliation, group membership, cooperation, empathy, and collective
. Humans exhibit strong tendencies toward in-group preference and out-group disfavor, and these tendencies may be amplified during periods of uncertainty, perceived threat, or social instability.
Identity-based narratives, memes and semiotics exert influence because they engage these neural systems, and adversarial cognitive operations can exploit identity dynamics by targeting perceptions of belonging, legitimacy, victimization, grievance, and collective
. The objective is to alter the social and emotional frameworks through which reality is interpreted, and in this way, affect individual and collective action.
Neurocognitive processes can be targeted indirectly or
. Most current cognitive warfare activities operate indirectly, by manipulating socio-environmental inputs via information ecosystems (e.g., digital media, social networks, algorithmic recommendation systems, news platforms, entertainment channels, and interpersonal communication) to influence neural processing to affect behavior “downrange.” Emotional content activates attentional systems; threat-related information engages defensive circuitry; social validation or disruption differentially activates reward networks; and narratives shape memory consolidation. With robust and/or repeated exposure, these effects accumulate such that beliefs become reinforced, attitudes become entrenched, and behavioral tendencies can become
. This approach is a subtle, yet powerful feature of cognitive engagement, as it exploits natural neurocognitive mechanisms via indirect means that can be difficult to detect and directly attribute.
Although indirect approaches to cognitive warfare are currently predominant, emerging technologies are increasingly enabling more direct assessment and potential modulation of neural activity. For example, advances in multimodal neuroimaging (e.g., convergent use of functional magnetic resonance imaging [fMRI], functional near infrared imaging [fNIR], magnetoencephalography [MEG], high-density quantitative electroencephalography [qEEG]) now afford ability for increasingly detailed observation, analyses and correlation of brain structure and functions. Brain-computer interfaces (BCIs) afford tools for sophisticated communication between neural systems and computational platforms, and neural decoding methods have made it possible to identify brain nodes and networks involved in perception, attention, intention, emotional state, and decision-making that could be targeted and modulated using ever more specific drugs, toxins, microbes, and devices (e.g., directable sonic and/or electromagnetic
). While limitations remain, these developments illustrate a notable trend toward increasing ability to assess, access and affect neurocognitive processes. Tactically and strategically, this affords capability for more diversified, and thus greater means of influence.
The convergence of neuroscience, behavioral science, and computational analytics is transforming understanding and accessibility of human cognition at scale. Historically, neuroscientific research has focused upon individuals, with studies conducted in controlled environments. While valuable, these approaches can be inadequate for understanding how cognitive processes occur and manifest effect in large populations, and/or how collective behavior arises from individual
.
However, as we have
, big data methods and technologies are affording capabilities to accumulate, assimilate, synthesize and analyze a huge amount of vastly different types and levels of information. Artificial intelligence systems can analyze big datasets to identify behavioral patterns, cognitive/emotional tendencies, preferences, vulnerabilities and volatilities, and do so in ways that enable individual-to-group and group-to-individual comparisons and norming. For example, machine learning systems are capable of integrating biological, psychological, social, cultural, economic, and informational variables simultaneously to identify patterns, correlations, and predictive relationships within datasets.
The resulting capability is referred to as population
. Population neuroanalytics enable improved understanding of neural, psychological, and behavioral processes at scale by identifying recurring patterns and relationships between neural mechanisms, psychological tendencies, social interactions, and collective action(s). While totally accurate (viz., “perfect”) prediction remains unrealistic, ever more sophisticated probabilistic models are now achievable.
A next step beyond population neuroanalytics is development of synthetic cognitive modeling. Advances in computational neuroscience, agent-based modeling, machine learning, and digital-twin technologies are feasible for creating virtual representations of individuals, organizations, and populations. Of course, such models do not replicate actual brains, but instead afford simulacra of cognitive and behavioral tendencies based upon known relationships among neural, psychological, sociological, cultural, and environmental variables; the strategic utility of these systems is their ability to evaluate possible futures. Indubitably, all models possess limitations, and human behavior remains inherently complex, adaptive, and often unpredictable. Yet even imperfect predictive capability can afford significant strategic advantage, as synthetic cognitive environments may become indispensable tools for operational planning, deterrence and defense.
To wit, synthetic cognitive modeling can provide valuable capabilities within the cognitive domain, given that such models may enable identification of several factors and functions, as summarized in Table 1.
• Emerging social tensions
• Declining institutional trust
• Radicalization pathways
• Information contagion dynamics
• Social fragmentation indicators
• Cognitive resilience factors
• Decision-making vulnerabilities
• Behavioral responses to crises
In effect, the convergent use of big data techniques and tools, and AI enables far more nimble and thus functionally adaptive cognitive engagement, to instantiate a shift from mass persuasion toward precision influence. In this light, near future cognitive operations could be likened to precision-guided weaponry directed against specific targets rather than generalized assault.
However, target specificity does not negate the viability or value of more broadly directed targeting.  Indeed, the cognitive condition of populations can be a critical strategic variable and leveraging factor. Historically, the extrapolation of individual data to collective relevance has been difficult, given that no two brains are identical. Individuals differ genetically, developmentally, culturally, socially, and experientially. Moreover, collective behavior emerges through interactions among individuals rather than simple aggregation of individual traits. This complexity has limited attempts to extrapolate directly from neuroscience to population behavior. But the aforementioned scientific and technological developments are reducing, if not overcoming many of these impediments; and thus, the “brain-as-battlespace” of cognitive warfare is poised upon a cusp of capability.
Throughout history, military power has depended upon understanding critical domains of engagement and effect. To be sure, the aforementioned convergence of neuroscience, big data, AI, biotechnology, and information technology creates a new engagement environment that we believe could be regarded as the milieu of neurocognitive strategic competition. Currently, states that successfully integrate these disciplines could acquire unprecedented capabilities to understand and shape human thought and behavior. The implications extend beyond military operations. Political stability, economic confidence, social cohesion, and national resilience all depend upon such cognitive factors.
Accordingly, we argue that cognitive security must become a central component of national security. To remain apace of, if not preferably ahead of peer-competitors’ and adversarial developments, we advocate that the DoW should establish an interdisciplinary and operationally focused
. Toward such an enterprise, the following lines of effort are proposed:
1.
, to develop methods and improved tools to assess cognitive vulnerabilities and resilience across military forces, governmental institutions, and critical populations.
2.
, toward advancing understanding of relationships among neural architectures and mechanisms, cognitive processes, behavioral dynamics, social cohesion, and strategic stability.
3.
to create systems capable of monitoring evolving cognitive and emotional trends that are relevant to national security.
4.
to develop technologies that enhance decision-making while preserving human judgment and ethical oversight.
5.
aimed at identifying methods to strengthen resistance against manipulation, misinformation, coercion, and adversarial influence.
6.
to monitor global developments in neuroscience, neurotechnology, AI-enabled behavioral systems, and related dual-use capabilities.
7.
to develop rigorous methodologies for measuring cognitive effects and evaluating operational outcomes.
8.
ensuring responsible development and use of cognitive-security capabilities.
Toward achieving these ends, we offer the following recommendations:
1.
The DoW should establish a permanent cross-functional organization integrating expertise from neuroscience, behavioral science, biotechnology, AI, strategic deterrence, and military planning.
2.
A dedicated intelligence effort should continuously monitor foreign developments in neurotechnology, computational neuroscience, cognitive warfare, AI-enabled behavioral analytics, and related dual-use capabilities. Particular attention should focus upon activities conducted by China, Russia, Iran, and North Korea.
3.
The Department should establish secure infrastructures capable of integrating behavioral, informational, sociological, and neurocognitive datasets while maintaining appropriate legal and ethical safeguards. Such architectures will be essential for future cognitive-security operations and analyses.
4.
Training, education, leader development, and force-preparation programs should incorporate cognitive-security principles. The objective should be development of cognitively resilient personnel, organizations, and populations capable of recognizing and resisting adversarial influence efforts.
5.
Long-term investment is required. Short funding cycles are insufficient for sustained advancement in neuroscience and technology, big data, and AI. A dedicated research portfolio should be established comparable to historical investments in nuclear deterrence, cyber security, and biodefense.
The future of strategic competition will be defined and determined by the ability to understand, influence, protect, and defend the human cognitive processes that shape perception, judgment, decision-making, and behavior. Advances in neuroscience are revealing the neural substrates that are involved in and subserve thought, emotion, and action. Concomitant advances in big data and AI are enabling unprecedented capacity to examine relationships between individual cognition and collective behavior.
Taken together, these developments have established cognition as a domain of tactical accessibility, strategic relevance and operational viability and value. Adversaries recognize this reality and are actively pursuing capabilities designed to exploit cognitive vulnerabilities, manipulate perceptions, degrade trust, and influence thought, emotion and
. The U.S. cannot afford to regard such developments as merely academic or theoretical but instead should acknowledge and respond to such advancements as emerging risks and threats to national security. Thus, the challenge and opportunity for DoW is to strengthen the scientific, technological, operational, and ethical foundations necessary to successfully secure and protect the neurocognitive domain.
Indubitably, success of an enterprise of this magnitude will necessitate sustained investment, interdisciplinary collaboration, strategic foresight, and whole-of-nation
. As previous generations developed doctrines for nuclear deterrence, and biological and chemical weapons governance and control, we opine that it is now vital to develop a coherent doctrine of cognitive security and neurostrategic competition. For in this emerging environment, strategic advantage will increasingly belong to those who most effectively understand and protect the biological, psychological and social dimensions that influence human thought, emotion, judgment, and action.
The views and opinions expressed in this essay are those of the authors and do not necessarily reflect those of the United States government, Department of War, or the National Defense University.
Dr. James Giordano is Head of the Center for Strategic Deterrence and Study of Weapons of Mass Destruction, and Program Lead for Disruptive Technology and Future Warfare of the Institute for National Strategic Studies at the National Defense University. He is also Professor Emeritus of Neurology, Biochemistry, and Ethics at Georgetown University Medical Center.
Dr. Robert Schmidle (LtGen, USMC, ret) is a Professor of Professional Practice in the Irregular Warfare Center at the Arizona State University.
_source.movement_title: 美国智库建议国防部设立认知安全机构应对神经战略竞争
_source.movement_abstract: 美国国防大学国家战略研究所詹姆斯·吉奥尔达诺博士与罗伯特·施米德尔博士发表文章，提出将认知安全确立为国家安全核心组成部分。文章指出，随着神经科学、大数据与人工智能的融合，大脑已成为新的战略竞争领域，即“神经认知战略竞争”。对手正积极利用神经技术、计算神经科学及AI行为分析系统，针对人类认知漏洞进行操纵，以影响感知、判断及行为。文章建议美国国防部（DoW）建立跨职能常设组织，整合神经科学、行为科学、生物技术及AI专家。具体行动包括：开发评估认知脆弱性与韧性的工具；建立监测全球神经技术及AI行为系统发展的情报机制，重点关注中国、俄罗斯、伊朗及朝鲜的活动；构建安全基础设施以整合多源数据；将认知安全原则纳入人员培训与部队准备；设立长期研究投资组合以支持相关技术发展。文章强调，未来战略优势将取决于对生物、心理及社会维度的理解与保护能力，需制定类似核威慑的连贯认知安全学说。

Of course, such models do not replicate actual brains, but instead afford simulacra of cognitive and behavioral tendencies based upon known relationships among neural, psychological, sociological, cultural, and environmental variables; the strategic utility of these systems is their ability to evaluate possible futures. Indubitably, all models possess limitations, and human behavior remains inherently complex, adaptive, and often unpredictable. Yet even imperfect predictive capability can afford significant strategic advantage, as synthetic cognitive environments may become indispensable tools for operational planning, deterrence and defense.
To wit, synthetic cognitive modeling can provide valuable capabilities within the cognitive domain, given that such models may enable identification of several factors and functions, as summarized in Table 1.
• Emerging social tensions
• Declining institutional trust
• Radicalization pathways
• Information contagion dynamics
• Social fragmentation indicators
• Cognitive resilience factors
• Decision-making vulnerabilities
• Behavioral responses to crises
In effect, the convergent use of big data techniques and tools, and AI enables far more nimble and thus functionally adaptive cognitive engagement, to instantiate a shift from mass persuasion toward precision influence. In this light, near future cognitive operations could be likened to precision-guided weaponry directed against specific targets rather than generalized assault.
However, target specificity does not negate the viability or value of more broadly directed targeting.  Indeed, the cognitive condition of populations can be a critical strategic variable and leveraging factor. Historically, the extrapolation of individual data to collective relevance has been difficult, given that no two brains are identical. Individuals differ genetically, developmentally, culturally, socially, and experientially. Moreover, collective behavior emerges through interactions among individuals rather than simple aggregation of individual traits. This complexity has limited attempts to extrapolate directly from neuroscience to population behavior. But the aforementioned scientific and technological developments are reducing, if not overcoming many of these impediments; and thus, the “brain-as-battlespace” of cognitive warfare is poised upon a cusp of capability.
Throughout history, military power has depended upon understanding critical domains of engagement and effect. To be sure, the aforementioned convergence of neuroscience, big data, AI, biotechnology, and information technology creates a new engagement environment that we believe could be regarded as the milieu of neurocognitive strategic competition. Currently, states that successfully integrate these disciplines could acquire unprecedented capabilities to understand and shape human thought and behavior. The implications extend beyond military operations. Political stability, economic confidence, social cohesion, and national resilience all depend upon such cognitive factors.
Accordingly, we argue that cognitive security must become a central component of national security. To remain apace of, if not preferably ahead of peer-competitors’ and adversarial developments, we advocate that the DoW should establish an interdisciplinary and operationally focused
. Toward such an enterprise, the following lines of effort are proposed:
1.
, to develop methods and improved tools to assess cognitive vulnerabilities and resilience across military forces, governmental institutions, and critical populations.
2.
, toward advancing understanding of relationships among neural architectures and mechanisms, cognitive processes, behavioral dynamics, social cohesion, and strategic stability.
3.
to create systems capable of monitoring evolving cognitive and emotional trends that are relevant to national security.
4.
to develop technologies that enhance decision-making while preserving human judgment and ethical oversight.
5.
aimed at identifying methods to strengthen resistance against manipulation, misinformation, coercion, and adversarial influence.
6.
to monitor global developments in neuroscience, neurotechnology, AI-enabled behavioral systems, and related dual-use capabilities.
7.
to develop rigorous methodologies for measuring cognitive effects and evaluating operational outcomes.
8.
ensuring responsible development and use of cognitive-security capabilities.
Toward achieving these ends, we offer the following recommendations:
1.
The DoW should establish a permanent cross-functional organization integrating expertise from neuroscience, behavioral science, biotechnology, AI, strategic deterrence, and military planning.
2.
A dedicated intelligence effort should continuously monitor foreign developments in neurotechnology, computational neuroscience, cognitive warfare, AI-enabled behavioral analytics, and related dual-use capabilities. Particular attention should focus upon activities conducted by China, Russia, Iran, and North Korea.
3.
The Department should establish secure infrastructures capable of integrating behavioral, informational, sociological, and neurocognitive datasets while maintaining appropriate legal and ethical safeguards. Such architectures will be essential for future cognitive-security operations and analyses.
4.
Training, education, leader development, and force-preparation programs should incorporate cognitive-security principles. The objective should be development of cognitively resilient personnel, organizations, and populations capable of recognizing and resisting adversarial influence efforts.
5.
Long-term investment is required. Short funding cycles are insufficient for sustained advancement in neuroscience and technology, big data, and AI. A dedicated research portfolio should be established comparable to historical investments in nuclear deterrence, cyber security, and biodefense.
The future of strategic competition will be defined and determined by the ability to understand, influence, protect, and defend the human cognitive processes that shape perception, judgment, decision-making, and behavior. Advances in neuroscience are revealing the neural substrates that are involved in and subserve thought, emotion, and action. Concomitant advances in big data and AI are enabling unprecedented capacity to examine relationships between individual cognition and collective behavior.
Taken together, these developments have established cognition as a domain of tactical accessibility, strategic relevance and operational viability and value. Adversaries recognize this reality and are actively pursuing capabilities designed to exploit cognitive vulnerabilities, manipulate perceptions, degrade trust, and influence thought, emotion and
. The U.S. cannot afford to regard such developments as merely academic or theoretical but instead should acknowledge and respond to such advancements as emerging risks and threats to national security. Thus, the challenge and opportunity for DoW is to strengthen the scientific, technological, operational, and ethical foundations necessary to successfully secure and protect the neurocognitive domain.
Indubitably, success of an enterprise of this magnitude will necessitate sustained investment, interdisciplinary collaboration, strategic foresight, and whole-of-nation
. As previous generations developed doctrines for nuclear deterrence, and biological and chemical weapons governance and control, we opine that it is now vital to develop a coherent doctrine of cognitive security and neurostrategic competition. For in this emerging environment, strategic advantage will increasingly belong to those who most effectively understand and protect the biological, psychological and social dimensions that influence human thought, emotion, judgment, and action.

He is also Professor Emeritus of Neurology, Biochemistry, and Ethics at Georgetown University Medical Center.

影响行动之所以成功，是因为信息（积极或消极）与预先存在的认知架构相互作用。与现有信念一致的叙述（即认知上一致的）可以迅速传播。挑战核心结构、价值和/或身份（即，认知上不一致的）的信息可以被拒绝，而不管客观准确性如何。因此，成功的认知参与取决于（1）理解大脑如何构建现实，以及（2）控制信息本身。
信任决定了信息是否被接受、拒绝、放大或忽略，因此也是认知战中最重要的变量之一。神经科学研究表明，信任感是通过大脑机制的相互作用而产生的，这些机制涉及社会联系、群体成员、合作、移情和集体
.人类表现出对内群体偏爱和外群体厌恶的强烈倾向，这些倾向在不确定、感知威胁或社会不稳定时期可能会被放大。
基于身份的叙事、模因和符号学发挥影响，因为它们涉及这些神经系统，而对抗性认知操作可以通过针对归属感、合法性、受害、不满和集体的感知来利用身份动态
.其目标是改变解释现实的社会和情感框架，并以这种方式影响个人和集体行动。

.大多数当前的认知战活动都是通过信息生态系统（例如，数字媒体、社交网络、算法推荐系统、新闻平台、娱乐频道和人际交流）操纵社会环境输入，间接影响神经处理，从而影响“下游”行为。情绪内容激活注意系统；威胁相关信息参与防御电路；社会认可或破坏不同程度地激活奖励网络；和记叙文形成记忆巩固。随着强烈和/或重复的暴露，这些影响会累积，从而使信念得到强化，态度变得根深蒂固，行为倾向可能变得
.这种方法是认知参与的一个微妙而强大的特征，因为它通过难以检测和直接归因的间接手段来利用自然的神经认知机制。
尽管认知战争的间接方法目前占主导地位，但新兴技术正越来越多地实现对神经活动的更直接评估和潜在调节。例如，多模式神经成像的进步（例如，功能性磁共振成像[fMRI]、功能性近红外成像[fNIR]、脑磁图[Meg]、高密度定量脑电图[qEEG]的集中使用）现在提供了对大脑结构和功能进行越来越详细的观察、分析和关联的能力。脑机接口（BCI）为神经系统和计算平台之间的复杂通信提供了工具，神经解码方法使得识别涉及感知、注意、意图、情绪状态和决策的脑节点和网络成为可能，可以使用更具体的药物、毒素、微生物和设备（例如，定向声波和/或电磁
).虽然局限性仍然存在，但这些发展说明了一个显著的趋势，即评估、访问和影响神经认知过程的能力不断提高。在战术上和战略上，这提供了更多样化的能力，从而提供了更大的影响手段。
神经科学、行为科学和计算分析的融合正在大规模地改变人类认知的理解和可及性。从历史上看，神经科学研究的重点是个人，研究是在受控环境中进行的。虽然这些方法很有价值，但对于理解认知过程如何在大量人群中发生和表现出来的影响，以及/或者集体行为如何从个体中产生，这些方法可能是不够的
.
然而，正如我们所
此外，大数据方法和技术提供了积累、吸收、综合和分析大量不同类型和级别的信息的能力。人工智能系统可以分析大数据集，以识别行为模式、认知/情感倾向、偏好、脆弱性和波动性，并以能够进行个体与群体以及群体与个体的比较和标准化的方式进行。例如，机器学习系统能够同时整合生物、心理、社会、文化、经济和信息变量，以识别数据集中的模式、相关性和预测关系。
由此产生的能力称为人口。
.群体神经分析通过识别神经机制、心理倾向、社会互动和集体行动之间的重复模式和关系，能够提高对神经、心理和行为过程的理解。虽然完全准确（即“完美”）的预测仍然是不现实的，但现在可以实现更加复杂的概率模型。
超越人口神经分析的下一步是综合认知建模的发展。计算神经科学、基于主体的建模、机器学习和数字孪生技术的进步对于创建个人、组织和群体的虚拟表示是可行的。当然，这样的模型并不复制真实的大脑，而是提供基于神经、心理、社会、文化和环境变量之间已知关系的认知和行为倾向的拟像。这些系统的战略效用是它们评估可能的未来的能力。毫无疑问，所有模型都有局限性，而人类行为本质上仍然是复杂的、适应性的，而且常常是不可预测的。然而，即使是不完美的预测能力也可以提供显著的战略优势，因为合成认知环境可能成为作战计划、威慑和防御不可或缺的工具。
也就是说，综合认知建模可以在认知领域内提供有价值的能力，因为这样的模型可以识别几个因素和功能，如表1所示。
•新出现的社会紧张局势
•机构信任度下降
•激进化途径
•信息传染动态
•社会分化指标
•认知弹性因素
•决策漏洞
•对危机的行为反应
实际上，大数据技术和工具以及人工智能的融合使用使得认知参与更加灵活，从而在功能上具有适应性，这体现了从大众说服向精确影响的转变。在这种情况下，不久的将来，认知作战可以被比作针对特定目标的精确制导武器，而不是一般的攻击。
然而，靶标特异性并不否定更广泛定向靶向的可行性或价值。事实上，人口的认知状况可能是一个关键的战略变量和杠杆因素。从历史上看，鉴于没有两个大脑是完全相同的，将个体数据外推到集体相关性是很困难的。个人在遗传、发展、文化、社会和经验方面存在差异。此外，集体行为是通过个体之间的互动而产生的，而不是个体特征的简单聚合。这种复杂性限制了从神经科学直接外推到群体行为的尝试。但是，上述科学和技术发展正在减少，如果不是克服其中许多障碍的话。因此，认知战争的“作为作战空间的大脑”正处于能力的尖端。
纵观历史，军事力量依赖于对交战和效果的关键领域的理解。可以肯定的是，前面提到的神经科学、大数据、人工智能、生物技术和信息技术的融合创造了一个新的参与环境，我们认为这可以被视为神经认知战略竞争的环境。目前，成功整合这些学科的国家可以获得前所未有的能力来理解和塑造人类的思想和行为。其影响超出了军事行动的范围。政治稳定、经济信心、社会凝聚力和国家恢复力都取决于这些认知因素。
因此，我们认为认知安全必须成为国家安全的核心组成部分。为了保持快速发展，如果不是更好地领先于同行竞争对手和对手的发展，我们主张道琼斯指数应该建立一个跨学科和业务重点。
.为实现这一目标，提出了以下努力方向：
1.
开发方法和改进工具，以评估军队、政府机构和关键人群的认知脆弱性和复原力。
2.
促进对神经结构和机制、认知过程、行为动力学、社会凝聚力和战略稳定性之间关系的理解。
3.
创建能够监测与国家安全相关的不断变化的认知和情感趋势的系统。
4.
开发增强决策能力的技术，同时保留人类判断和道德监督。
5.
旨在确定加强对操纵、错误信息、胁迫和对抗性影响的抵制的方法。
6.
监测神经科学、神经技术、人工智能行为系统和相关双重用途能力的全球发展。
7.
开发用于测量认知效果和评估操作结果的严格方法。
8.
确保负责任地开发和使用认知安全能力。
为了实现这些目标，我们提出以下建议：
1.
陶氏化学应该建立一个永久性的跨职能组织，整合来自神经科学、行为科学、生物技术、人工智能、战略威慑和军事规划的专业知识。
2.
专门的情报工作应持续监测外国在神经技术、计算神经科学、认知战争、人工智能行为分析和相关军民两用能力方面的发展。应特别关注中国、俄罗斯、伊朗和朝鲜的活动。
3.
该部门应建立安全的基础设施，能够整合行为、信息、社会学和神经认知数据集，同时保持适当的法律和道德保障。这样的架构对于未来的认知安全操作和分析是必不可少的。
4.
培训、教育、领导者发展和部队准备计划应纳入认知安全原则。目标应该是培养具有认知弹性的人员、组织和人群，使其能够识别和抵制对抗性的影响。
5.
需要长期投资。短的融资周期不足以推动神经科学和技术、大数据和人工智能的持续发展。应建立与核威慑、网络安全和生物防御方面的历史投资相当的专门研究组合。
战略竞争的未来将由理解、影响、保护和捍卫塑造感知、判断、决策和行为的人类认知过程的能力来定义和决定。神经科学的进展正在揭示与思维、情感和行动有关并为其服务的神经基质。伴随而来的大数据和人工智能的进步，使得研究个体认知和集体行为之间关系的能力达到了前所未有的水平。
总之，这些发展已经将认知确立为战术可达性、战略相关性和作战可行性和价值的领域。对手认识到这一现实，并积极追求旨在利用认知弱点、操纵感知、降低信任和影响思想、情感和
.美国不能将此类发展仅仅视为学术或理论上的发展，而应承认并将此类发展视为对国家安全的新风险和威胁。因此，陶氏面临的挑战和机遇是加强必要的科学、技术、操作和伦理基础，以成功保护神经认知领域。
毫无疑问，这种规模的企业的成功将需要持续的投资、跨学科合作、战略远见和整个国家
.由于前几代人发展了核威慑以及生物和化学武器治理和控制的理论，我们认为，现在至关重要的是发展认知安全和神经战略竞争的连贯理论。因为在这种新兴环境中，战略优势将越来越多地属于那些最有效地理解和保护影响人类思想、情感、判断和行动的生物、心理和社会维度的人。
本文所表达的观点和意见是作者的观点和意见，并不一定反映美国政府、战争部或国防大学的意见。
詹姆斯·乔尔达诺（James Giordano）博士是战略威慑和大规模杀伤性武器研究中心（Center for Strategic Deterrence and Study of Weapons of Mass Destruction）的负责人，也是美国国防大学（National Defense University）国家战略研究所（Institute for National Strategic Studies）破坏性技术和未来战争项目负责人。他也是乔治敦大学医学中心神经病学、生物化学和伦理学的荣誉退休教授。
Robert Schmidle博士（LtGen，USMC，RET）是亚利桑那州立大学非常规战争中心的专业实践教授。
