Many have inevitably drawn comparisons with Russia’s invasion of Ukraine and the role played by fake separatist movements created by the Kremlin to justify Moscow’s expansionist agenda in eastern Ukraine’s Donbas region. When separatist propaganda about “People’s Republics” first began appearing in Ukraine in the years prior to the onset of Russian aggression in 2014, it was not initially taken seriously.
Recent references to a “Narva People’s Republic” appear to refer to the entire Ida-Viru County in northeastern Estonia rather than the city of Narva alone. Like Ukraine’s Donbas, Ida-Viru County was subject to an extended period of russification. During the Soviet occupation following World War II, large numbers of Russian-speakers from various parts of the Soviet Union were settled in Narva and in newly built Soviet industrial cities in the region.
With a current population that remains dominated by Russian-speakers and ethnic Russians, this would seem to make Ida-Viru County ripe for the Kremlin’s influence operations and grievance politics. However, the Estonian government has invested significantly in the region’s economic development and cultural integration.
Also, the fact that many residents of Estonia’s northeast have family links to Russia means they are well aware that they currently enjoy a far better standard of living than most people across the Narva River in the Russian Federation. With Estonia, like Ukraine, one must avoid the fallacy of conflating language with loyalty.
The fact that a grassroots separatist movement is unlikely to develop in Ida-Viru County will not necessarily prevent Russia from using the separatist narrative to advance its agenda. When efforts to cultivate a local separatist movement in the Donetsk and Luhansk regions of Ukraine proved insufficient in 2014, the Kremlin sent in Russian citizens and military personnel without insignia. Soon after, they were followed by an undeclared invasion force.
Russia’s goal in Estonia might not be military conquest. It is often suggested that Moscow could aim to test NATO’s collective security commitments and discredit the alliance by launching a relatively minor incursion and claiming a small chunk of Estonian territory on the pretext of protecting compatriots. _source.movement_title: 爱沙尼亚应对虚拟分离主义运动及俄方潜在渗透策略分析
_source.movement_abstract: 近期，爱沙尼亚社交媒体上出现所谓“纳尔瓦人民共和国”虚拟分离主义运动，其模式与2014年俄罗斯在乌克兰东部建立“人民共和国”相似。爱沙尼亚内政安全部门认定该运动为俄罗斯信息行动，但对外情报局质疑其是否涉及俄政府直接参与。记者调查发现该行动规模较小，疑似由圣彼得堡关联人员主导。爱沙尼亚东北部伊达-维鲁县因历史俄化政策存在俄语人口比例高的特点，但政府已通过经济和文化整合措施强化控制。居民普遍意识到自身生活水平远超对岸俄罗斯地区，语言与忠诚度不应混淆。尽管俄罗斯可能尝试通过小规模渗透测试北约反应，但爱沙尼亚评估2026年及未来一年内不会面临军事威胁。政府强调社会整体安全理念，反对将本国描绘为脆弱或依赖外部安全。北约盟友需保持警惕但避免过度反应，关注分离主义叙事在社交媒体中的传播趋势。
_source.post_location: 华盛顿特区西北L街1400号
_source.title: Could Russia use fake separatists to destabilize Estonia and discredit NATO?
_source.trans_cont:
最近几周，有关邻国爱沙尼亚亲俄分离主义运动的言论在社交媒体上频繁出现。所谓的“人民共和国”明显呼应了克里姆林宫在2014年春季俄罗斯入侵初期在乌克兰东部建立的“人民共和国”。然而，并非所有人都认为这个虚拟运动值得关注。

爱沙尼亚内部安全局近年来因其一系列成功行动而获得广泛尊重，该机构将“纳尔瓦人民共和国”倡议视为一项信息宣传活动。与此同时，爱沙尼亚对外情报局则怀疑有任何直接的俄罗斯政府参与。

一名来自爱沙尼亚报纸的记者最近成功加入了一个Telegram聊天群组，并揭露了“纳尔瓦人民共和国”实际上是由一个很可能位于爱沙尼亚境外、显然与圣彼得堡有联系的人所领导的小型行动。鉴于该行动规模较小，爱沙尼亚及社交媒体上对此是否值得强调展开了热烈的讨论。

许多人不可避免地将这一情况与俄罗斯入侵乌克兰以及克里姆林宫创建虚假分离主义运动以正当化莫斯科在乌克兰东部顿巴斯地区扩张主义议程的行为进行了比较。在2014年俄罗斯侵略开始前的几年里，有关“人民共和国”的分离主义宣传最初并未受到重视。

最近提到的“纳尔瓦人民共和国”似乎指的是爱沙尼亚东北部的伊达-维鲁县，而不仅仅是纳尔瓦市本身。与乌克兰的顿巴斯地区一样，伊达-维鲁县曾经历了一段长期的俄罗斯化。在二战后苏联占领期间，大量来自苏联各地的俄语使用者被安置在纳尔瓦以及该地区新建的苏联工业城市中。

目前，该地区的人口仍以俄语使用者和俄罗斯族人为主，这似乎使其成为克里姆林宫影响行动和煽动不满情绪的肥沃土壤。然而，爱沙尼亚政府在该地区的经济发展和文化融合方面投入了大量资源。

此外，许多爱沙尼亚东北部居民与俄罗斯有家庭联系，他们清楚地知道，他们目前的生活水平远高于俄罗斯联邦纳尔瓦河对岸的大多数人。正如乌克兰一样，必须避免将语言与忠诚混为一谈的谬误。

尽管基层分离主义运动在伊达-维鲁县不太可能发展起来，但这并不一定阻止俄罗斯利用分离主义叙事来推进其议程。当2014年在顿涅茨克和卢甘斯克地区培养本地分离主义运动的努力未能奏效时，克里姆林宫派遣了没有军衔的俄罗斯公民和军事人员。不久之后，他们被一支未宣而战的入侵部队所跟随。

俄罗斯在爱沙尼亚的目标可能并非军事征服。经常有人认为，莫斯科可能试图通过发动一次相对较小的入侵并声称占领爱沙尼亚一小块领土，以此来测试北约的集体安全承诺并损害联盟的声誉，借口是保护侨民。然而，鉴于爱沙尼亚的严格法律，即使是最小的违规行为也会受到严厉惩罚。在这种情况下，爱沙尼亚不会等待北约的反应。

爱沙尼亚官员对任何将该国描绘为特别脆弱或过度依赖他国安全的描述都极为敏感。自2014年俄罗斯入侵乌克兰以来，不断有各种问题询问“爱沙尼亚是否真的如此脆弱？”这种说法遭到了强烈的反对。

同样，爱沙尼亚官员批评了导致波罗的海地区迅速反应的军事演习，认为这些演习夸大了波罗的海国家自身的安全态势，甚至到了不切实际的地步。与邻近的芬兰、拉脱维亚和立陶宛一样，爱沙尼亚采用了一种“全社会参与”的安全概念，这一点不容忽视。

由于在乌克兰遭受了巨大的损失，俄罗斯军队目前被认为没有能力发动对爱沙尼亚的入侵。在2026年的年度报告中，爱沙尼亚对外情报局虽然清楚地认识到克里姆林宫的扩张野心，但评估认为，俄罗斯在本年度或很可能在下一年对任何北约成员国发动军事攻击的可能性极低。

难怪爱沙尼亚的外交和国防政策一直专注于团结支持乌克兰，以应对俄罗斯的侵略。也难怪俄罗斯的一些势力希望制造爱沙尼亚面临威胁的假象。迄今为止，爱沙尼亚对社交媒体上关于所谓分离主义运动的言论反应通常较为克制。随着这一叙事引起媒体关注，我们可以预期它会被进一步推动和重复。爱沙尼亚的北约盟友应效仿塔林的做法，保持警惕但冷静。

_source.evidence: 文章主要描述了俄罗斯利用社交媒体制造虚假的‘纳尔瓦人民共和国’分离主义运动，试图破坏爱沙尼亚稳定并抹黑北约。虽然文章涉及认知域（信息战、舆论操纵），但根据标签定义，[涉我事件] 特指涉及中国大陆（作为被攻击对象）的事件。本文中的被攻击对象是爱沙尼亚和北约，与中国大陆无直接关联。文章描述的是具体的舆论攻击行动（制造虚假分离主义运动），属于认知域对抗行动，因此最符合 [行动动向] 的定义（相关领域的具体作战、对抗等行动及其动向，如具体的舆论攻击行动）。

_source.content:
The end may be in sight for the current war in the Middle East, with its massive U.S. and Israeli air strikes on Iran and Iranian attacks on U.S. regional allies and Gulf shipping. Even then, however, hostilities may not stop. One plausible future scenario is that the Iranian regime and Israel remain in a state of low-level conflict that involves cyberattacks, sabotage, terrorism, and the occasional overt military strike, with the United States perhaps joining in from time to time. For Israel, this will be a way to keep Iran weak and off balance, while Tehran will be striking back out of vengeance, to legitimize its tottering regime, and to restore deterrence.
The future of the Iranian regime is unclear, but one plausible scenario—perhaps the most plausible—is that it will emerge from the war weak but unbowed, and perhaps even more radical. Regime change is possible but unlikely, and the decision to choose Mojtaba Khamenei, the son of assassinated Supreme Leader Ali Khamenei, as his successor signals defiance and a strong role for the hardline Islamic Revolutionary Guards Corps (IRGC).
This regime might retreat to a corner and lick its wounds, but it might also seek revenge. With U.S. intelligence assistance, Israel killed not only Ali Khamenei, but also Iran’s defense minister, the IRGC chief, and other senior officials—and these deaths are on top of the large numbers of security officials that Israel killed during the Twelve-Day War in 2025. Israel also decimated the leadership of key proxies, such as the Lebanese Hezbollah. In 2012, Iran and Hezbollah retaliated for the assassination of Iranian scientists by bombing a busload of Israeli tourists in Bulgaria. More recently, Iran has sought to assassinate senior U.S. officials involved in the 2020 killing of IRGC paramilitary leader Qassem Soleimani, among other retaliatory plots. Given the far greater scale of the 2025 and 2026 assassinations and the higher profile of those killed, Iran’s incentives for striking back are high.
If revenge is not enough of a motive, a desire to restore deterrence may be. In general, Iranian officials are likely to believe that there is nothing they can do to alleviate U.S. and Israeli hostility, so they must instead deter or degrade their enemies before receiving a fatal blow. Before the series of conflicts triggered by the Hamas terrorist attack on Israel on October 7, 2023, Iran relied on its vast missile and rocket arsenal and strong proxy groups to deter U.S. and Israeli attacks. Since then, Israel has decimated Hezbollah and Hamas, two of Iran’s most important proxies, and the 2025 and 2026 wars have destroyed or degraded much of Iran’s missile and rocket forces. Militarily, Iran is weak and seemingly at the mercy of its foes. Iran may continue to back proxies and use what limited stockpiles it has to ensure that Israel, the United States, and other perceived aggressors know that they will pay a price if they strike Iran. This may also include continued strikes on, or at least threats against, the Gulf states, so they lobby the United States to be more accommodating.
The biggest question mark is whether Iran will seek a nuclear weapon. On the one hand, much of Iran’s program is buried in the rubble of the 2025 U.S. and Israeli strikes, but U.S. and Israeli officials remain concerned that Iran could restart the program. Pursuing nuclear weapons would be a provocative step for Iran—Iran’s nuclear program helped spark two wars, after all. In the regime’s eyes, however, the U.S. abrogation of the Iran nuclear deal and subsequent attacks on Iran, even when Iran was not believed to be weaponizing its nuclear program, are proof that the United States and Israel are hostile. The regime might feel that it will be attacked regardless of whether it does or does not pursue nuclear weapons.
Finally, the postwar regime leaders may think that continued conflict is in their political interest. Even before the latest war, Iran faced rampant inflation, rising poverty, and other economic problems. These problems helped spark the massive protests throughout Iran that the regime suppressed brutally in January 2026. The destruction of the latest war will worsen this already disastrous situation. Having an external enemy, especially Israel and the United States, would be a way for the regime to justify repression at home and deflect blame for ongoing economic problems.
Just as Iran has reasons to keep the war going, so too does Israel. Israeli leaders seek to keep Iran and its proxies weak as long as the regime remains hostile. Well before October 7, Israeli leaders talked of the “campaign between the wars.” The idea is to disrupt enemy forces to prevent buildup, bolster deterrence to reduce the likelihood of attack, and develop operational and intelligence access should more force be needed. In practice, this has meant limited, and at times covert, attacks, including airstrikes, cyber operations, and other measures that make any future war more likely to go in Israel’s favor. For example, Israel targeted antiaircraft missiles going from Iran to the Lebanese Hezbollah via Syria in 2013 and conducted cyberattacks on Iranian nuclear facilities in 2021.
If Israel judges that Iran remains hostile, it is likely to conclude that a future war is probable and that more limited operations are necessary to ensure that Iran is weak and deterred and, should deterrence fail, faces defeat in any future war. Under this approach, Israel need not rely on Iran’s compliance with any ceasefire or diplomatic agreement. Instead, Israel can feel secure because its opponents are weak. Israel also emphasizes that it must restore deterrence, which it believes failed, thus allowing the October 7 attacks. Constant use of force makes clear that Israel will defend itself.
Israel is already applying this approach in Lebanon and Syria. Although the all-out war between Israel and Hezbollah ended in 2024, Israel has kept up airstrikes and assassinations as well as maintained a limited ground presence in Lebanon that has since grown in the latest round of conflict. In areas of Syria near the Israeli border, the Israeli military has conducted raids and seized weapons, and the Israeli Air Force has hit air defenses, military infrastructure, and other targets throughout Syria.
In the future, limited Israeli operations could reduce Iranian weapons stocks, destroy command infrastructure, and kill Iranian scientists and leaders. All this can be done largely by airstrikes, resulting in relatively few Israeli casualties and avoiding the diplomatic costs and on-the-ground complexities that come with occupying territory. Israeli leaders could also calibrate the operations according to their domestic political conditions and the tolerance of international partners.
Such an approach, however, necessitates additional attacks over time as Iran rebuilds. Iran, like Hamas in planning October 7, may also adapt and develop new methods of challenging Israel that existing defenses are not designed to counter. Israel’s strategy of repeated preventative strikes also risks feeding extremist narratives within Iran, discrediting moderates who might otherwise challenge the Iranian regime.
For the United States, the “wars after the war” would deepen a familiar alliance-management dilemma. Israel may prefer a strategy of repeated preventive blows to keep Iran and its proxies weak, while Gulf partners may want the United States to protect shipping and deter Iran so they can regain their status as safe havens for trade and investment. At the same time, Gulf partners likely want Washington to restrain Israel enough to avoid endless escalation that undermines trade, investment, and domestic stability.
Even if the United States tries to stay out of future rounds, Iran’s perception that the United States and Israel act in lockstep increases the risk to Washington. U.S. bases, commercial networks, diplomats, shipping, and perhaps the homeland itself would remain exposed to recurring harassment and retaliation.
Finally, such conflicts create a strategic distraction for Washington. A low-level Israel-Iran conflict would keep pulling Washington back into the region through air and missile defense, maritime protection, intelligence support, cyber defense, and occasional strikes. That would mean a continuing drain on senior policymakers’ attention, military assets, and munitions at a time when official U.S. strategy identifies homeland defense and deterring China as top priorities.
Daniel Byman is the director of the Warfare, Irregular Threats, and Terrorism Program at the Center for Strategic and International Studies in Washington, D.C.
_source.movement_title: 中东战后伊朗以色列低烈度冲突持续，美国陷入战略两难
_source.movement_abstract: 中东当前战争可能接近尾声，但美以对伊朗及伊朗对美以盟友的打击行动表明冲突或将转入低烈度阶段。伊朗政权可能在战争后更趋激进，通过网络攻击、破坏活动和偶发军事行动维持对抗。以色列则采取预防性策略，削弱伊朗及其代理武装力量，如黎巴嫩真主党。美国面临战略困境：既要支持以色列维持威慑，又要避免激化与海湾国家的矛盾。伊朗核问题存疑，尽管2025年打击行动损毁其核设施，但美以情报部门仍担忧其可能重启核计划。经济困境和2026年初的镇压抗议事件使伊朗政权更依赖外部敌人转移国内矛盾。以色列在黎巴嫩和叙利亚持续开展空袭和斩首行动，以消耗伊朗军力并降低未来战争风险。美国需在地区安全与战略资源分配间寻求平衡，避免陷入长期消耗战，同时应对中国等其他战略优先事项。

当前中东地区的战争可能接近尾声，美国和以色列对伊朗发动的大规模空袭，以及伊朗对美国地区盟友和海湾航运的攻击，都表明局势正在发生变化。然而，即使如此，敌对行动可能不会停止。一个合理的未来情景是，伊朗政权和以色列将保持一种低水平的冲突状态，包括网络攻击、破坏、恐怖主义以及偶尔的公开军事打击，美国也可能偶尔参与其中。对以色列而言，这是保持伊朗软弱和失衡的一种方式，而德黑兰则会出于复仇心理进行反击，以合法化其摇摇欲坠的政权，并恢复威慑力。

伊朗政权的未来尚不明确，但一个合理的场景——也许是最有可能的——是它将从战争中走出，虽然虚弱但依然强硬，甚至可能更加激进。政权更迭是有可能的，但可能性不大，而选择阿里·哈梅内伊之子莫塔哈里·哈梅内伊作为继任者，表明了对峙的意志和强硬派伊斯兰革命卫队（IRGC）的重要作用。

这个政权可能会退缩一隅，舔舐伤口，但也可能寻求报复。借助美国情报支持，以色列不仅杀死了阿里·哈梅内伊，还杀死了伊朗国防部长、IRGC负责人和其他高级官员，这些死亡人数还叠加了2025年十二日战争期间以色列杀死的大量安全官员。此外，以色列还摧毁了关键代理人组织的领导层，例如黎巴嫩真主党。2012年，伊朗和真主党因伊朗科学家被暗杀而报复，轰炸了一辆载有以色列游客的巴士。最近，伊朗试图暗杀参与2020年暗杀IRGC准军事领导人卡西姆·苏莱曼尼的美国高级官员，以及其他报复行动。鉴于2025和2026年暗杀行动的规模更大，以及被暗杀者的知名度更高，伊朗的报复动机非常强烈。

如果复仇不足以成为动机，恢复威慑力可能是一个原因。总体而言，伊朗官员可能认为他们无法缓解美国和以色列的敌意，因此必须在遭受致命打击前威慑或削弱敌人。在2023年10月7日哈马斯对以色列发动恐怖袭击引发一系列冲突之前，伊朗依靠其庞大的导弹和火箭弹库以及强大的代理人组织来威慑美国和以色列的攻击。此后，以色列摧毁了伊朗最重要的两个代理人组织——真主党和哈马斯，而2025和2026年的战争摧毁或削弱了伊朗大部分导弹和火箭弹力量。从军事角度来看，伊朗已经虚弱，似乎完全依赖于其对手。伊朗可能会继续支持代理人组织，并利用其有限的库存，以确保以色列、美国和其他被视为侵略者的国家知道，如果他们攻击伊朗，将付出代价。这可能还包括对海湾国家的持续袭击或至少威胁，以促使他们游说美国采取更加宽容的立场。

最大的疑问是伊朗是否会寻求核武器。一方面，伊朗的核计划大部分已被2025年美国和以色列的空袭摧毁，但美国和以色列官员仍担心伊朗可能重启该计划。追求核武器对伊朗来说是一个挑衅性的举动——伊朗的核计划实际上引发了两次战争。然而，在政权眼中，美国撕毁伊朗核协议并随后对伊朗发动攻击，即使当时伊朗并未被认定正在武器化其核计划，也证明了美国和以色列的敌意。政权可能认为，无论是否追求核武器，都将遭到攻击。

最后，战后政权领导人可能会认为，持续的冲突符合他们的政治利益。即使在最近的战争之前，伊朗就面临着严重的通货膨胀、贫困上升和其他经济问题。这些问题促成了2026年1月伊朗大规模抗议活动的爆发，而政权残酷地镇压了这些抗议活动。最近的战争破坏只会使这一已经灾难性的局势更加恶化。拥有外部敌人，尤其是以色列和美国，将是政权在国内镇压和转移经济问题责任的一种方式。

正如伊朗有理由继续战争一样，以色列也有同样的理由。以色列领导人希望在政权保持敌对态度的情况下，尽可能长时间地削弱伊朗及其代理人。早在10月7日之前，以色列领导人就谈论过“战间行动”。其想法是扰乱敌方力量，防止其增强，加强威慑以减少攻击的可能性，并在需要更多力量时发展操作和情报能力。实际上，这意味着有限的、有时是秘密的攻击，包括空袭、网络行动和其他措施，使未来战争更可能有利于以色列。例如，2013年，以色列针对从伊朗经叙利亚运往黎巴嫩真主党的防空导弹进行了打击，并在2021年对伊朗核设施进行了网络攻击。

如果以色列判断伊朗仍然敌对，它可能会得出未来战争可能发生，并且需要更有限的行动来确保伊朗软弱并受到威慑，如果威慑

In an industrial zone on the outskirts of Abu Dhabi, Emirati state-backed artificial intelligence (AI) company G42 has poured 100,000 cubic meters of concrete to
a cluster of data centers the size of Berkeley, California. The campus will use NVIDIA chips and Oracle cloud services. It will
a region-specific version of ChatGPT across the government and vital sectors. It is the
AI infrastructure project outside the United States, and it’s built on US technology.
Five hundred miles to the west, in Riyadh, the Saudi company Humain has broken ground on its own vast national AI project. US infrastructure
this project, too. NVIDIA and Qualcomm provide the chips, Amazon the cloud, and Cisco the networking.
And in the Negev desert, the United States is
four thousand acres to build Fort Foundry One, a joint Israeli-US tech and industrial park for advanced computing, semiconductor production, and AI development.
The United States, through government and industry, is building an AI infrastructure alliance in the Middle East, and it may write the next chapter of regional integration.
These projects represent a realization that AI, the technology powering the fourth industrial revolution, will define the twenty-first century. A World Economic Forum study estimates that AI will
14 percent of global gross domestic product (GDP) by 2030. Countries will need access to cloud and compute like they need water and power plants. And they are turning to US companies to provide it.
A creative blend of diplomacy and economic policy has facilitated these developments. Last year, the State Department unveiled
, a new coalition of countries working together to secure access to AI inputs, from critical minerals to semiconductors. The Commerce Department, for its part,
a program to promote AI exports and
the sale of advanced chips to the United Arab Emirates (UAE) and Saudi Arabia.
In combination, these initiatives aim to pool the contributions of trusted nations, yielding a secure supply chain that produces data centers running on US chips and applications built on the United States’ foundational models. In this vision, US systems will form the bedrock of the world’s AI, much as the world
on Microsoft software when computers reached mass adoption. The new alliance also mitigates reliance on China, which
nearly 80 percent of the world’s silicon, the building block for AI chips.
For the partner countries, Pax Silica and its related initiatives offer an invitation into the United States’ AI tent. The participating countries are betting that the United States will build the best infrastructure, and they are counting on Washington to keep providing partners with largely open access to chips rather than reverting to stricter export rules with more conditions and caps.
This carries profound implications for the Middle East. Among Pax Silica’s twelve signatories are three of the Middle East’s four AI leaders: Israel, the UAE, and Qatar. The fourth, Saudi Arabia, hasn’t joined yet, but it already relies heavily on US chips and cloud.
All four countries are racing to embed AI into their national infrastructure to secure their economic futures. Each brings different strengths to AI development. And they’re all looking to the United States for the anchor technology. This dynamic opens a new track for regional integration.
In the near term, the United States should establish the Middle East as a hub for American-led AI. This would deepen Washington’s bilateral relationships in the region as partner countries use US models and chips to build applications for their critical sectors.
Israel is set to grow from startup nation to indispensable tech infrastructure ally. The US-led supply chain will benefit from Israeli chip design, cloud security, and AI applications. Next year, NVIDIA will start
a campus in Kiryat Tiv’on for chip research, further establishing Israel as its largest research-and-development base outside the United States.
Meanwhile, the UAE is using its capital, land, and energy to build some of the biggest compute hubs in the world, anchoring a push to apply AI across the country. Saudi Arabia is also building sovereign infrastructure to apply AI across sectors, transforming an economy that today relies on oil and gas for
of its GDP. The Iran war’s disruption to the flow of physical goods through the Strait of Hormuz validates the Gulf countries’ plans to make advanced technology a centerpiece of their economic diversification.
Under these initiatives, a new type of bloc will likely emerge in the region—one that aligns with the United States for core economic interests, not just national security interests. Each member of the bloc will see the incentive to preserve the new US-led tech order.
This lays a foundation for cooperation between the members. The UAE-Israel relationship offers a natural place to start. After the signing of the Abraham Accords in 2020, Israel-UAE bilateral trade
in 2022 and has
in years since. The relationship will expand to include AI infrastructure collaboration. For example, Emirati hospitals could feed patient scans into an Israeli oncology model, building a new system for cancer detection.
In the long term, American tech leadership holds the promise of slowly deepening the Saudi-Israeli relationship beyond security coordination to encompass economic cooperation. For now, full Saudi-Israeli diplomatic normalization will have to wait. Crown Prince Mohammed bin Salman already reached a defense agreement with the United States and acquired access to the most advanced US chips without making concessions on normalization. And Saudi domestic politics remain too difficult for normalization without movement on the Palestinian issue. AI’s promise will not override these persistent geopolitical realities.
But opportunities for limited cooperation will emerge, and the United States should serve as the bridge, advancing the principles of the Abraham Accords even before their formal expansion. Israel and Saudi Arabia can cooperate indirectly on AI infrastructure in the absence of diplomatic relations by working through American companies. Every step toward interconnected economic infrastructure builds the incentive to protect that infrastructure, driving momentum for further cooperation in a way that diplomatic and security ties alone cannot.
When Egyptian President Anwar Sadat addressed Israel’s Knesset in 1977, taking the first step towards the first Arab-Israeli peace treaty, he focused squarely on peace and security. He didn’t invoke economic cooperation. In the 1994 Israel-Jordan peace treaty, the countries did agree to economic cooperation in the form of trade and water sharing, but the deal centered on security.
The leaders behind those deals pursued peace at the diplomatic level. Any economic cooperation would have been a bonus. They likely didn’t imagine a day when a new technology would define power and prosperity in the Middle East and encourage deep economic integration among former adversaries.

_source.movement_title: 美国与中东国家共建AI基础设施联盟
_source.movement_abstract: 文章介绍了美国与中东多国合作建设AI基础设施的项目。阿布扎比的G42公司建设大型数据中心集群，使用NVIDIA芯片和Oracle云服务；沙特Humain公司启动国家级AI项目，同样依赖美国芯片和云服务；以色列与美国合作建设Fort Foundry One科技园区。美国通过外交与产业政策推动Pax Silica联盟，联合以色列、阿联酋、卡塔尔等国构建基于美国技术的AI供应链体系。这些项目旨在减少对中国半导体的依赖（中国目前占据全球80%硅供应），通过共享算力基础设施深化区域经济整合。文章指出，AI技术将重塑21世纪经济格局，预计2030年贡献全球GDP的14%。中东国家正通过AI基础设施合作推动经济转型，例如阿联酋发展医疗AI应用，沙特推进能源产业AI化。尽管沙特与以色列尚未实现全面外交关系正常化，但可通过美国企业间接开展AI技术合作。这种以经济利益为核心的新型技术联盟，为中东国家间合作提供了新路径，但受制于巴勒斯坦问题等传统地缘政治因素。
_source.post_location: 华盛顿特区西北L街1400号
_source.title: American AI leadership can open a new chapter for Middle East integration
_source.trans_cont:
在阿布扎比郊区的工业区，由阿联酋支持的AI公司G42正在为一个相当于加州伯克利大小的数据中心群浇筑10万立方米的混凝土。该园区将使用NVIDIA芯片和Oracle云服务，并将在政府和关键领域部署ChatGPT的地区版本。这是美国以外的AI基础设施项目，其技术基础来自美国。
在500英里以西的利雅得，沙特公司Humain已开始建设其庞大的国家AI项目。该项目同样依赖美国的基础设施。NVIDIA和Qualcomm提供芯片，亚马逊提供云服务，思科提供网络服务。
而在内盖夫沙漠，美国正在为建设占地四千英亩的Fort Foundry One，一个联合以色列和美国的高科技和工业园区，用于先进计算、半导体制造和AI开发。通过政府和产业，美国正在中东建设一个AI基础设施联盟，这可能会书写区域一体化的新篇章。
这些项目体现了对AI技术的共识，即AI作为第四次工业革命的核心技术，将定义21世纪。世界经济论坛的一项研究估计，到2030年，AI将贡献全球GDP的14%。各国将需要像水和发电站一样依赖云和计算资源，而他们正转向美国公司来提供这些资源。
外交与经济政策的巧妙结合促成了这些发展。去年，国务院推出了“Pax Silica”，一个新的国家联盟，旨在确保对AI输入资源（从关键矿产到半导体）的访问。商务部则推出了一个促进AI出口和向阿联酋和沙特阿拉伯出售先进芯片的计划。
这些举措旨在汇集可信赖国家的贡献，建立一个安全的供应链，生产运行在美国芯片上的数据中心和基于美国基础模型的应用程序。在这个愿景中，美国系统将成为全球AI的基石，正如世界在计算机普及时依赖微软软件一样。新的联盟也减少了对中国（占全球近80%的硅，即AI芯片的基础）的依赖。
对于参与国家而言，“Pax Silica”及其相关举措邀请它们加入美国的AI阵营。参与国家相信美国将建设最好的基础设施，并依赖华盛顿继续为合作伙伴提供开放的芯片访问，而不是重新实施更严格的出口规则。
这对中东地区具有深远影响。在“Pax Silica”的十二个签署国中，有三个中东AI领导者：以色列、阿联酋和卡塔尔。第四个，沙特阿拉伯尚未加入，但其已严重依赖美国芯片和云服务。
这四个国家都在努力将AI嵌入国家基础设施，以确保其经济未来。每个国家在AI发展方面都有不同的优势，他们都依赖美国提供核心技术。这种动态为区域一体化开辟了新的路径。
短期内，美国应将中东确立为美国主导的AI枢纽。这将加深华盛顿与该地区伙伴国家的双边关系，因为这些国家使用美国模型和芯片来为其关键领域构建应用。
以色列将从初创国家发展为不可或缺的科技基础设施盟友。美国主导的供应链将受益于以色列的芯片设计、云安全和AI应用。明年，NVIDIA将在基里亚特·提维翁开设一个芯片研究校园，进一步确立以色列作为其最大的海外研发基地。
与此同时，阿联酋正利用其资本、土地和能源建设世界上最大的计算中心之一，推动AI在国家范围内的应用。沙特阿拉伯也在建设主权基础设施，以在各个领域应用AI，转型其目前依赖石油和天然气占其GDP大部分的经济。伊朗战争对霍尔木兹海峡货物流动的干扰，验证了海湾国家将先进技术作为经济多元化核心的计划。
在这些倡议下，该地区可能会出现一种新的联盟——这种联盟基于核心经济利益与美国结盟，而不仅仅是国家安全利益。每个成员都将看到维护新美国主导的科技秩序的激励。
这为成员之间的合作奠定了基础。阿联酋与以色列的关系是一个自然的起点。在2020年亚伯拉罕协议签署后，以色列和阿联酋双边贸易在2022年增长，并在之后几年持续增长。两国关系将扩展到包括AI基础设施合作。例如，阿联酋的医院可以将患者扫描数据输入以色列的肿瘤模型，建立新的癌症检测系统。
长期来看，美国的科技领导地位有望逐步加深沙特和以色列之间的关系，超越安全协调，涵盖经济合作。目前，沙特和以色列的全面外交正常化仍需等待。王储穆罕默德·本·萨勒曼已与美国达成防务协议，并获得最先进的美国芯片，而无需在正常化上做出让步。此外，沙特国内政治仍过于复杂，除非巴勒斯坦问题有所进展，否则无法实现正常化。AI的前景无法改变这些持续的地缘政治现实。
但有限合作的机会将出现，美国应作为桥梁，推动亚伯拉罕协议的原则，甚至在正式扩展之前。在没有外交关系的情况下，以色列

In 2019, the author, with Arnel David, argued that the United States military’s conception of lethality was dangerously narrow—focused almost exclusively on kinetic destruction while neglecting strategic influence as a decisive instrument of war. That argument has been validated by events: adversaries have waged and won influence campaigns at a fraction of the cost of conventional warfare, while the United States has continued to pay an astronomical bill for kinetics-first strategies with diminishing strategic returns. This article revisits and builds on the 2019 thesis, surveys the strategic ledger since then, and introduces the Power and Ideology Lethality (PIL) simulation platform—a new analytical tool designed to help practitioners plan, assess, and wargame influence competition as a core component of lethal strategy.
In February 2019, the author, with Arnel David,
in these pages that the United States military’s understanding of lethality was dangerously incomplete. The concept had become a defining priority of the Department of Defense (DoD)—appearing across modernization strategies, acquisition frameworks, and doctrinal literature—yet it was treated almost exclusively as a physical phenomenon: the ability to find, fix, and destroy enemy forces. We argued then that this was insufficient. To view lethality only through a physical lens limits its full potential. Lethality at the strategic level, we contended, must also include the capacity to break an adversary’s will to fight. And that capacity is increasingly exercised not through firepower, but through influence. We have used influence to support kinetic action. This paper argues that this order of events is inverted: kinetic action should operate within the framework of strategic influence, not the other way around.
The strategic competition between the United States and its rivals has intensified. The cost of kinetic warfare—in blood, treasure, and strategic credibility—has grown exponentially. Meanwhile, peer and near-peer competitors have continued to invest heavily in influence-based strategies, reshaping political environments, undermining alliances, and projecting power without firing a shot. The gap between what the United States understands as lethality and what its adversaries practice as strategy has not closed. If anything, it has widened.
This piece returns to the 2019 argument—not to relitigate it, but to stand on it and build on it. The world has changed in ways that make our original warning more urgent. We survey those changes, examine the cost of inaction, and introduce a new analytical tool—the Power and Ideology Lethality (PIL) simulation platform—designed to help practitioners think about influence lethally and strategically. PIL is the doctrinal equipment this argument demands.
The 2019 article identified a fundamental conceptual failure in the DoD’s understanding of its own organizing principle. The term
had become something everyone claimed to understand, but no one could coherently define. In practice, it defaulted to the physical and the tactical: weapons systems, targeting speed, and force protection. What was missing was any serious reckoning with lethality at the strategic level—the capacity not simply to destroy enemy forces, but to compel an enemy to stop fighting.
Here is the inversion that the 2019 article pointed toward, and that the intervening years have confirmed: kinetic operations do not achieve strategic decisions on their own. They set the conditions under which influence achieves a decision. If the strategic return on kinetics has been inadequate despite overwhelming physical success—and it has been, repeatedly—then the physical is no longer the decisive variable. It is the setup for the influence punch. The most expensive bill in modern military history was run up by a doctrine that had the sequence backwards.
Wars are not decided by the annihilation of forces alone. As we saw in Iraq, the destruction of the Iraqi Army only led to a prolonged asymmetric war. Wars end when one side concludes that the contest is no longer worth its cost. The will to fight—an adversary’s political resolve, domestic legitimacy, coalition cohesion, and narrative control of the conflict—is therefore as much a target as any weapons system. And influence, properly understood, is the mechanism through which that target is engaged.
We defined strategic influence as the use of the elements of national power—diplomatic, military, economic, with and through information—to shape the information and operational environment to erode the enemy’s will. Lt. Gen. (ret.) James Dubik
foreign influence operations as the single most important strategic-level preparation that civilian and military leaders must make for the next war. The Special Operations Forces community understood this instinctively and through decades of experience. The rest of the joint force had not caught up.
That diagnosis has not changed. What has changed is the price of ignoring it.
The years since 2019 have provided a running demonstration of influence lethality in action—mostly by adversaries.
Russia’s renewed invasion of Ukraine in February 2022 combined kinetic operations with an information campaign of considerable sophistication. Moscow sought to fracture Western coalition support, delegitimize the Ukrainian government, and shape the information environment both domestically and internationally—sustaining the Russian will to fight while eroding it elsewhere. The kinetic campaign has been costly and, in many respects, underperforming. The influence campaign has been more durable: exploiting fault lines in Western publics, amplifying war fatigue, and contesting the narrative architecture of the conflict across multiple platforms simultaneously.
China, meanwhile, has
a long-game strategy of displacing American influence—not primarily through force, but through economic leverage, technological dependency, institutional access, and narrative shaping. The Confucius Institute case warrants a label it rarely receives: Lethal Influence in the homeland. China invested systematically in educational and cultural influence operations at American universities for nearly two decades, reshaping curricula, suppressing discussion of sensitive topics, and curating a generation of students’ understanding of China—without a single shot fired on American soil. As Bottomley
, by 2023, fewer than five of the roughly 100 Confucius Institutes once operating on US campuses remained—not because China’s strategy failed, but because American institutions finally recognized what was happening and moved to close them. The asymmetry is stark: China spent an estimated $8 billion on public diplomacy in 2020 alone, compared to roughly $2 billion by the United States. The competition for influence is not hypothetical. It is funded, structured, and ongoing—and it reaches inside US borders.
Non-state actors have not stood still either. Violent extremist organizations, criminal networks, and proxy forces continue to demonstrate that narrative warfare—the contest over who controls the meaning of events—can be as strategically consequential as any kinetic operation. Recruitment, radicalization, and the erosion of state legitimacy in contested spaces remain influence-driven phenomena.
The cost of kinetic approaches, meanwhile, has become impossible to ignore. Vietnam received 13 million tons of high explosives—more than six times the weight dropped in all theaters during World War II. The United States killed an estimated one to two million people. It lost the war. Iraq and Afghanistan produced variations on the same lesson: tactical lethality delivered at enormous cost produced no strategic decision. The physical destruction of forces does not compel adversaries to abandon political objectives. It may, in fact, harden them—generating civilian casualties that fuel hostile narratives, strengthen recruitment, and sustain the will to fight against the United States.
The bill for a kinetics-first strategy is astronomical. The strategic return has been inadequate. And yet the conceptual framework that produced these outcomes—lethality as destruction—persists.
It would be a mistake to conclude that the United States does not engage in influence operations. It does—extensively. Public diplomacy, information operations, strategic communications, civil affairs, psychological operations, and foreign internal defense are all influence activities conducted worldwide by the U.S. government and military elements.
The problem is doctrinal, not operational. The United States does not consider these activities to be lethal. They are treated as supporting efforts—force multipliers at best, soft-power adjuncts at worst—rather than as core instruments of strategic compellence. The planning architecture, resource allocation, and assessment frameworks of the US military continue to treat kinetic action as the decisive variable and influence as the supporting one. The strategic logic runs backward.
The gray zone—that contested space of competition below the threshold of conventional conflict—is fundamentally an influence environment. Gray zone operations
political objectives through integrated campaigns, mostly using nonmilitary tools, operating below key escalatory thresholds, moving gradually toward objectives rather than seeking rapid, decisive results. Adversaries have designed their strategies around this space precisely because US conventional superiority makes direct military confrontation unattractive. That workaround is effective because the United States has no coherent strategic framework for competing in it.
Countering gray zone competition requires treating influence as a lethal instrument: targeted, resourced, assessed, and integrated into strategic planning at the same level as kinetic capabilities. The US military does not currently do this. What it needs is not more influence activity. It needs a doctrinal architecture—and analytical tools—that make influence legible as a form of lethality.
Recognizing a problem is not enough. Practitioners need equipment. The Power and Ideology Lethality (PIL) Simulation Platform is equipment—built specifically to operationalize what this article argues and to give intelligence (S-2) and operations (S-3) staffs a rigorous framework for planning, assessing, and wargaming influence competition alongside kinetic operations.
PIL is a theory-driven, agent-based geopolitical simulation engine that
the behavior of nation-states and other actors across the full spectrum of competitive instruments—not just kinetic military action, but diplomatic, economic, informational, cyber, technological, space, and gray-zone operations. The architecture embodies the argument: influence operations are not peripheral categories in PIL. They are first-class domains, treated as structurally equivalent to kinetic action in the model’s move-selection logic. A narrative legitimacy strike can be more strategically permanent than a sunk ship. PIL is designed to see both and to assess both on the same strategic terms.
Consider a concrete example. A challenger state operating as a ‘regional patron’ deploys a sequence of economic coercion moves, coordinated information operations, and proxy pressure against a US partner nation—incrementally eroding that partner’s will to host U.S. basing rights, without ever crossing the threshold of armed conflict. Traditional wargaming struggles to model this: the moves are non-kinetic, the effects are political and psychological, and the timeline is measured in months or years rather than hours. PIL models the full move sequence, assesses the legitimacy and coalition coherence costs at each step, and surfaces the countermove options available to the United States and its partners—including influence countermoves that legacy planning tools cannot represent.
PIL is built on role theory as developed in international relations scholarship. States do not simply maximize interests—they perform roles. A hegemon, a challenger, a spoiler, a regional patron: each role carries behavioral expectations, resource constraints, and characteristic move repertoires. PIL models 15 such roles, and role assignment can change dynamically during a simulation in response to external shocks, resource depletion, or competitive pressure. Delegitimizing an adversary’s claimed role is itself a form of strategic lethality—and PIL makes that target visible and plannable.
PIL also incorporates a modernized event ontology—the Policy Instrument and Leadership Observatory Taxonomy (PILOT)—that substantially expands the legacy Conflict and Mediation Event Observations (CAMEO) coding framework. CAMEO was built for a different world: it could not code a state-sponsored botnet operation, a supply chain coercion move, a coordinated influence campaign, or an electronic warfare event, because those categories did not exist in its ontology. Keeping CAMEO as the analytical standard for event data in 2026 is analogous to navigating great-power competition with a map drawn before the internet existed. PILOT
native vocabulary for all these domains. It gives analysts the language to see what legacy frameworks could not.
One concern the 2019 article raised directly bears repeating here: artificial intelligence (AI) and machine-learning tools must be held suspect until vetted. PIL is not a black box. It is a transparent, theory-driven platform in which every move, every probability weight, and every outcome can be traced back to its underlying logic. A commander does not have to trust an algorithm—they can interrogate the model’s reasoning at every step. PIL supplements human expertise; it does not supplant it. Scenario outputs can be shared and audited as readily in a spreadsheet, making the platform accessible to the analyst and commander alike. This is explainable AI in the service of strategic judgment, not a replacement for it.
In 2019, we warned that an exclusively physical understanding of lethality was insufficient for the strategic environment the United States faced. That warning was not heeded with the urgency the situation demanded. The years since have supplied the evidence.
Competitors have continued to invest in influence-based strategies. The cost of kinetics-first campaigns has mounted. The gap between what the United States understands as lethality and what its adversaries practice as strategy remains dangerously wide. And the institutional culture of the DoD—its planning frameworks, resource priorities, and assessment architectures—continues to treat influence as a supporting capability rather than a decisive one.
The argument is not that kinetic force is irrelevant. It is that kinetic force is insufficient—and that a strategic culture which cannot conceive of influence as lethal will continue to spend enormously, fight hard, and struggle to achieve decisive outcomes. The inversion must be completed: kinetics sets the conditions; influence achieves the decision.
Wars end when one side decides to quit the field. The objective of the strategy is to compel that decision. In the 21st century, the most powerful mechanisms for achieving that objective are often not weapons. They are narratives, networks, legitimacy, and the sustained shaping of the information environment. The most decisive blows may be struck not with weapons, but with influence. Building the doctrine, the institutions, and the analytical tools to deliver those blows strategically is the most important work the US military has left undone. PIL is the weapons system for that fight.
_source.movement_title: 战略影响力与动能：重新定义杀伤力的新框架PIL平台
_source.movement_abstract: 文章指出美国国防部对杀伤力的理解存在根本性缺陷，过度依赖动能摧毁而忽视战略影响力。2019年作者与Arnel David提出这一观点，后续事件验证了该论断：俄罗斯在乌克兰战争中通过信息战削弱西方联盟支持，中国通过长期经济文化渗透削弱美国影响力，非国家行为体则通过叙事战争影响战略目标。文章强调战略影响力应与动能行动同等重视，因为战争胜负取决于削弱对手战斗意志而非单纯物理摧毁。美国当前军事规划仍将影响力建设视为辅助手段，导致战略回报不足。为此，作者介绍了Power and Ideology Lethality (PIL)模拟平台，该工具基于国际关系角色理论，可对经济胁迫、信息战、灰区竞争等非动能手段进行建模评估，使影响力成为战略决策的核心要素。PIL采用PILOT事件分类体系，突破传统CAMEO框架局限，并通过透明算法实现可解释的人工智能分析，帮助美军完善战略影响力规划框架。
_source.title: Information Lethality Revisited: Strategic Influence and the Future of War
_source.trans_cont:
2019年，作者与Arnel David共同提出，美国军方对致命性的理解过于狭隘，几乎只关注动能破坏，而忽视了战略影响力作为战争决定性工具的重要性。这一观点已被现实所验证：对手通过低成本的影响力行动赢得了战争，而美国却继续为以动能为主的策略支付高昂代价，且战略回报却在下降。本文重新审视并发展了2019年的论点，回顾了此后战略局势的变化，并介绍了“权力与意识形态致命性”（PIL）模拟平台——一种新的分析工具，旨在帮助从业者将影响力竞争作为致命性战略的核心组成部分进行规划、评估和模拟推演。
2019年2月，作者与Arnel David在这些页面上指出，美国军方对致命性的理解存在严重缺陷。这一概念已成为国防部（DoD）的核心优先事项——出现在现代化战略、采购框架和理论文献中——但几乎只被当作一种物理现象：找到、锁定并摧毁敌方力量的能力。我们当时认为，这种理解是不够的。仅通过物理视角看待致命性会限制其全部潜力。在战略层面，致命性还应包括打破对手战斗意志的能力。而这种能力越来越多地不是通过火力，而是通过影响力来实现。我们已将影响力用于支持动能行动。本文认为，这一顺序是颠倒的：动能行动应在战略影响力框架内进行，而不是相反。
美国与竞争对手之间的战略竞争日益激烈。动能战争的成本——在生命、财富和战略信誉上的代价——呈指数级增长。与此同时，竞争对手继续大量投资于基于影响力的策略，重塑政治环境，削弱联盟，且无需开火即可展示力量。美国对致命性的理解与对手实际运用的策略之间的差距并未缩小，反而进一步扩大。
本文回到2019年的论点——不是为了重演，而是站在其基础上进行扩展。世界的变化使我们最初的警告更加紧迫。我们回顾这些变化，审视不作为的成本，并介绍了一种新的分析工具——“权力与意识形态致命性”（PIL）模拟平台，旨在帮助从业者以致命和战略的方式思考影响力。PIL是这一论点所要求的理论装备。
2019年的文章指出了国防部对其自身组织原则理解中的根本概念性失败。该术语已成为每个人都声称理解，但无人能清晰定义的概念。实际上，它默认为物理和战术层面：武器系统、目标锁定速度和力量保护。缺失的是对战略层面致命性的严肃审视——不仅仅是摧毁敌方力量，而是迫使敌方停止战斗的能力。
2019年的文章指出的这一倒置，以及近年来的验证表明：动能行动本身无法实现战略决策。它们为影响力实现决策创造了条件。如果尽管在物理上取得压倒性胜利，动能的战战略回报仍不充分——事实上确实如此——那么物理因素已不再是决定性变量。它只是影响力打击的铺垫。现代军事史上最昂贵的账单是由一个顺序颠倒的理论造成的。
战争并不单靠力量的歼灭决定。正如我们在伊拉克看到的，伊拉克军队的毁灭反而导致了长期的不对称战争。战争结束于一方认为代价不再值得。战斗意志——对手的政治决心、国内合法性、联盟凝聚力和对冲突的叙事控制——因此与任何武器系统一样，都是目标。而影响力，如果正确理解，就是实现这一目标的机制。
我们将战略影响力定义为利用国家权力的要素——外交、军事、经济，以及通过信息——来塑造信息和作战环境，以削弱敌方意志。前陆军少将詹姆斯·杜比克认为，外国影响力行动是文职和军事领导人必须为下一场战争做出的最重要的战略层面准备。特种作战部队社区本能地理解这一点，并通过数十年的经验认识到这一点。其余的联合部队尚未跟上。
这一诊断并未改变。变化的是忽视它的代价。
自2019年以来，影响力致命性在行动中得到了持续的演示——主要由对手实现。
2022年2月，俄罗斯对乌克兰的再次入侵结合了动能行动与高度复杂的宣传活动。莫斯科试图削弱西方联盟支持，使乌克兰政府失去合法性，并在国内外塑造信息环境——维持俄罗斯的战斗意志，同时削弱它。动能行动代价高昂，且在许多方面表现不佳。影响力行动则更为持久：利用西方公众中的分歧，放大战争疲劳，并在多个平台上同时争夺冲突的叙事架构。
与此同时，中国则采取了长期战略，以取代美国的影响力——并非主要通过武力，而是通过经济杠杆、技术依赖、制度准入和叙事塑造。孔子学院案例值得一个很少被使用的标签：本土的致命影响力。中国在过去的二十年里系统性地投资于美国大学的教育和文化影响力行动，重塑课程，压制敏感话题的讨论，并塑造一代学生对中国的基本认知——而这一切都在美国本土未开一枪。正如Bottomley所指出
_source.trans_title: 信息致死性再探：战略影响力与战争的未来
_source.evidence: 文章核心在于重新审视和构建关于‘杀伤力（Lethality）’的战略理论框架，特别是将‘影响力（Influence）’定义为一种战略层面的杀伤力。文章回顾了2019年的论点，分析了美国国防部（DoD）在认知和教条上的不足，并提出了新的理论工具（PIL模拟平台）来支持这一理论框架的落地。虽然文中提到了俄罗斯、中国等对手的行动（涉我事件/行动动向），但这些是作为论据来支撑其理论观点的。文章的主要贡献在于提出新的战略概念、教条修正建议以及理论分析工具，而非描述具体的作战行动、部队组建或单纯的武器技术研发。因此，最符合的标签是‘理论政策’。

An ex-Army employee that had top-secret clearance has been charged with leaking classified information, according to the Department of Justice (DOJ).
In a Wednesday press release, the DOJ said that 40-year-old Courtney Williams of North Carolina was arrested by the FBI on Tuesday. Williams was indicted by a federal grand jury on Wednesday regarding “her alleged transmission of classified national defense information to individuals not authorized to receive it, including a journalist,” according to the DOJ.
“Clearance holders accept a solemn obligation to protect the classified information entrusted to them,” John A. Eisenberg, assistant attorney general for national security, said in a statement in the release.
“That they do so is critical to the security of our Nation. When clearance holders violate that trust, the National Security Division will act swiftly to hold them accountable.”
The DOJ said that Williams had “a Top Secret / Sensitive Compartmented Information security clearance” and was an employee of a special military unit (SMU) for six years starting in 2010, per court documents.
From 2022 to 2025, Williams, who worked at Fort Bragg, allegedly talked to a journalist on multiple occasions on the phone and by text, the DOJ said.
“During this period, Williams and the Journalist had over 10 hours of telephone calls and exchanged more than 180 messages. In one such message, the Journalist identified themselves as a journalist and stated that they sought information about the SMU in support of an upcoming article and book,” the DOJ said in its press release.
“After these communications with Williams, the Journalist published a book and article that named Williams as a source and attributed specific statements to her. Some of these statements contained classified national defense information. In addition to her disclosures to the Journalist, Williams also made unauthorized disclosures of national defense information via her social media accounts.”
_source.movement_title: 美国前陆军雇员被起诉泄露机密信息
_source.movement_abstract: 美国司法部宣布，一名前陆军雇员因涉嫌泄露机密信息被起诉。40岁的北卡罗来纳州居民Courtney Williams被联邦调查局逮捕，其曾持有绝密/敏感隔离信息安全许可，并在2010年至2016年期间任职于特别军事单位。据司法部披露，Williams在2022年至2025年期间多次通过电话和短信与一名记者沟通，期间累计通话超10小时，互发信息逾180条。该记者随后出版了包含Williams作为信源的书籍和文章，其中部分内容涉及机密国防信息。此外，Williams还被指控通过社交媒体账户擅自披露国防信息。司法部国家安全助理部长John A. Eisenberg强调，安全许可持有人泄露机密信息将面临快速追责。
_source.title: Ex-Army employee with top-secret clearance charged with leaking information to journalist
_source.trans_cont:
一名曾拥有最高机密权限的前美军雇员被指控泄露机密信息，据美国司法部（DOJ）称。  
在周三的一份新闻稿中，DOJ表示，40岁的北卡罗来纳州法院威廉斯（Courtney Williams）于周二被联邦调查局（FBI）逮捕。据DOJ称，周三，威廉斯因“涉嫌向未经授权的个人，包括一名记者，传递机密的国防信息”被联邦大陪审团起诉。  
司法部国家安全事务助理总检察长约翰·A·艾森伯格（John A. Eisenberg）在新闻稿中表示：“拥有权限的人接受了一项庄严的义务，即保护交托给他们的机密信息。”  
“他们履行这一职责对于保障我们国家的安全至关重要。当权限持有人违反这一信任时，国家安全部门将迅速采取行动追究其责任。”  
司法部表示，威廉斯拥有“最高机密/敏感特情信息”安全权限，并自2010年起在特种军事单位（SMU）工作了六年，根据法院文件。  
据司法部称，从2022年到2025年，威廉斯在佛罗里达州布拉格堡工作期间，据称多次通过电话和短信与一名记者联系。  
司法部在新闻稿中表示：“在此期间，威廉斯与记者进行了超过10小时的电话交谈，并交换了超过180条信息。其中一条信息中，记者自称是记者，并表示他们正在为即将发表的文章和书籍寻找有关SMU的信息。”  
“在与威廉斯的这些交流之后，记者出版了一本著作和一篇文章，将威廉斯列为消息来源，并归因于她一些具体的言论。其中一些言论包含机密的国防信息。除了向记者披露信息外，威廉斯还通过她的社交媒体账号未经授权地泄露了国防信息。”
_source.trans_title: 前军队雇员，拥有最高机密权限，被指控向记者泄露信息

Ukraine recently survived the fourth winter of Russia’s full-scale invasion. That is not a figure of speech. During the winter months, Moscow’s clear intention was to freeze millions of Ukrainians into submission by bombing power and heating infrastructure amid subzero temperatures.
Russia has employed similar tactics during each wartime winter, but the scale of the latest bombing campaign was unprecedented. In January, United Nations officials
regular strikes on energy infrastructure across seventeen regions of Ukraine. By the end of the winter season, all of Ukraine’s thermal power plants had been damaged or destroyed.
In Kyiv, thousands of residential buildings were left without central heating for extended periods. The municipal authorities reported
as a result of power and heating outages, but some volunteers who visited freezing apartments remain skeptical that the official statistics tell the full story.
Ukraine was able to endure the hardships of the past winter because it adapted and improvised. In doing so, the country laid the foundations for an operational doctrine to keep cities warm when civilian infrastructure comes under systematic attack. This has practical applications beyond the borders of wartime Ukraine.
The model of heating infrastructure resilience that has emerged in Ukraine in recent years is based on decentralization and speed. When centralized heating plants became high-value targets for Russian drones and missiles, Ukrainian operators pivoted toward mobile
. Greater reliance on these compact systems created the conditions to generate both electricity and heat independently of the wider grid.
By November 2025, Ukraine’s district heating sector was operating 182 cogeneration units alongside almost 250 block-modular boilers. This made it possible to create so-called “energy islands” for hospitals, water utilities, and residential heating. While European procurement cycles can often be measured in years, Ukrainian operators were able to install these decentralized heating and energy solutions in a matter of days.
Ukraine’s response was not planned in advance; it was improvised under fire. As Russia’s bombing campaigns have intensified over the past four years, Ukraine has developed a rapid repair doctrine complete with pre-positioned spare parts, emergency communication protocols, and decision-making at the municipal level that cuts through the bureaucratic hierarchy.
An
by the International Energy Agency (IEA) published in February 2026 found that Ukraine’s comprehensive emergency response capabilities could offer important lessons for the international community. The immediate neighborhood stands to gain most from studying Ukraine’s experience.
Across Central and Eastern Europe, district heating is the primary way cities stay warm. Poland, Slovakia, the Czech Republic, Hungary, and the Baltic states all depend on centralized systems similar to Ukraine’s that date back to the Soviet era. This makes them potentially vulnerable if adversaries choose to target civilian infrastructure.
For now, the region is unprepared. Crisis protocols are untested, while limited municipal budgets are more likely to be spent on boiler maintenance than cyber security. Meanwhile, there are signs that the threat to civilian infrastructure is not limited to bombardment and could also include a cyber dimension.
In January 2024,
shut down heating to over six hundred apartment buildings in Lviv in western Ukraine. This was the first known use of this method to disrupt municipal heating systems. Researchers have identified similarly exposed systems in Lithuania and Romania.
In late 2025, a
targeted a large Polish combined heating and power plant serving nearly half a million customers. A probe into the incident found
to the Russian security services and revealed that the attackers had penetrated the system months in advance.
Ukraine knows what these attacks look like, how they escalate, and how to keep heat flowing in spite of them. However, the European providers who need this information do not always have it. There are some signs that European attention is beginning to turn toward collective cyber defense and infrastructure resilience. Proposals for joint European cyber defense capabilities are now on the table, but the pace of the debate does not match the scale of the threat.
The institutional infrastructure for knowledge exchange already exists. Europe’s
connects Ukraine to its European neighbors and has signed memorandums specifically on district heating coordination. Meanwhile, the
sets out thirty actions for crisis resilience across the EU. However, there is currently no mechanism to translate Ukraine’s hard-won knowledge into systematic European preparedness.
Ukraine did not choose to become Europe’s laboratory for civilian heating infrastructure under attack, but it is now institutionalizing the results. In early March, Ukraine’s
approved energy resilience plans for every region of the country built around four pillars: Critical infrastructure protection, additional cogeneration capacity, decentralized heating supply, and decentralized water supply.
Ukraine is turning wartime improvisation into national doctrine. The question is whether the country’s European neighbors will absorb this knowledge before they have to learn the same lessons first-hand.

_source.movement_title: 乌克兰去中心化供暖经验为欧洲提供重要借鉴
_source.movement_abstract: 乌克兰在应对俄罗斯大规模入侵的第四个冬季中，通过去中心化能源系统和快速响应机制有效保障了民生供暖。俄方持续对能源设施实施轰炸，导致乌克兰多地热电厂受损，市政供暖中断。乌克兰采用移动式联合发电装置和模块化锅炉构建“能源孤岛”，在数日内完成设施部署，形成独立供能体系。2026年国际能源署报告指出，乌克兰的应急响应经验对欧洲具有重要借鉴意义，尤其对依赖苏联时期集中供暖系统的中东欧国家。2024年初，利沃夫市曾发生首次针对市政供暖系统的网络攻击，2025年底波兰联合供热厂遭俄方网络攻击，暴露出欧洲在基础设施网络安全方面的薄弱。尽管欧洲已建立知识共享机制和危机应对框架，但尚未将乌克兰经验转化为系统性防护措施。乌克兰已制定全国能源韧性计划，涵盖关键设施保护、增建联合发电装置、去中心化供能和供水体系四大支柱，其战时应变正转化为国家政策，欧洲邻国需及时吸收相关经验以避免被动应对。
_source.post_location: 华盛顿特区西北L街1400号
_source.title: Ukraine’s heating system resilience offers lessons for European neighbors
_source.trans_cont:
乌克兰最近成功度过了俄罗斯全面入侵的第四次寒冬。这不是修辞手法。在冬季期间，莫斯科的明确意图是在零下温度下通过轰炸电力和供暖基础设施，将数百万乌克兰人逼入困境。
俄罗斯在每次战时冬季都使用了类似的战术，但最近一次轰炸行动的规模是前所未有的。1月，联合国官员报告称，俄罗斯对乌克兰十七个地区的能源基础设施进行了定期袭击。到冬季结束时，乌克兰所有的热电厂都已遭到破坏或摧毁。
在基辅，成千上万的住宅楼在很长一段时间内失去了集中供暖。市政当局报告称，由于电力和供暖中断，许多居民受到影响，但一些志愿者访问了寒冷的公寓，仍对官方统计数据是否完整表示怀疑。
乌克兰之所以能够度过过去冬天的艰难时期，是因为它进行了适应和创新。通过这样做，该国为在民用基础设施遭受系统性攻击时保持城市温暖奠定了操作性理论基础。这种做法在战时乌克兰之外也有实际应用。
近年来，乌克兰出现的供暖基础设施韧性模式基于去中心化和快速响应。当集中供暖厂成为俄罗斯无人机和导弹的高价值目标时，乌克兰操作人员转向了移动式系统。对这些紧凑系统的更大依赖，创造了在不依赖更广泛电网的情况下独立发电和供热的条件。
到2025年11月，乌克兰的区域供暖部门正在运行182台联合发电系统和近250台模块化锅炉。这使得能够为医院、水务设施和住宅供暖创建所谓的“能源孤岛”。虽然欧洲的采购周期通常以年为单位，但乌克兰操作人员能够在几天内安装这些去中心化的供暖和能源解决方案。
乌克兰的应对措施并非事先计划，而是在战火中即兴发挥。随着过去四年俄罗斯轰炸行动的加剧，乌克兰发展出了一套快速修复理论，包括预先部署的备用零件、紧急通讯协议以及在市政层面做出决策，从而绕过官僚等级制度。
国际能源署（IEA）于2026年2月发布的一份报告发现，乌克兰全面的应急响应能力可以为国际社会提供重要的经验教训。该地区的邻国最有可能从研究乌克兰的经验中获益。
在中欧和东欧，区域供暖是城市保持温暖的主要方式。波兰、斯洛伐克、捷克共和国、匈牙利以及波罗的海国家都依赖于与乌克兰相似的集中式系统，这些系统可以追溯到苏联时代。这使它们在对手选择攻击民用基础设施时可能变得脆弱。
目前，该地区尚未做好准备。危机应对机制尚未经过考验，而有限的市政预算更可能用于锅炉维护而非网络安全。与此同时，有迹象表明，对民用基础设施的威胁不仅限于轰炸，还可能包括网络维度。
2024年1月，俄罗斯关闭了乌克兰西部利沃夫市超过六百栋公寓楼的供暖。这是首次已知使用这种方法来干扰市政供暖系统。研究人员在立陶宛和罗马尼亚也发现了类似暴露的系统。
2025年底，一个网络攻击针对了波兰一家为近五十万客户服务的大型联合供暖和发电厂。对事件的调查发现该攻击与俄罗斯安全机构有关，并揭示攻击者早在数月前就已渗透系统。
乌克兰了解这些攻击的模式、升级方式以及如何在攻击中保持供暖。然而，需要这些信息的欧洲供应商并不总是拥有这些信息。有一些迹象表明，欧洲对集体网络安全和基础设施韧性开始关注。现在，联合欧洲网络安全能力的提案已摆上桌面，但辩论的速度与威胁的规模不相匹配。
知识交流的制度基础设施已经存在。欧洲的“欧洲邻国连接计划”将乌克兰与欧洲邻国连接起来，并签署了关于区域供暖协调的专门备忘录。同时，欧盟的《危机韧性行动计划》提出了三十项行动。然而，目前尚无机制将乌克兰获得的经验转化为系统的欧洲准备。
乌克兰并未选择成为欧洲民用供暖基础设施在攻击下的试验场，但现在它正在制度化这些成果。2026年3月初，乌克兰的议会批准了针对全国每个地区的能源韧性计划，该计划围绕四个支柱：关键基础设施保护、额外联合发电能力、去中心化供暖供应和去中心化供水供应。
乌克兰正在将战时的即兴应对转化为国家理论。问题是，该国的欧洲邻国是否会在亲身体验相同教训之前吸收这些知识。
_source.trans_title: 乌克兰供暖系统的韧性为欧洲邻国提供了借鉴

_source.content:
China was behind the sudden dismissal of Myanmar junta chief propagandist Maj-Gen Zaw Min Tun late last month after his involvement in procuring restricted Chinese drones was flagged by Beijing, according to a source familiar with the matter.
The Irrawaddy
broke the news
about his removal as junta spokesman, a post he had occupied since the military coup in 2021. The reason behind his dismissal remained unclear at the time.
However, The Irrawaddy learned that the purge stemmed from information delivered by Chinese Special Envoy Deng Xijun during his visit to Naypyitaw on March 13. Deng provided evidence that Zaw Min Tun brokered the sale of Chinese drones to a Myanmar company, despite Beijing restricting their purchase outside of China.
The type of drone, size and timing of the deal, and parties involved, remain unknown.
Beijing also took action against the Chinese drone company for violating its restriction order.
Junta media reported that Deng met with regime Foreign Minister Than Swe during his visit.
Junta chief Min Aung Hlaing ordered an investigation against Zaw Min Tun, who admitted to earning a brokerage fee of around US$ 20,000 for the drone deal, a source in Naypyitaw told The Irrawaddy. His confession triggered his immediate dismissal from all duties—as deputy minister of information, director of Army Public Relations and Psychological Warfare, and information chief of the National Defense and Security Council (NDSC). He was replaced by Brigadier General Ye Yint Aung, director of the Directorate of Public Relations and Psychological Warfare.
Zaw Min Tun is the latest in a string of high-ranking junta officials axed after tip-offs by China. In late January, Lieutenant General
Tun Tun Naung
was ousted as home affairs minister after Beijing informed Naypyitaw that he was profiting from scam centers in northern Shan State.
Zaw Min Tun has vanished from public life since his dismissal, absent from major regime events such as the Armed Forces Day parade on March 27. Speculation regarding his removal had ranged from the regime chief’s displeasure over reports of his recent spinal surgery to the ongoing fuel crisis and corruption cases involving his wife.
Other sources said his fall came after Min Aung Hlaing had handpicked him as his new regime’s information minister as reward for his tireless parroting of junta claims since the coup.
Known as
master of the junta’s ‘skyful of lies
,’ Zaw Min Tun shameless peddling of regime narratives includes his declaration that ousted State Counselor Daw Aung San Suu Kyi was corrupt, a smear that remains unfounded despite a series of trials since 2021.
His response when the military was ethnic armed groups and their allied People’s Defense Forces overran the military in northern Shan State in 2023 was equally brazen. He dismissed the historic humiliation as merely “a temporary tactical retreat.”
The junta has so far been unable to reclaim the majority of the territory lost since then.
_source.movement_title: 中国特使介入致缅甸军政府宣传主管因违规采购无人机被免职
_source.movement_abstract: 【缅甸伊洛瓦底网站报道】据缅甸伊洛瓦底网站报道，缅甸军政府宣传主管、少将佐敏吞（Zaw Min Tun）于上月末被突然免职，直接原因系中国特使邓锡军（Deng Xijun）于3月13日访问内比都期间向军政府高层提供证据，指证其违反中国出口管制规定，促成中国无人机向缅甸公司非法销售。佐敏吞承认从中收取约2万美元佣金，随即被解除信息部副部长、陆军公共关系与心理战局局长及国防与安全委员会信息主管等职务，由少将耶印昂（Ye Yint Aung）接任。此次清洗系继今年1月内政部长吞吞昂（Tun Tun Naung）因涉缅北诈骗中心利益输送被中国通报后，又一名因中方情报介入而被罢免的高层官员。佐敏吞自2021年政变以来长期担任军政府首席发言人，因系统性散布虚假信息被外界称为“谎言大师”，其近期缺席3月27日建军节阅兵等公开活动，引发对其健康状况及家庭涉腐传闻的猜测。军政府尚未收复2023年在掸邦北部失守的多数领土，其宣传口径持续否认战败事实。
_source.title: Chinese Drone Deal Behind Downfall of Myanmar Junta’s Chief Propagandist
_source.trans_cont:
据一位了解情况的消息人士称，中国在上个月末突然解职缅甸军方宣传部长少将扎温·敏丁一事上有所迟疑，原因是北京指出其涉及采购受限制的中国无人机。《伊洛瓦底》杂志率先披露了他被解除军方发言人职务的消息，该职位自2021年军事政变以来一直由他担任。当时其被解职的原因尚不清楚。

然而，《伊洛瓦底》了解到，此次清洗源于中国特使邓锡军3月13日访问内比都期间提供的信息。邓锡军提供了证据，显示扎温·敏丁在中方限制其无人机出口至缅甸的情况下，仍促成了一家缅甸公司购买中国无人机。无人机的型号、交易规模、时间及涉及方尚不清楚。

北京同时对涉事的中国无人机公司采取了行动，因其违反了限制购买令。军方媒体称，邓锡军在访问期间会见了军方外交部长丹梭。军方领导人敏昂莱下令对扎温·敏丁展开调查，一名内比都消息人士告诉《伊洛瓦底》，扎温·敏丁承认从中收取了约2万美元的中介费。他的供认导致其立即被解除所有职务——包括信息部长、陆军公共关系与心理战局局长以及国家安全与国防委员会（NDSC）信息主管。他由少将耶因丁·昂取代，后者是公共关系与心理战局总监。

扎温·敏丁是继中国情报泄露后被解职的又一名高级军方官员。1月底，少将吞吞那昂因北京通知内比都称其从掸邦北部的诈骗中心获利而被解职。自被解职后，扎温·敏丁已淡出公众视野，缺席了3月27日的建军节阅兵等重要军方活动。关于其被解职的猜测包括军方领导人对其近期脊椎手术报道的不满、持续的燃料危机以及其妻子涉及的腐败案件。

其他消息人士称，其倒台源于敏昂莱亲自挑选他担任新政权的信息部长，以表彰其自政变以来不遗余力地重复军方说法。被称为军方“谎言满天飞”的操盘手，扎温·敏丁肆无忌惮地传播军方叙事，包括宣称被推翻的国务资政昂山素季腐败，尽管自2021年以来多次审判均未证实这一指控。2023年军方与少数民族武装及其盟友人民防卫军在掸邦北部攻占军方据点时，他的回应同样大胆，称这一历史性耻辱只是“一次暂时的战术撤退”。截至目前，军方仍未能收复大部分失地。
_source.trans_title: 中国无人机交易导致缅甸军政府首席宣传官下台

_source.content:
With most attention in Washington focused on the Middle East, Ukraine’s defense private sector has recently been on a tour across the U.S., trying to catch the attention of lawmakers and investors to showcase their impressive cutting-edge and affordable mass-production capabilities. And despite the occasional Ukraine political whirlwind in D.C., the majority of Americans and Congress support Ukraine on a bipartisan level.
Yet one of the persistent problems among Ukraine’s partners is that many still view Ukraine as a problem to be solved rather than an opportunity to be seized. That perception may be the single greatest challenge Ukraine faces in the eyes of leaders across the democratic world.
The Kremlin understands this dynamic well, which is why it heavily invests in propaganda worldwide. Propaganda is relatively cheap — but its influence on perception can be enormous. Moscow has worked to reinforce a narrative that Ukraine is inherently corrupt and incapable of being a successful democracy. Ukraine has been countering the Kremlin’s efforts, but the sheer scale of its propaganda operations poses a challenge.
This can be witnessed in a familiar conversational pattern about Ukraine’s economy. For decades, Western decision-makers have delivered the same message: Ukraine has “great potential.” But the conversation rarely moves beyond the predictable caveats — there is corruption and red tape, and perhaps it is better to wait. This hesitancy is reflected in Ukraine’s historically low foreign direct investment.
The same dynamic appears in Western discussions about aid conditionality. Ukraine is told that if it implements reforms, it will receive greater financial support. In principle, this approach makes sense. In practice, it often turns into inaction.
Conditionality is necessary. But instead of vacillation, Ukraine’s partners should be tripling down on support for reforms. That includes expanding resources for anti-corruption watchdogs and strengthening institutions that ensure transparency, accountability and structure.
At the same time, Ukraine itself must radically transform how the world sees its government. The most effective way is implementing sweeping bold reforms — particularly in its judicial institutions. Ukraine must spotlight those efforts and demonstrate, beyond doubt, that it has permanently disposed of its Soviet-inherited residue of corruption. Importantly, a trustworthy court system reduces risk for investors and businesses.
Ukraine’s long-term economic success will depend on competition and entrepreneurship across its regions and cities. As such, Ukraine and its partners must create an environment that both encourages innovation and protects it, meaning reliable access to capital and strong intellectual property rights.
A change in perception also requires a change in the narrative about what Ukraine actually is. Too often, Western policymakers view Ukraine primarily as a geopolitical hedge, a buffer zone — a label Ukrainians strongly dislike — between Russia and Europe. A far more accurate description is that Ukraine can become an exporter of stability, security and resilience.
For example, Ukraine covers roughly 233,000 square miles, making it the largest country in Europe by landmass, roughly the size of Texas. It is larger than France, Spain or Sweden, but its population is less than half of Germany’s and roughly half that of France and the United Kingdom.
Ukraine can become a leading economic giant in Europe. Ukrainians are innovative, and the country has already demonstrated remarkable technological capacity. In just four years, despite a full-scale war, Ukraine has rapidly developed a massive ecosystem of hundreds of drone manufacturers and defense startups.
If the U.S. commits to a Ukrainian victory, Ukraine will become a success story of democratic resilience that has fully switched from a war-torn country to a hub of security and stability. Ukraine’s story is truly unique for 21st-century Europe — no other country has a battlefield-tested economy on such a scale. Ukraine’s iterative progress amid constant shocks is remarkable, offering nearly every sector an opportunity to strengthen resilience.
Although Russia terrorizes the country daily, Ukraine’s GDP grew in 2024 by approximately 2.9 percent, delivering an estimated $190.7 billion in output. Ukraine also remains the leading sunflower oil supplier to the European Union and consistently leads as a top global sunflower oil exporter.
This Ukraine perception shift has clear implications for U.S. policy. If the U.S. does not take advantage of what Ukraine’s innovative economy has to offer, other countries will, including China.
A victorious Ukraine would send a powerful signal to other post-Soviet countries that they can finally leave Russia’s orbit and become growing democracies. This would also create new opportunities for the U.S. abroad.
Russia has traditionally viewed the U.S. as a strategic adversary, seeking its downfall, and has never fully accepted its defeat in the Cold War. But Russia is also at its weakest point since the full-scale invasion began. Ukraine is primed to deliver the U.S. a lasting Kremlin defeat like never before, and at no human cost to U.S. soldiers.
Ukraine is a gold mine for democracy, being handed to the U.S. on a platter. It would be naive and short-sighted for us to ignore it.
Ilya Timtchenko is a nonresident fellow with the Transatlantic Defense and Security Program at the Center for European Policy Analysis. He is the founder and CEO of HawkNation LLC and a board member at First Aid of the Soul, a nonprofit providing trauma-informed mental health support to Ukrainians affected by the war.
_source.movement_title: 乌克兰经济转型与国际认知挑战
_source.movement_abstract: 乌克兰近期组织国防企业在美国开展宣传活动，向立法者和投资者展示其先进的大规模生产能力和成本优势。尽管美国国会和民众普遍支持乌克兰，但国际社会仍存在将其视为问题而非机遇的固有认知。克里姆林宫通过低成本宣传策略强化乌克兰腐败和民主失败的叙事，导致西方决策者长期以\"潜力\"而非现实价值看待乌克兰经济。当前乌克兰在司法体系改革、吸引外资、保障知识产权等方面亟需突破，其2024年国内生产总值逆势增长2.9%至1907亿美元，葵花籽油出口量保持全球领先地位。文章指出美国若不把握乌克兰战场验证的经济韧性，其他国家（包括中国）将抢占机遇。一个转型成功的乌克兰可成为后苏联国家摆脱俄罗斯影响的典范，为美国提供无人员伤亡的持久战略优势。乌克兰国土面积相当于得克萨斯州，人口虽不及德国一半，但已形成数百家无人机制造商和国防初创企业的创新生态系统。
_source.title: Ukraine is not a charity case — it is a strategic opportunity
_source.trans_cont:
在美国的大部分关注都集中在中东地区时，乌克兰的国防私营部门最近在美国各地进行巡回访问，试图引起国会议员和投资者的注意，展示其令人印象深刻的尖端技术和可负担的批量生产能力。尽管华盛顿偶尔会出现乌克兰政治风波，但大多数美国人和国会仍以跨党派的方式支持乌克兰。
然而，乌克兰的合作伙伴中存在一个持续的问题，即许多人仍然将乌克兰视为需要解决的问题，而不是需要抓住的机会。这种看法可能是乌克兰在全球民主国家领导人眼中面临的最大挑战。
克里姆林宫深知这种动态，因此在全球范围内大力投资宣传。宣传成本相对较低，但对公众认知的影响却可能非常巨大。莫斯科努力强化一种叙事，即乌克兰本质上腐败且无法成为成功的民主国家。乌克兰一直在对抗克里姆林宫的努力，但其宣传规模庞大，构成了挑战。
这种现象可以从关于乌克兰经济的常见对话模式中看到。几十年来，西方决策者一直传递着同样的信息：乌克兰“潜力巨大”。但对话很少超越这些可预测的警告——存在腐败和官僚主义，也许最好等待。这种犹豫不决反映在乌克兰历史上较低的外国直接投资水平上。
同样的动态也出现在西方关于援助条件性的讨论中。乌克兰被告知，如果实施改革，将获得更多的财政支持。从原则上讲，这种方法是有道理的。但在实践中，它往往导致不作为。
条件性是必要的。但与其犹豫不决，乌克兰的合作伙伴应加大对改革的支持力度。这包括扩大对反腐败监督机构的资源，并加强确保透明度、问责制和制度化的机构。
同时，乌克兰自身必须彻底改变世界对其政府的看法。最有效的方法是实施广泛的、大胆的改革，特别是在司法机构方面。乌克兰必须突出这些努力，并明确证明其已彻底摆脱了苏联遗留的腐败。重要的是，一个值得信赖的法院系统可以降低投资者和企业的风险。
乌克兰的长期经济成功将取决于其各地区和城市之间的竞争和创业精神。因此，乌克兰及其合作伙伴必须创造一个既鼓励创新又保护创新的环境，这意味着可靠的资本获取和强大的知识产权保护。
改变看法还需要改变对乌克兰实际是什么的叙述。西方政策制定者往往将乌克兰主要视为一个地缘政治缓冲区，即在俄罗斯和欧洲之间的屏障——这是乌克兰人强烈反感的标签。一个更准确的描述是，乌克兰可以成为稳定、安全和韧性的出口国。
例如，乌克兰国土面积约23.3万平方英里，是欧洲面积最大的国家，大致相当于德克萨斯州的大小。它比法国、西班牙或瑞典大，但人口不到德国的一半，大约是法国和英国的一半。
乌克兰可以成为欧洲领先的经济大国。乌克兰人富有创新精神，该国已经展示了显著的技术能力。在短短四年里，尽管面临全面战争，乌克兰迅速发展出数百家无人机制造商和国防初创企业的庞大生态系统。
如果美国承诺支持乌克兰取得胜利，乌克兰将成为民主韧性的成功典范，从一个战乱国家转变为安全与稳定的中心。乌克兰的故事是21世纪欧洲独一无二的——没有其他国家拥有如此规模的经过战场检验的经济。乌克兰在不断冲击中取得的逐步进展令人印象深刻，为几乎每个行业提供了增强韧性的机会。
尽管俄罗斯每天都在恐吓乌克兰，但乌克兰2024年的GDP增长了约2.9%，产出估计达到1907亿美元。乌克兰仍然是欧洲联盟最大的葵花籽油供应国，并且持续位居全球葵花籽油出口国前列。
这种对乌克兰的看法转变对美国政策有明确的影响。如果美国不利用乌克兰创新经济所提供的机会，其他国家将会，包括中国。
乌克兰的胜利将向其他前苏联国家发出一个强有力的信号，表明他们终于可以摆脱俄罗斯的轨道，成为不断发展的民主国家。这也将为美国创造新的国际机会。
俄罗斯传统上将美国视为战略对手，寻求其失败，并从未完全接受冷战的失败。但自全面入侵开始以来，俄罗斯也处于其最弱的时期。乌克兰正准备为美国带来前所未有的、持久的克里姆林宫失败，且不会对美国士兵造成任何人员伤亡。
乌克兰是民主的金矿，美国几乎将其奉送到手中。忽视它将是天真且短视的。
伊利亚·季姆琴科是欧洲政策分析中心跨大西洋国防与安全计划的非居民研究员。他是HawkNation LLC的创始人兼首席执行官，也是First Aid of the Soul非营利组织的董事会成员，该组织为受战争影响的乌克兰人提供基于创伤知情的心理健康支持。

The Psychology of Fear That Surrounds the Strait of Hormuz: The Strait of Hormuz remains at the center of the conflict in Iran. Breaking down the psychology, fear increasingly engulfs the Strait of Hormuz issue. It is more than a traditional cost-benefit analysis in major military conflicts. And it is this dynamic that might decide what happens next in the Iran crisis as well as in global energy markets.
Due to the ideology of the Islamic Republic, the pressures exerted on many politicians worldwide due to rising energy prices and the ripple effects on relations with the adversaries of the People’s Republic of China (PRC) and Russia, etc., these non-empirical forces exert considerable influence on this situation.
To say that the tensions in the Strait become more complex by the day is an understatement.
But the dilemma is how to undo this Gordian Knot — to reopen the Strait of Hormuz and ensure that actions taken do not make the situation worse.
Accomplishing that task requires some detailed comprehension of just how the minds of Iran’s clerical rulers and its Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps (IRGC) work in relation to this issue.
A recent essay from the Jewish Institute for National Security of America (JINSA) goes into some detail about the dynamics involved.
What is required is a full realization that Iran’s actions are largely psychological warfare — designed to amplify anxiety and influence shipping markets.
Countering this fear psychology means having a full understanding of several important factors.
This requires “focusing on objective maritime realities, maintaining operational awareness, and engaging in proactive, small acts of defiance against alarmism,” according to these analysts.
Without physically closing the Strait of Hormuz or denying the sea to the U.S. Navy, Iran has managed to bring Gulf shipping nearly to a halt.
Consequently, the global economy has been upended.
U.S. President Donald Trump’s promises of retribution against Iran have minimal effect in these circumstances.
While the Islamic Republic continues to interfere with the free movement of commerce, say the Israeli analysts, “shippers will refuse to transit these waters as long as the perceived risks remain prohibitive and Iran’s maritime threats appear plausible—even if they no longer nearly as formidable” as they once were.
Just last week, on April 1, the famous World Economic Forum (WEF) organization pointed out that there are additional issues at stake in the world economy with the closure of the Strait, beyond just energy prices. Nine other commodities are seeing their positions on the world market affected by the closure.
“The shipping crisis in the Strait of Hormuz is now “the largest supply disruption in the history of the global oil market”, according to the head of the International Energy Agency, Fatih Birol. But while “focus remains on the 11 million barrels of oil and 140 billion cubic metres of gas usually in daily global circulation, the impact extends far beyond energy,” says the WEF.
“As the conflict in Iran continues, the blockage also exposes a deeper vulnerability: the Middle East’s role as a primary supplier of non-oil commodities. From the fertilizers essential for global food security to the minerals powering the energy transition, the current shortages are reshaping supply chains in real time.”
According to the estimates of the JINSA analysts, the main threats to shipping and to the U.S. forces are “mainly in the Gulf, not the Strait. As its other anti-ship capabilities are degraded, Iran will have greater incentive to prolong the war and raise its costs by dotting the Gulf—currently devoid of U.S. surface ships—with naval mines.
“Just as shipping is easier to stop than to restart in wartime,” state these analysts. “[Sea] mines work in Iran’s favor by being relatively easy to deploy, difficult to clear, and potentially paralyzing to seaborne traffic.”
The current conflict, including Iranian attacks on tankers and other commercial vessels, has shrunk shipping through the Strait by 90 percent and bottled up 600 international trading ships inside the Gulf.
A majority of the 10 percent that remains free to pass through the Gulf are Iranian oil exports, which amount to some 1.0-1.5 million barrels per day, plus ships from the PRC and other friendly countries that Tehran “permits” safe transit.
At this point, no U.S. surface ships are operating in the Hormuz or the Gulf, meaning that control of these zones has been ceded to Iran by Washington.
President Trump has issued threats of retaliation against Iran should they interdict commercial ships transiting the Strait.
But the perceived risks of doing so, along with insurance firms refusing to indemnify those vessels, will likely effectively close this waterway anyway.
Until friendly warships and US-flagged vessels show they can sail through the Strait unimpeded, the psychological anxiety holding them back will continue to be in place.
The only way to break this hold is for the U.S. and its allies and partners to reassert naval predominance over this most important of the world’s waterways.
Reuben F. Johnson has thirty-six years of experience analyzing and reporting on foreign weapons systems, defense technologies, and international arms export policy. Johnson is the Director of Research at the Casimir Pulaski Foundation. He is also a survivor of the Russian invasion of Ukraine in February 2022. He worked for years in the American defense industry as a foreign technology analyst and later as a consultant for the U.S. Department of Defense, the Departments of the Navy and Air Force, and the governments of the United Kingdom and Australia. In 2022-2023, he won two awards in a row for his defense reporting. He holds a bachelor’s degree from DePauw University and a master’s degree from Miami University in Ohio, specializing in Soviet and Russian studies. He lives in Warsaw.
_source.movement_title: 伊朗利用心理战封锁霍尔木兹海峡致航运量下降九成
_source.movement_abstract: 【美国犹太国家研究所网站2026年4月报道】美国犹太国家研究所（JINSA）分析指出，伊朗通过心理战策略而非物理封锁，成功导致霍尔木兹海峡航运量下降90%，约600艘国际商船滞留波斯湾。尽管美国未实施物理封锁，但伊朗伊斯兰革命卫队（IRGC）的威胁及保险拒保导致航运中断。国际能源署（IEA）指出，除每日1100万桶石油和1400亿立方米天然气外，化肥及关键矿产供应链亦受冲击。世界经合组织（WEF）警告，该危机已演变为全球最大供应中断事件。JINSA分析师认为，伊朗利用水雷等低成本手段制造恐慌，迫使商船停运。目前仅10%的航运为伊朗出口及获许可的友好国家船只。美国前总统特朗普的报复威胁未能缓解局势，因航运商仍视风险过高。分析师建议，唯有美军及盟友重新确立在该海域的制海权，展示安全通行能力，方能打破心理封锁，恢复全球能源及商品供应链稳定。
_source.title: Psychology As Warfare: Iran Never Physically Closed the Strait of Hormuz. It Just Used Fear Instead Psychology As Warfare: Iran Never Physically Closed the Strait of Hormuz. It Just Used Fear Instead

霍尔木兹海峡恐惧心理分析：霍尔木兹海峡仍然是伊朗冲突的中心。剖析这种心理，恐惧正日益笼罩着霍尔木兹海峡问题。这不仅仅是在重大军事冲突中传统的成本效益分析。正是这种动态可能会决定伊朗危机以及全球能源市场的下一步发展。
由于伊斯兰共和国的意识形态，全球许多政界人士因能源价格上涨以及对中华人民共和国（PRC）和俄罗斯等对手关系的连锁反应而受到压力，这些非经验性因素对该局势产生了重大影响。
说霍尔木兹海峡的紧张局势每天变得更加复杂，这还算是低估了。
但困境在于如何解开这个 Gordian 结——重新开放霍尔木兹海峡并确保采取的行动不会使局势恶化。
完成这一任务需要对伊朗神职统治者及其伊斯兰革命卫队（IRGC）在这一问题上的思维方式有详细的了解。
最近，美国国家安全犹太研究所（JINSA）的一篇文章详细探讨了其中的动态。
所需的是充分认识到伊朗的行动在很大程度上是心理战，旨在加剧焦虑并影响航运市场。
应对这种恐惧心理需要全面理解几个重要因素。
根据这些分析人士的说法，这要求“关注客观的海上现实，保持操作意识，并采取积极的小规模反抗行动来对抗恐慌情绪”。
在没有实际关闭霍尔木兹海峡或阻止美国海军通行的情况下，伊朗已使海湾航运几乎陷入停滞。
因此，全球经济被打乱。
在这种情况下，美国总统唐纳德·特朗普对伊朗的报复承诺几乎没有效果。
以色列分析人士指出，尽管伊朗继续干扰商业自由流动，但只要人们认为风险仍然很高，且伊朗的海上威胁看起来可信，船运商就会拒绝通过这些水域——即使这些威胁不再像以前那样强大。
就在上周，4月1日，著名的世界经济论坛（WEF）指出，霍尔木兹海峡的关闭对世界经济的影响不仅限于能源价格，还有其他九种商品的世界市场地位也受到影响。
国际能源署（IEA）负责人法提赫·比罗尔表示：“霍尔木兹海峡的航运危机现在是全球石油市场历史上最大的供应中断。”但世界经济论坛指出：“虽然关注点仍然集中在每天全球流通的1100万桶石油和1400亿立方米天然气上，但影响远超能源领域。”
“随着伊朗冲突的持续，封锁也暴露了中东作为非石油商品主要供应国的深层脆弱性。从对全球粮食安全至关重要的肥料到推动能源转型的矿物，目前的短缺正在实时重塑供应链。”
根据JINSA分析人士的估计，对航运和美国部队的主要威胁“主要在海湾，而不是海峡。随着伊朗的其他反舰能力被削弱，伊朗更有动机延长战争并提高成本，通过在目前没有美国水面舰艇的海湾布设海军水雷来实现这一目标。”
这些分析人士指出：“在战争中，停止航运比重新启动更容易。”“水雷对伊朗有利，因为它们部署相对容易，清除困难，且可能瘫痪海上交通。”
当前冲突，包括伊朗对油轮和其他商船的袭击，已使通过霍尔木兹海峡的航运减少了90%，并将600艘国际商船困在海湾内。
目前仍有10%的船只可以自由通过海湾，其中大部分是伊朗的石油出口，每天约100万至150万桶，加上中国等友好国家的船只，这些船只得到德黑兰“允许”安全通行。
目前，没有美国水面舰艇在霍尔木兹海峡或海湾活动，这意味着华盛顿已将这些区域的控制权让渡给伊朗。
特朗普总统曾威胁对伊朗进行报复，如果他们拦截通过海峡的商业船只。
但对采取此类行动的感知风险，以及保险公司拒绝赔偿这些船只，可能会使这条水道实际上关闭。
直到友好战舰和美国注册船只展示出它们能够无阻碍地通过海峡，这种心理焦虑将继续存在。
打破这种局面的唯一方法是，美国及其盟友和伙伴重新确立对该世界最重要航道的海上主导地位。
雷宾·约翰逊拥有36年分析和报道外国武器系统、国防技术和国际军售政策的经验。约翰逊是卡西米尔·普拉斯基基金会的研究主任。他也是2022年2月俄罗斯入侵乌克兰的幸存者。他曾在美国国防工业工作多年，担任外国技术分析师，后来成为美国国防部、海军和空军部门以及英国和澳大利亚政府的顾问。2022至2023年，他连续两年获得国防报道奖项。他拥有印第安纳大学德保罗分校的学士学位和俄亥俄州迈阿密大学的硕士学位，专攻苏联和俄罗斯研究。他现居华沙。
_source.trans_title: 心理战：伊朗从未实际封锁霍尔木兹海峡，而是以恐惧代替
_source.evidence: 文章主要分析了伊朗利用心理战（恐惧心理）封锁霍尔木兹海峡的策略及其对全球能源市场的影响。虽然文中提到了中国（PRC）作为受影响的利益相关方（如油价波动、贸易关系），但文章的核心焦点是伊朗的战术行动（心理战、封锁威胁）和地缘政治分析，而非专门针对中国大陆发起的特定敌情攻击事件（如针对中国的舆论战、认知攻击等）。同时，文章未涉及具体的军事演习、新部队组建、武器技术研发或政策发布。因此，该文章属于认知域范畴（心理战分析），但不符合前6类具体标签的定义，归为[其他]。
